input.content:
# Characters

## Arthur Prescott (POV throughout)

Age thirty-eight. Junior partner at Garside & Prescott, Winckley Square, Preston. Sixteen years with
the firm; twelve as a qualified solicitor; before that, articles under Henry Garside himself. He has
tried one previous contested probate action and won, though it was nothing like this.

Prescott is methodical, privately warm, formally restrained. He does not perform emotion but it shows
in what he notices. Unmarried; the firm is the work of his life. His professional faith — absorbed
from Garside over two decades — is that the file does not forget. He is good at knowing when a loose
end exists. He is not good at leaving it alone.

He believes the second codicil is a forgery from the caveat onward. Belief is not proof, and the
difference between them is where Garside & Prescott earns its cost recovery. His interior life
surfaces as displacement: what he sees in the strong-room register, what the mill tells him when he
visits, what the Fairhurst household on Bank Parade makes him notice about his own life. He does not
name his grief for Garside. He finds it, repeatedly, in work Garside built better than the occasion
required.

Voice in narration: exact, dry, capable of observational wit, and occasionally capable of the plain
sentence that carries disproportionate weight because everything before it has been controlled.

## Walter Eccleston

Age approximately fifty. Manager of Vale Mill for fifteen years — the position he expected to inherit
along with the residue. He is competent at the mill; his men like him; orders came in, in the good
years, partly because of him. He was genuinely fond of Josiah, as Josiah was fond of him, for the
twenty years before the reconciliation with Margaret.

He has persuaded himself he is correcting a late sentimentality rather than committing a felony. The
codicil was a soft mood; Josiah said so. Walter spent 1924 to 1926 waiting for Josiah to put it
right, carrying the debt on the expectation, and Josiah died without doing so. He is not a monster.
He is also not innocent, and has not been since October 1926.

His exposure at the hearing — handing him the original first codicil and watching him read the word
*or* for the first time in his life — is staged by the brief to hurt. Prescott's register at that
moment is procedural and almost apologetic. Walter goes down.

Never POV. Appears through attendance notes, letters, and as observed by Prescott.

**Walter always says "and her issue" when he quotes the first codicil in dialogue.** This is the
plot device itself — Josiah told him "I've left it to Margaret and her issue after her" — and it is
characterization, not record error. Walter has repeated this version: in R4 (June 1925), to his wife,
and once to Prescott. He has never in his life had the executed text before his eyes.

## Henry Garside

Age approximately seventy-four. Senior partner, now dead. He dies at his desk in December 1926 — his
heart, while the Eccleston action is still gathering speed. Garside drew the will in 1919 and the
first codicil in 1924, using "or her issue" for a niece because he knew Wills Act s.33 gave him no
protection against lapse. He trained Prescott. He handed him the firm's ethos: the file does not
forget; the document is the witness; the signed paper is the record.

Garside is present throughout as the book's standing displacement object. Prescott finds the file
built with more care than the occasion required, and each such discovery is Garside. His handwriting
is in the strong-room register for twenty years. What he left behind is what wins the case.

## Edgar Fairhurst

Approximately forty-five. Schoolmaster, Preston. Husband of the late Margaret. Lives at Bank Parade
with his children. He cannot fund a probate action. He enters the caveat; he consents to the
administrator pendente lite; he cooperates fully. He is the face that reminds Prescott, when the work
becomes procedure against persons, what the stake is. Not a fool; not a lawyer.

## Nora Fairhurst

Nineteen. Older child of Margaret and Edgar. She appears at Bank Parade — she has opinions, a voice,
a sense of what her mother was and what she was to have had. She is not simply a cause. The reader
should feel the stake through her.

## George Fairhurst

Sixteen. Younger child. Less present in the book than Nora; not scenery.

## Mr. Booth

The firm's managing clerk. Has run the Garside & Prescott office since 1911. He knows where every
document is. He is the institutional memory of the place, loyal to it. After Garside's death, the
firm is Prescott and Mr. Booth. He does not editorialize; he acts.

## Secondary and off-page characters

**Josiah Eccleston** — died October 1926, eighty-one. Cotton spinner, magistrate, owner of Eccleston
Hall and Vale Mill. Drew his will in 1919; made the first codicil in 1924 after the genuine
reconciliation with Margaret. His voice enters through correspondence and what those who knew him
say. He was capable of late sentiment; he was also capable of stubbornness about it. He told Walter
what he had done — "I've left it to Margaret and her issue after her; you'll not want for the mill
if you earn it" — and never said it again in those terms.

**Margaret Fairhurst** (née Eccleston) — died May 1925, before Josiah. Josiah's niece; Walter's
cousin. The reconciliation was genuine. Her death, before Josiah's, is what activates the lapse
problem — without "or her issue" the gift would fail entirely, and the estate would go back to
Walter.

**Thurston & Marsh** — Walter's solicitors, Preston. They produce the second codicil, act for Walter
in the probate action, and eventually take instructions to abandon.

**The administrator pendente lite** — a neutral Preston accountant appointed by the court while the
action is pending. He can collect assets and pay debts but cannot distribute. His monthly figures
are how Prescott — and the reader — watch the mill bleed.

**The carter** — died of influenza, 28 September 1926. One of the two attesting witnesses named on
the second codicil, chosen because he could not be cross-examined. His genuine signatures on earlier
estate papers exist for comparison.

**The gardener** — sailed to Canada, mid-October 1926, no fixed address. The other attesting witness.
The application for a commission to examine him abroad fails; this is the calendar-against-Prescott
beat. His genuine signatures exist; he never testifies.

**Two handwriting experts** — one retained by each side. They split honestly and remain split. The
book does not reconcile them. The one licensed irresolution.

**Mr. Holt** — Walter's bank manager (named in R4). Present only through correspondence.

# Style

## Register

Third person limited, past tense, Arthur Prescott throughout. The narrative voice is Prescott's
sensibility: dry, precise, professionally restrained, and capable of landing weight in a plain
sentence. The nearest exemplars are Dorothy L. Sayers's *Unnatural Death* (1927) — procedural pace,
the investigator's eye for documents and professional detail, observational wit that lives in
noticing rather than performance — and Freeman Wills Crofts's method novels: patient accumulation
of evidence, a calendar-against-the-investigator pressure that never lets up, the slow foreclosure
of each innocent explanation. This is not pastiche of either.

The book loves documents the way its narrator does. When a document is quoted verbatim, it stands as
a set-off passage and the prose gets entirely out of the way. No frame, no gloss, no comment on the
language in the paragraph that follows. The document is its own meaning.

Interiority is noticing and deciding, not ruminating. Prescott thinks in the professional vocabulary
— instruments, dates, custody, recitals — and his emotional life surfaces as displacement: onto
objects (the strong-room, the register in Garside's hand), onto procedure (the file that is better-
built than it needed to be), onto what he sees in other people's houses. He does not name his grief
for Garside; he finds it in the work Garside left behind.

## Sentence rhythm

Mid-range and exact. Short declaratives (8–12 words) cluster at moments of weight or decision; they
are a rhythm, not a default. Complex sentences earn themselves through precision: a long sentence in
this register holds several legal specifications in syntactic suspension, not several subordinate
feelings. Period vocabulary — "the instrument," "the executed original," "the strong-room register,"
"letters of administration with the will annexed" — is the furniture of this world. Use it without
gloss; context carries it.

Average sentence length: 18–26 words. Maximum for any single sentence: 45 words (for a sentence
enumerating legal specifications); beyond that, split it.

## Chapter movement

Most chapters centre on a single professional act. The compounding mechanism (every chapter closes a
door) means each chapter earns its place through a foreclosure: something is fixed in evidence at
the end that was not fixed at its start. Documents enter as set-off passages within chapters; the
prose resumes from the same narrative level afterward. The calendar countdown (days to the hearing)
appears in every chapter but varies its position — beginning, middle, or end — and must not close
every chapter like a metronome.

## Tonal register

Sober and quiet. No chase, no violence, no confrontation until the hearing. The tension is
procedural: is the record sufficient? Is there time? Period-true affect: professionals who do not
perform emotion, who are not cold but who would rather show grief in what they do than say it. When
the weight lands, it lands in plain sentences, because the sentences around it have been controlled.

## Fair-play planting

The two forms of the clause — *or her issue* in R2, *and her issue* in R3's recital and in Walter's
dialogue — are each printed verbatim, in plain view, before the discovery chapter, without the
narration ever underlining the variance. The reader is invited to notice. The narration does not help
them notice, and does not penalize them for missing it.

Walter's spoken misquotation appears exactly three times before the discovery, pinned in the brief
(R4 printed as a financial exhibit; Walter to Prescott at the funeral caveat meeting; Walter,
kindly, to Nora and George at Bank Parade). No further occasions.

## Lean-into patterns

Patterns the drafter and editors should NOT treat as failures, because this register depends on them.

- **Verbatim document quotation:** printing a canonical text in full is fair-play planting, not
  padding. R1–R3 may each appear at most two or three times in full before the discovery; after the
  discovery, they are referenced by name or fragment. Within that ceiling, printing the full text is
  the contractual act of fair-play.
- **Displacement onto objects:** Prescott's grief for Garside surfaces through professional
  discovery (the file built too precisely, the procedure followed beyond what was required), not
  through direct sentiment. This is not evasion; it is the register's correct form of interiority.
  Do not compress it.
- **The plain sentence that lands hard:** mid-register prose earns the occasional sentence of
  disproportionate weight by controlling everything around it. Do not follow such a sentence with a
  gloss; do not precede it with a softening qualifier. The weight is produced by the contrast.
- **Period-legal vocabulary as texture:** "the executed original," "due execution," "solemn form,"
  "the recital," "letters of administration with the will annexed" — these are not jargon insertions.
  They are how this world is described by someone who lives in it. Use them; do not italicize or
  explain them.

## Failure modes

The AI-author patterns most tempting in this story's register. The drafter should actively avoid
these; the compression pass should cut them.

- **Sentence-after-the-sentence** — Prescott's narrated noticing must be allowed to land without the
  next sentence explaining what it was. When an observation has weight, the prose earns it by
  stopping. A gloss sentence immediately after ("He had not expected that to matter as much as it
  did") deflates the whole register.
- **Meta-commentary on cognition** — "He noted that," "It occurred to him that," "She registered" —
  these are labels for thinking that Prescott's perspective already performs. The professional
  sensibility is shown through what he attends to, not through naming the act of attention.
- **Post-scene subtext naming** — after a document is quoted, the narrative must not explain what it
  "really" meant. The paragraph after a document insert continues the scene; it does not annotate the
  text. This is also a fair-play rule: the reader must encounter the document uninterpreted.
- **Emotional structural analysis** — the register does not explain grief. It shows the strong-room
  register in Garside's hand. Any passage that begins to anatomize Prescott's feelings about
  Garside's death must be cut back to the displacement form.
- **Redundant transition / re-summary** — Prescott does not recap what the file contains. He works
  forward. A paragraph that begins "So far Prescott had established…" belongs in a different kind of
  detective novel.

# Continuity

Hard facts that must not break in later drafting. Facts 1–4 are architectural binding constraints
written directly into the brief; they are reproduced here because every audit, editor, and repair
pass reads this file and must respect them. Facts 5–24 are research-confirmed and architecturally
set.

---

## Inviolable document constraints (from the brief)

1. **The document variance is by design and inviolable.** The registered text of `first-codicil`
   (R2) contains the words *"or her issue"*. The registered text of `second-codicil` (R3) contains
   the words *"and her issue"* in its recital. This one-word variance is the book's engine. Any
   finding, by any pass, that these two registered texts disagree with each other is a finding that
   the engine is working. No continuity, audit, or repair pass may ever reconcile, correct, or
   repair either text toward the other.

2. **Walter's spoken misquotation is deliberate characterisation, not record drift.** Walter
   Eccleston, quoting the first codicil in *dialogue*, always says *"and her issue."* This is the
   plot device itself — the root is Josiah's own spoken account to Walter in March 1924: "I've left
   it to Margaret and her issue after her." Walter has repeated this version ever since. No
   continuity, audit, or repair pass may correct Walter's spoken words toward the registered records.
   Only narrator-framed document quotations must match the record.

3. **Document texts are inviolable.** Repair passes may never alter any word inside the quotation of
   any canonical document text (R1–R5, registered under their record ids). This includes punctuation,
   capitalisation, and the or/and distinction.

4. **Verbatim fidelity is achieved by prevention.** Drafters must call `read_record` before every
   re-quotation of any of R1–R5. No pass should expect an audit to catch a drifted in-prose
   quotation; none should introduce one.

---

## Story and structural facts

5. **Single POV throughout.** Arthur Prescott, third person limited, past tense. No other POV
   chapters. Off-page events reach the book only through period-true channels — correspondence,
   attendance notes, depositions, opposing solicitors' letters, what witnesses say in the room.
   Verbatim document inserts are records, not POV breaches.

6. **The will** was executed 3 June 1919, typed, held in the strong-room of Garside & Prescott.
   It gives the residue of the estate to Walter Eccleston absolutely and appoints Walter sole
   executor (R1).

7. **The first codicil** was executed 15 March 1924, typed, held in the strong-room of Garside &
   Prescott from the day of execution (R2). It revokes clause 4 of the will entire — both the gift
   *and* the executorship. It gives the residue to Margaret Fairhurst *or her issue* absolutely. No
   copy, draft, or carbon of it ever existed outside Garside & Prescott: the original in the
   strong-room, the letter-book carbon of the covering correspondence (which never left the office),
   and nothing else. Drafters must not invent a copy at the Hall or elsewhere.

8. **The second codicil** is dated 14 August 1926 (R3). It was forged by Walter Eccleston. He forged
   it in the approximately six days the despatch-box stood at the mill in his keeping — in late
   October or early November 1926 — after R5 (dated 2 November 1926) had given him the date of the
   first codicil in writing. He dated it 14 August to predate his access to the box.

9. **The origin of Walter's misquote.** In March 1924, Josiah told Walter what he had done: "I've
   left it to Margaret and her issue after her; you'll not want for the mill if you earn it." That
   spoken sentence — not any document — is the root of Walter's version. Walter repeated "and her
   issue" in R4 (June 1925), to his wife, and to Prescott.

10. **Walter has never read the executed first codicil.** He heard it read aloud once — September
    1926, at the Hall, when Josiah (failing) had Garside fetch the codicil from the strong-room and
    read it to the assembled family. The strong-room register records the fetch and same-day return
    in Garside's hand. Garside read the instrument entire, including its date. Prescott was present,
    carrying the deed-box. Walter was present. Walter heard "or her issue" but his memory had already
    encoded "and," and one hearing aloud did not correct it. He has never had the text before his
    eyes.

11. **The despatch-box.** Inventoried, with Prescott present, approximately a week after Josiah's
    death: no second codicil in it at that point. Stood approximately six days at the mill in
    Walter's keeping. Walter produced the second codicil after that period.

12. **The attesting witnesses.** The carter died of influenza on 28 September 1926. The gardener
    sailed to Canada in mid-October 1926 without leaving a fixed address. Both are beyond
    examination. Their genuine signatures on earlier estate papers exist for comparison with the
    attestations on the second codicil. The application for a commission to examine the gardener
    abroad fails on the ground of no traceable address — this is the calendar-against-Prescott beat.

13. **The executor point.** The first codicil revoked clause 4 entire — gift and executorship both.
    If the second codicil fails, there is no executor. The grant is letters of administration with
    the will annexed, to Edgar Fairhurst as guardian of the minor children. Walter is not the
    executor under any surviving instrument; drafters must not write Walter acting as executor, and
    must not write "probate granted" to the children's side (it is administration, not probate).

14. **Both children are minors.** Majority was twenty-one under 1926 law (reduced only by the Family
    Law Reform Act 1969). Nora Fairhurst is nineteen; George Fairhurst is sixteen.

15. **Josiah's death:** October 1926, age 81. **Margaret Fairhurst's death:** May 1925, before
    Josiah. **Henry Garside's death:** December 1926, at his desk, his heart.

16. **The administrator pendente lite** is a neutral Preston accountant appointed by the court. He
    can collect assets and pay debts but cannot distribute. His monthly figures on the estate's
    condition are how Prescott (and the reader) watch the mill bleed.

17. **The firm's financial position.** Garside & Prescott carries the action at its own risk; costs
    are recoverable only if the action succeeds.

18. **The hearing** is in the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division of the High Court, London.
    Documents travel by post; counsel appears in London; Prescott manages evidence from Preston.

19. **The discovery.** Late, alone, on the eve of final hearing preparation, Prescott re-reads the
    propounded second codicil against the strong-room original of the first — file discipline, not
    intuition. He sees the ninth word. The discovery rests on K1 (the R2/R3 comparison) plus R4
    pulled from exhibits already in the record. Nothing material enters the book after the three-
    quarter mark that the reader has not already seen.

20. **The exposure.** At the hearing (or in its immediate face), Walter is handed the original first
    codicil and reads the word *or* for the first time in his life. Walter's counsel takes
    instructions; the action is abandoned.

21. **The handwriting experts split** honestly and remain split. The book does not reconcile them.
    Text convicts; typewriter and ink evidence narrows provenance to the mill office but never closes
    it alone.

22. **Walter's cover story (fixed).** Walter's account: Josiah must have typed the codicil himself
    (or had it typed) on one of his days at the mill office, and laid it in the despatch-box.
    Walter says he found it going through insurance papers after the funeral.

23. **The mill sale.** Walter's sale contract is conditioned on "a grant of representation
    establishing the vendor's title." Failure of the second codicil makes that grant impossible.

24. **"Or her issue" is the professionally correct substitutional gift** for a niece (a collateral
    relative) because Wills Act 1837 s.33 protects against lapse only for gifts to the testator's
    own descendants. Garside used "or" deliberately. "And her issue" potentially creates only a
    class gift with ambiguous construction. The legal distinction is one of construction clarity,
    not necessarily outcome, but a careful 1924 draftsman would have used "or."

25. **The clean ending is the contract.** The forgery is proven on the page; Walter's authorship is
    established; the action collapses; the estate passes under the 1924 codicil (letters of
    administration with the will annexed). Criminal consequence begins and is stated plainly, not
    dramatized. No withheld answer; no final-page unsettling; no ambiguity about the central
    question. The editor and reader passes must not re-complicate it.

26. **The compounding mechanism is strict.** Every chapter closes or materially narrows one named
    innocent explanation of the second codicil. A fact once established must not be re-walked. The
    enumerated doors are: (a) the machine; (b) Josiah's presence; (c) the witnesses; (d) the
    profession; (e) the firm; (f) the habit; (g) the despatch-box; (h) the September reading;
    (i) the date asymmetry.

input.content:
# Glossary

**Administrator pendente lite** — A neutral administrator appointed by the court to manage a
deceased's estate while a contentious probate action is pending. Can collect assets and pay debts;
may not distribute to any beneficiary. In this book: a Preston accountant, his monthly figures the
reader's window onto the mill's deterioration.

**Administration of Estates Act 1925 (AEA 1925)** — In force 1 January 1926. Its central reform for
this story: all of a deceased's estate (real *and* personal) now vests in the personal
representative, not directly in the heirs. A sale conditioned on "a grant of representation
establishing the vendor's title" is the correct post-1925 formulation.

**Attestation clause** — The clause in a will or codicil, signed by the attesting witnesses,
recording that the instrument was executed in the testator's presence. Creates a rebuttable
presumption of due execution.

**Caveat (probate)** — A formal notice lodged at the Probate Registry preventing any grant of
representation from issuing. The caveator states their contrary interest; if they enter an
appearance, the caveat persists until the court resolves the dispute. Edgar Fairhurst enters the
caveat on behalf of the minor children.

**Codicil** — A supplementary document to a will, executed with the same formalities (Wills Act 1837
s.9 and s.10), that adds to, alters, or revokes the will's provisions.

**Common form** — Routine, uncontested grant of probate on the executor's oath. Vulnerable to
challenge for up to thirty years; not appropriate here, where the instrument is disputed.

**Deed box** — A painted steel box with a hinged lid, used by solicitors to hold a client's
documents. The Eccleston deed box is black, "ECCLESTON" in white on the lid.

**Due execution** — Compliance with Wills Act 1837 s.9: the will or codicil is signed by the
testator, in the presence of two witnesses present at the same time, each of whom attests and signs
in the testator's presence. A facially correct attestation clause raises a presumption of due
execution (*omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta*).

**Engrossment** — The final fair copy of a legal document, on good paper, ready for execution. By
the 1920s, engrossment is typically typed rather than handwritten in a provincial solicitors' office.

**Issue** — In English legal usage: all lineal descendants — children, grandchildren, and further.
"Or her issue absolutely" in R2 means the gift passes to Margaret's children (and potentially
grandchildren) if she predeceases Josiah.

**Lapse** — Failure of a testamentary gift when the legatee predeceases the testator. The failed
gift falls back into residue (or, if the residuary gift itself fails, on intestacy). Wills Act 1837
s.33 prevents lapse for gifts to the testator's own children or remoter descendants; it does not
extend to nieces or other collateral relatives. Margaret is Josiah's niece; s.33 affords her no
protection.

**Letter-book** — The firm's bound record of outgoing correspondence, carbon-copied from the 1920s
onward. The letter-book carbon of R5 (Garside & Prescott's November 1926 notice letter) survives as
a corroborating exhibit.

**Letters of administration with the will annexed** — A grant issued when no executor is able or
willing to act. Gives the administrator the same powers as an executor. If the second codicil fails,
the grant goes to Edgar Fairhurst as guardian of the minor children; Walter's executorship was
revoked by the first codicil.

**Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division (PDA Division)** — The division of the High Court that
heard contentious probate matters in 1926. Created by the Judicature Acts 1873–75; renamed by the
Administration of Justice Act 1970.

**Probate in solemn form** — Proof of a will in open court, with all interested parties cited. Has
res judicata effect — binds everyone who appeared or was cited. The correct procedure when the
instrument's validity is in dispute.

**Recital** — The explanatory clause in an instrument, recording background facts. In the second
codicil the recital quotes the terms of the first codicil. A recital has no operative legal effect;
an error in a recital is probative evidence about the maker's knowledge of the underlying document.

**Short time** — The period term for reduced-hours working: running a mill for fewer days or hours
than normal to reduce output while keeping the workforce partially employed. The standard state of
the Lancashire weaving industry in 1926. Vale Mill is working short time throughout the book.

**Solemn form** — See *Probate in solemn form*.

**Strong-room** — A fireproof vault (typically in the basement or a reinforced ground-floor room of
a solicitors' office) holding original deeds, wills, and clients' title documents.

**Strong-room register** — The bound ledger recording every deposit and withdrawal from the strong-
room: date, document described, clerk's signature. Garside's handwriting is in this register for
twenty years. It records the September 1926 fetch and same-day return of the first codicil.

**Substitutional gift** — A gift drafted so that a secondary donee takes if the primary donee cannot.
"Unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst or her issue absolutely" (R2) is a substitutional gift: Margaret
takes if living at Josiah's death; her issue take if she has predeceased. The word "or" makes the
substitution express and unambiguous — the formulation a careful 1924 draftsman uses for a niece
because s.33 affords no statutory fallback.

**Trustee Act 1925, s.27** — Allows a personal representative to advertise in the *London Gazette*
for creditors and claimants; after two months, the representative who distributes is protected from
unknown creditors. The Gazette advertisement for any solicitor who took Josiah's testamentary
instructions falls within standard post-death estate administration.

**Vale Mill** — A stone weaving mill above Ribchester, on the hillside above the Ribble valley
floor. Owned through the Eccleston estate; managed by Walter Eccleston for fifteen years. Working
short time throughout; mortgaged; Walter's sale contract conditioned on the estate grant.

**Winckley Square** — A Georgian square in Preston, developed from 1799, by the early twentieth
century the centre of the town's legal profession. Garside & Prescott occupies a town house on the
square.

**Wills Act 1837 s.9** — The statutory formality requirements for a valid will (and, by s.10, a
codicil): in writing; signed by the testator; signature made or acknowledged in the presence of two
witnesses present at the same time; each witness attests and signs in the testator's presence.

# Themes

## The record against memory

The book's whole engine is the divergence between text and memory — and the principle that memory,
however sincere, is not evidence. Josiah told Walter what he had done; Walter carried those words for
two years, wrote them to his bank, said them to his wife, told his dead cousin's children what their
mother was to have had. He was not lying about what he remembered. What he remembered was wrong by
one word, because he had never read the executed text, and the spoken sentence Josiah gave him was
not the same as the instrument Garside drew.

The same divergence runs through the handwriting experts: two honest men, looking at the same
signature, arriving at opposite conclusions. The book does not sneer at them. The limit of honest
memory and honest perception is not a villain's alibi — it is the condition under which all of them
operate. The file does not forget because the file is not human.

## Procedure as justice

Prescott is not a detective. He has no authority to arrest, no dramatic confrontation to stage, no
genius for intuitive leaps. He can build a record. A record, if it is thorough enough, constrains
what is possible — forecloses the innocent explanations, one by one, until what remains must be what
happened. The compounding mechanism is this theme enacted structurally: the calendar shrinks, the
record grows, and the growing record is justice advancing at the pace justice advances when it is
done properly rather than narratively. The book trusts that this is sufficient — and asks the reader
to trust it.

## The cost of expectation

Walter's crime is not greed in the simple sense. He was owed the mill. He had carried it for fifteen
years; he had been told it was his; he had borrowed against it in good faith; the debt had compounded
while Josiah's sentimentality ran its course. The first codicil was, in Walter's reading, a temporary
aberration — Josiah would put it right; Josiah said so; and then Josiah died without doing so. The
forgery is the act of a man who had waited as long as he could wait and decided to close the account
himself. The book will not let him be simply wrong; it insists on the logic of his position. What it
refuses to permit is the conclusion that the logic made him right. The quiet corruption the book
traces — from the spring of 1924 to the autumn of 1926 — is the compound interest on believing
oneself owed something that belongs to someone else.

## Grief converted to procedure

Prescott cannot grieve for Garside directly; it is not the register of the man or the book. What he
can do is find the file better than it needed to be. Find the strong-room register more precise than
the occasion required. Find, at the end, that Garside's habit of exactitude — a professional habit,
unremarkable for forty years — is what convicts the forger. The old man is everywhere in the record,
and the record is what wins.

Prescott's grief is therefore useful; it is the fuel of the method. The discovery is not a detective's
triumph — it is a clerk's reflex, a check run late at night that turns out to matter. The procedure
Garside taught him is what Prescott enacts in Garside's place. That this is also cold is true. The
book leaves both propositions on the table.

# Drafter guidance — The Probate of Eccleston

## Voice register

The target register is procedural-literary: the considered, precise, professionally dry sensibility
of a 1920s English solicitor's narration, capable of landing weight in plain sentences. The two
closest exemplars:

- **Sayers, *Unnatural Death* (1927):** procedural investigation sustained through
  document and witness, observational wit that lives in noticing rather than performance, emotional
  weight carried by restraint rather than by statement — "He had not known Mr. Garside well enough
  to be quite certain that he had known him at all" is the kind of sentence this register can hold.

- **Crofts (method novels):** patient accumulation of evidence across chapters that feel spare
  rather than eventful; a calendar pressure on the investigator that never resolves until it must;
  each chapter closes one door and the closed door is the chapter's payoff.

This is not pastiche of either. Prescott's voice is his own — a probate man, not a detective, and
the distinction matters in every scene he appears in.

## Sentence-length expectations

- Average sentence length: **18–26 words** (longer than a thriller, exact rather than expansive)
- Maximum for any single sentence: **45 words** (for a sentence enumerating legal specifications);
  beyond that, split it
- Short declaratives (8–12 words) cluster at moments of weight or decision: **three in a row is a
  rhythm, four is a tic** — vary after three
- Long sentences in this register enumerate legal specifications, not feelings; a sentence that gets
  long because it is elaborating an emotion is the wrong kind of long sentence

## Chapter-opening conventions

Chapters open in process — Prescott already in the middle of a professional act: examining a
document, composing a letter, receiving a visitor, walking to a meeting. The reader arrives halfway
through something. No abstract observation openings ("The autumn of 1926 brought…"). No summary of
what the previous chapter established. No weather paragraph that is only weather. If weather appears
in the opening sentence, it is doing two things.

## Chapter-ending conventions

The chapter ends when the door is closed — the new record item fixed, the foreclosure made. The last
substantive paragraph is the closure itself; a summary sentence after it is redundant. Target
distribution across a 20-chapter manuscript:

- **6 resolved-beats** — door closed, record extended, Prescott moves on
- **4 coda** — a quiet displacement image: the office at night, the register in Garside's hand, the
  mill working short time, Bank Parade in a specific light
- **4 turn** — new information reorganises the record (Garside's death; the refused commission; the
  discovery; the hearing pivot)
- **3 mid-action cuts** — a proceeding broken off, a letter arriving at a bad time
- **3 declarative-close** — a plain statement of what has been established

No run of more than two chapters in the same ending mode. The calendar countdown must not close
every chapter — vary its position (beginning, middle, end); on average once per chapter.

## POV strategy

Single POV, Arthur Prescott, throughout — no exceptions. Off-page events (Walter's finances, the
children's lives, the mill's condition between visits) reach the book only through period-true
channels: letters, attendance notes, depositions, opposing solicitors' correspondence, witness
testimony in the room. A verbatim document insert (R1–R5 printed as set-off passages) is a record
within a chapter, not a POV breach. Prescott must be present at, or the recipient of, every scene.

## Dialogue density

Sparse but load-bearing. Professional exchanges between Prescott and witnesses, opposing solicitors,
Mr. Booth — functional, formal, producing the record. No banter; no extended social exchange. The
book's weight is carried by documents and procedure. Dialogue tags are spare: "said," "asked." No
qualifying tags ("as if to say," "which meant"). When Walter speaks about the first codicil, what he
says is governed by the brief's fair-play plant: the drafter must have read `canon/continuity.md`
item 2 before writing any such line.

## Document inserts

When R1–R5 are printed in full or substantial excerpt, they stand as **set-off passages** — visually
distinct, indented or preceded and followed by a blank line. The prose before the insert ends where
the document begins; the prose after resumes the scene from the same narrative level. No gloss
paragraph between the end of the insert and the next prose. No sentence commenting on the
language of the document. The document is its meaning.

Before every re-quotation of any of R1–R5, the drafter must call `read_record` with the appropriate
record id and reproduce the text verbatim. The critical pair: `first-codicil` contains *"or her
issue"*; `second-codicil` contains *"and her issue"* in its recital. These must never be equalised.

## Comic timing and tonal balance

Wit exists and is welcome. It lives in Prescott's noticing — a detail that is unexpected but exact,
a sentence that reveals an absurdity by naming it precisely, in the manner of Sayers's observational
comedy in professional settings. The timing is in the sentence's last clause or final word; a follow-
up sentence explaining the observation kills it. Comic passages are short and surrounded by gravity;
the gravity is what makes them land.

## Anti-defaults — what the drafter must actively avoid in this register

- **Do not open chapters on extended abstract interiority.** Prescott's interior life surfaces
  through displacement — what he notices about the office, the register, the Fairhurst household —
  not through reflection as a chapter-opening mode. No more than one sentence of interior thought
  before a sensory anchor or professional act.

- **Do not gloss a document after quoting it.** The paragraph following a document insert continues
  the scene; it does not explain what the document meant. This is also a fair-play rule.

- **Do not summarise prior chapters.** "So far Prescott had established…" belongs in a different
  kind of detective novel. The file does not recap.

- **Do not write more than one interior sentence of direct feeling.** When Prescott must acknowledge
  Garside's death or the children's situation, one sentence and back to procedure. Two sentences is
  a speech; three is editorialising.

- **Do not add Walter's spoken misquotation beyond the three pinned occasions.** The brief fixes
  exactly where "and her issue" appears in Walter's dialogue (R4 as financial exhibit; Walter to
  Prescott at the caveat meeting; Walter to Nora and George at Bank Parade). Adding further
  occasions tips the reader too explicitly and breaks the fair-play architecture.

- **Do not write a summation-of-triumph.** Prescott's register at the exposure is procedural and
  almost apologetic. There is no scene in which Prescott explains the proof to another character;
  the proof is in the record, and the record speaks.

- **Do not write Walter as a villain.** He is a man who went wrong under compound pressure. When he
  appears (through letters, through what others say, through the one or two direct meetings), he
  should be recognisably a person: competent, liked by his men, once genuinely fond of Josiah. His
  exposure must hurt, not satisfy.

# Plotter guidance — The Probate of Eccleston

## POV count and rotation

Single POV throughout: Arthur Prescott, third person limited, past tense. There is no rotation and
no exception. All 18–24 chapters belong to Prescott. Off-page events (Walter's finances, the mill's
condition between visits, the children's circumstances) reach the plot only through period-true
channels — correspondence, attendance notes, depositions, third-party testimony in the room. The
plotter must design the chapter sequence so that every door closure can be witnessed or received
by Prescott.

## Chapter-shape preferences

The dominant shapes are:

- **Single-scene document examination** — Prescott reads or receives a document; its implications
  are worked out within the chapter; the chapter's door is closed. Most chapters in Movement II.
- **Witness interview** — Prescott meets a witness (or reads a deposition); testimony fixes a
  fact. One or two chapters.
- **Correspondence chapter** — a letter received and its consequences managed. Efficient for
  calendar-gate beats and for introducing Walter through his solicitors.
- **Site visit** — the mill, Bank Parade, Eccleston Hall (once each, deliberately placed). These
  are the displacement chapters and the stake chapters.

Intercut chapters (Prescott managing two parallel developments in one chapter) are rare — use at
most twice, and only when the calendar is most constrained. Pure interiority chapters do not exist:
Prescott is always doing something, even when what he is doing is re-reading.

## The compounding mechanism — strict enforcement

This is the anti-sag spine of the book. Every chapter's outline row must name:

1. **Which door it closes** (select from the nine enumerated in `canon/continuity.md` item 26):
   - (a) the machine
   - (b) Josiah's presence
   - (c) the witnesses
   - (d) the profession (no solicitor anywhere took instructions for a revocation)
   - (e) the firm (no request for the codicil's text ever reached Garside & Prescott)
   - (f) the habit (every instrument of Josiah's adult life was drawn by the firm)
   - (g) the despatch-box (inventoried with no codicil; six days at the mill)
   - (h) the September reading (what the register records; what was read aloud; who was present)
   - (i) the date asymmetry (how Walter had the date but not the text; R5 as the source)

2. **The new record item** — the document produced, the deposition sworn, the custody fact fixed
   — that closes the door. The record item is the vehicle of the foreclosure, not a substitute for
   it. A chapter that produces evidence but forecloses nothing is not earning its place.

3. **The prior chapter's fact it tightens** — the compounding step. This chapter's closure must
   reference an established fact from an earlier chapter. The ladder must be visible.

4. **Days remaining to the hearing** — monotonically decreasing across the manuscript. Must not
   always appear at the same structural position in the chapter. Appears in every chapter. The
   refused commission is the one occasion the calendar moves against Prescott (days lost, not
   gained). At least one chapter should show the calendar costing Prescott in real time.

A door once closed must not be re-opened or re-walked in a later chapter. The record is permanent.

## The three movements

**Movement I — first quarter (4–6 chapters, ~10,000–14,000 words):**
The two codicils surface; the caveat is entered; Garside dies; the action and firm pass to Prescott.
Chapters here establish: the office and the strong-room culture; Josiah's death and the estate;
the first codicil (R2 must appear in full at least once, establishing the fair-play plant for the
reader — do this early, before Walter's first spoken misquotation); the firm's financial exposure;
Walter, glimpsed through the caveat meeting (one attendance note, his one spoken misquotation to
Prescott); Garside's death as the structural hinge. Doors closed in Movement I: (g) the despatch-
box (initial inventory); (h) the September reading (the strong-room register entry surfaced early).

**Movement II — middle half (8–12 chapters, ~22,000–28,000 words):**
The building of the record, foreclosure by foreclosure. The nine doors are distributed here (some
take two chapters for the full closure). Key beats:
- The negative canvass of the profession and the Gazette advertisement: (d)
- The firm-records check — no request for the codicil's text: (e)
- Josiah's correspondence and diary: (f) and (b)
- The mill visit: Prescott sees the typewriter (begins (a)); the mill office; short time. This
  chapter closes (b) (Josiah's last confirmed visit to the mill was May 1926).
- The typewriter identification report: closes (a) (machine in the mill office, not the Hall or
  any solicitors').
- The witnesses thread: (c) — the carter's death confirmed; the commission application for the
  gardener; the refusal (calendar-against beat, near the end of Movement II).
- R4 as financial exhibit: printed in full, unremarked, in the chapter covering Walter's mortgage
  and the sale contract. Its language ("and her issue") is not commented on.
- Walter to Nora and George at Bank Parade: third pinned misquotation; the Bank Parade chapter
  is one of two human-stake chapters (alongside the first Bank Parade visit with Edgar).
- The administrator pendente lite's first monthly figures: the mill bleeding in the ledger.
- The Garside displacement thread: Prescott keeps finding the file built more precisely than
  occasion required. This accumulates across three or four chapters without announcement.

**Movement III — final quarter (4–6 chapters, ~12,000–18,000 words):**
The discovery; the corroboration; the hearing; the aftermath.
- **Discovery chapter:** Late, alone, Prescott re-reads the propounded codicil against the strong-
  room original — file discipline, not intuition. He sees the ninth word. The chapter rests on K1
  (the R2/R3 comparison) plus R4 already in the record. Nothing material enters here that the
  reader has not seen.
- **Corroboration chapter:** the recital-variance closes (i) — the date was in Walter's hands in
  writing from R5; the text was not. Walter's misquotation is habitual (R4, the deposition of the
  bank manager or wife), written, and dated fourteen months before the codicil. The proof chain
  stated honestly: variance + closed doors = Walter as the only remaining candidate.
- **Hearing chapter:** Walter is handed the original first codicil; reads "or" for the first time;
  counsel takes instructions; action abandoned. Prescott's register is procedural, almost
  apologetic. The two handwriting experts remain split; this is confirmed at the hearing, not
  resolved.
- **Final chapter:** What the outcome costs and buys — the children, Walter, the mill, the firm.
  Criminal consequence begins and is stated plainly, not dramatized. Every opened account closed.

## Ending-mode distribution

For a 20-chapter manuscript (adjust proportionally for other lengths):
- 6 resolved-beats (Movement II door-closures)
- 4 coda (quiet displacement chapters: the office at night, the register, the mill visit end, the
  final chapter)
- 4 turn (Garside's death; refused commission; discovery; hearing)
- 3 mid-action (correspondence received at a bad moment; a proceeding broken off)
- 3 declarative-close (plain statement of what has been established)

No run of more than two chapters in the same ending mode. The coda endings cluster around the human-
stake chapters (Bank Parade, mill visit, Garside displacement). The turn endings mark the four
structural pivots.

## Chapter target words

- Standard chapter: 2,000–3,000 words
- Document-heavy chapters (two documents quoted in full): 1,500–2,000 words
- Major set pieces (discovery, hearing): up to 3,500–4,000 words
- Final chapter (aftermath): 1,500–2,500 words
- Total target: **45,000–55,000 words**; ceiling 70,000; the shorter book is the better book if
  every door is closed and every thread is settled

## Fair-play architecture constraints

**The three Walter misquotation occasions (pinned, non-negotiable):**
1. R4 printed in full as a financial exhibit — in a Movement II chapter on Walter's mortgage and
   sale contract; unremarked by the narration
2. Walter to Prescott, at the early caveat meeting in Movement I — mid-sentence, not the topic of
   the sentence
3. Walter, kindly, to Nora and George at Bank Parade — in a Movement II human-stake chapter

No additional occasions. The plotter must ensure these three are spread across the manuscript (not
consecutive chapters) and that each is doing other work in its scene.

**The reader's fair-play access:**
R2 must appear in full before Walter's first spoken misquotation. The reader must have seen "or her
issue" before they hear "and her issue" from Walter's mouth. Place R2's full first printing in the
early chapters of Movement I.

**Nothing new after three-quarters:** No document, witness, or fact that materially advances the
proof may be introduced after the three-quarter mark. The discovery re-reads what already exists.
The plotter must ensure all nine doors have at least begun to close by the end of Movement II.

## Genre-specific structural conventions

This is Golden Age fair-play detection in a literary register, not a thriller. The structural
conventions:

- **Patient accumulation** over dramatic revelation — the book's tension is procedural, not
  physical; the reader follows the record's growth rather than a chase
- **Calendar pressure** as the structural counterweight to the record's growth — the hearing date is
  fixed and approaching; it must feel like a genuine constraint, not a backdrop
- **The clean ending is the contract** — fully resolved; the forgery proven on the page; Walter's
  authorship established; the estate disposed of; criminal consequence stated. The editor and reader
  passes must not re-open it.
- **One licensed irresolution:** the handwriting experts split and remain split. This is not a
  defect; it is part of the book's argument about the limits of expert evidence. Do not resolve it
  in the outline.

# Reader guidance — The Probate of Eccleston

## Intended audience

Adult readers of literary detective fiction — specifically readers who know and value the Golden Age
fair-play tradition (Sayers, Crofts, Christie) and are comfortable with a patient, procedural pace
in a literary register. This is not a cozy mystery and not a thriller. The reader is invited to
solve the puzzle before Prescott does; the book assumes they will try. The satisfaction is
intellectual and emotional in equal measure, and the two are not in tension.

## Brief-adherence checks to perform

In addition to general craft review, the Reader must answer each of the following as a yes/no with
evidence:

**1. Fair-play contract: is every necessary fact on the page before the discovery?**
R2 ("or her issue") must appear verbatim before the discovery chapter. R3's recital ("and her
issue") must appear verbatim before the discovery chapter. R4 must appear in full as a financial
exhibit before the three-quarter mark. If any of these are absent or appear only at or after the
discovery, the fair-play contract is broken. This is a **structural failure, severity: critical**.

**2. Walter's misquotation — exactly three planted occasions before the discovery?**
The brief pins the count and locations: R4 printed as exhibit (financial thread chapter); Walter to
Prescott at the early caveat meeting (mid-sentence); Walter to Nora and George at Bank Parade.
Fewer than three: the fair-play plant is too thin. More than three: the variance is over-signalled
and the fair-play effect is compromised. Either count is a finding; extra occasions are the more
common risk.

**3. Single POV discipline: every chapter in Prescott's perspective?**
Flag any passage that accesses another character's interior, or that narrates an event Prescott
could not have witnessed and no period-true channel has relayed to him. This includes any scene
centred on Walter's private actions, any interior access to Edgar or Nora, and any scene at the
mill or Hall that Prescott did not visit.

**4. The compounding mechanism: does every chapter close a door?**
Each chapter should close or materially narrow at least one of the nine enumerated doors (machine,
Josiah's presence, witnesses, profession, firm, habit, despatch-box, September reading, date
asymmetry). Flag any chapter that consists entirely of atmosphere, recap, or procedural activity
without a foreclosure. Flag any door that is re-walked after it has been closed.

**5. Calendar monotonicity: do the days decrease without exception?**
The days remaining to the hearing must be named in every chapter and must decrease monotonically
(with one exception: the refused commission, where the calendar moves against Prescott). Flag any
chapter where the days are absent, or where they appear to have increased.

**6. The ending is complete: does it answer every opened question?**
The last movement must resolve: (a) Was the second codicil a forgery? (b) Who made it? (c) How is
the authorship proven? (d) What happens to the estate? (e) What happens to Walter? (f) What happens
to the children and the firm? Any withheld answer is a **structural failure**. The clean, fully-
resolved ending is the contract of the book; the Reader must not flag it as over-neat or suggest
re-complicating it.

**7. Document fidelity: does every verbatim quotation of R1–R5 match the registered text exactly?**
Call `read_record` for each of R1–R5 and compare. Any divergence — even a single word — is a
**critical finding**. The sole exception: Walter speaking from memory in dialogue (not quoting a
document as narrator) always says "and her issue" — this is correct and must not be flagged as a
continuity error.

**8. Quotation ceiling: is the verbatim ceiling respected?**
R1, R2, and R3 should each appear in full at most two or three times before the discovery chapter.
After the discovery, they should be referenced only by name, date, or brief fragment. Excess
full-text quotation of the same document is a continuity finding (over-quotation as filler).

## What "good" looks like for this book

A good chapter of *The Probate of Eccleston* opens in the middle of a professional act, proceeds
through procedural accumulation that closes one named door, and ends with the foreclosure fixed —
then stops. The legal vocabulary is used precisely and without gloss. The period texture is present
without becoming a standing display of research. Document inserts are clean: they stand, the prose
continues from the same narrative level, nothing follows that explains the insert.

The register is correct when it reads like a man who notices things precisely but does not explain
what noticing them means. When the displacement object (the strong-room register, the file built too
carefully, Bank Parade in a specific light) carries emotional weight without a sentence naming the
emotion — that is the register working.

The Garside thread is working when it accumulates through small, specific discoveries across the
middle movement — details in the file that were more precise than occasion required — without any
summary paragraph declaring their significance. It is *not* working if it is announced ("He thought
of Garside again") or if it is concentrated into one scene that functions as a grief chapter.

The Walter misquotations are working as fair-play when a reader paying careful attention will notice
the "and/or" variance each time Walter speaks — but only if they are paying attention, and only
because they are comparing against R2 which they have already read, not because the narration flags
the contrast. The narration must never flag it before the discovery.

## What to flag explicitly if the manuscript drifts

**1. Extended abstract interiority at chapter openings.**
If more than four sentences of Prescott's reflection appear before the first sensory anchor or
professional act, name it as register drift. The literary attractor produces this; the book does
not want it.

**2. Gloss paragraphs after document inserts.**
If the paragraph following any document insert explains what the document "really" meant or
summarises its significance, cut it or flag it as a failure mode. This is both a register failure
and a fair-play violation — the reader must encounter the document uninterpreted.

**3. Grief articulated directly.**
If Prescott's feelings about Garside are expressed in more than one direct sentence (not
displacement), flag it as over-articulation. The displacement mechanism is doing that work; direct
sentiment is the wrong register for this book.

**4. The ending re-complicated.**
If the final movement withholds any of the six answers in check 6, or introduces ambiguity about
the forgery's authorship, flag it as a structural failure. The editor and compression passes must
not re-open the ending. The clean resolution is the book's contract with its reader.

**5. Thriller-pace drift.**
If chapters have shortened to 1,000 words or fewer without document content to explain the
compression, if physical peril has entered, or if the pace has become punchy and cliffhanger-
dominant, name it as register drift in the wrong direction.

**6. Walter as villain.**
If the narration (through Prescott's observations) has tilted toward contempt for Walter — if his
exposure is satisfying rather than painful — flag the tonal balance. The brief requires that the
exposure hurt. A Walter who is simply a bad man does not hurt.

## What to applaud

- **The displacement mechanism working in accumulation.** If Prescott's grief for Garside surfaces
  consistently through specific professional discoveries across the middle movement — the file built
  too well, the procedure followed beyond what was required — without announcement or summary,
  defend this from any compression impulse that would trim the individual instances for efficiency.
  The accumulation is the effect; removing the instances removes the effect.

- **The plain sentence that lands hard.** If the manuscript has a sentence that carries
  disproportionate weight because everything before it has been exact and controlled, defend it from
  any impulse to contextualise or cushion it. A gloss sentence after it destroys it.

- **The fair-play subtlety of the Walter occasions.** If the "and/or" variance in Walter's dialogue
  is present but not flagged by the narration, and if a reader paying attention will notice it while
  a reader not paying attention will not — the fair-play contract is being honoured. Defend this
  subtlety from any impulse to make the variance more visible before the discovery.

- **The compounding mechanism producing visible accumulation.** If each chapter's foreclosure
  visibly tightens a prior chapter's established fact — if the record's growth is perceptible as
  accumulation rather than repetition — name this as structural success and defend it.

- **Procedural texture used without explanation.** If the legal vocabulary (engrossment, the
  recital, letters of administration with the will annexed) is used correctly and in context,
  without a glossing sentence, and if the reader's understanding is carried by context rather than
  by explanation, this is the register working. Do not flag unexplained legal terms as inaccessible;
  they are period texture.
