# Chapter 13 — The Fairhursts

**One-line summary:** Second visit to Bank Parade: Nora reports that Walter called last week and told her and George what their mother was to have had — his version of the first codicil's terms enters the record; the human stake is renewed at the case's midpoint.

---

## POV and Tense
Arthur Prescott — third person limited, past tense.

## Setting / Time
Bank Parade, Avenham district, Preston. April/May 1927. A spring afternoon; the parks visible from the terrace window; the parlour recognisable from the first visit.

## Chapter Shape
**Bottle — witness interview with human texture.** One location; near real-time. Prescott visits to take a deposition from Edgar on the administrator's figures and to discuss progress with the family. Nora and George are present; the chapter carries the human stake.

## Ending Mode
**Coda.** The chapter closes quietly: Prescott walks back from Bank Parade in the spring evening. The children are still people; the stake is not abstract. He does not name what the visit does to the dry record accumulating at his desk.

---

## Goal, Obstacle, Action Beats

**Prescott's goal:** Update Edgar on the case's progress; obtain whatever the family can provide as further evidence; and ensure the children are not simply abstractions in the brief.

**Obstacle:** The children live in a state of suspended uncertainty — the estate will come to them, or it will not; they are minors and cannot act; they must wait. Prescott must manage the communication of what is uncertain without either over-promising or withdrawing the human reality of what is at stake. Also: George is sixteen and finding the situation harder than he shows.

**Beats:**

1. **Arrival:** Prescott walks from Winckley Square again; Bank Parade in spring is a different place from the November visit — the parks greener, the light longer. The house is the same. Nora opens the door.

2. **The figures:** Edgar and Prescott discuss the administrator's figures — the mill bleeding, the estate's position, the hearing timeline. Edgar asks the question all clients ask: how confident is the firm? Prescott says: the record is building; the hearing date is fixed; the firm is confident but not yet in a position to say it is complete. This is honest; it is also controlled.

3. **George:** Briefly present — a sixteen-year-old under sustained uncertainty. He asks a direct question about what happens to the mill if the action fails. Prescott answers plainly: the estate passes to Walter under the second codicil; the mill is sold under Walter's sale contract; the money goes to Walter and his creditors. George says nothing further. He has understood.

4. **Nora's account of Walter's visit [PINNED MISQUOTATION 3 ON PAGE]:** Nora mentions, in the course of conversation about the estate, that Walter Eccleston came to call last week. He was kind; he seemed genuinely fond of their mother. He told them what their mother had been to receive — explained the first codicil and what it meant. He said — and Nora quotes him with evident accuracy — that Josiah had made a codicil "giving everything to our mother and her issue, which meant us." She is repeating Walter's words: "and her issue." She adds: Walter said their uncle had always meant to put it right, and he was sorry it had come to this. Prescott takes down the substance. He does not correct or remark on Walter's phrase.

5. **Nora's character:** She is nineteen, clear-eyed, and not given to sentimentality about the money. She is given to sentimentality about her mother. She says she thinks her mother would have been uncomfortable being made the subject of a legal action; she says she hopes the record will be enough. Prescott says he believes it will be. He believes this; it is also what a solicitor says to a client.

6. **The displacement:** Something in this visit — the spring light, Nora's directness, the March 1924 letter from Josiah to Margaret (mentioned in passing, the tone of it) — settles the case for Prescott in the way that cases must be settled before the work will come right. He does not name this. He gathers his notes and prepares to go.

7. **The close:** Prescott declines tea again; he has a train to catch or a brief to finish. He walks back through the parks, the river below. The hearing is 155 days away. He has what he came for, and more than what he expected.

---

## Outcome / Turn
Misquotation 3 is in the record — not flagged, not underlined, but in the working note from the visit, in Nora's words as reported to Prescott. Walter told the children "and her issue." He did not know, at that moment, that he was saying the wrong word. He said it kindly, without any consciousness that it was wrong. That is the cruelest thing about it.

## New Question or Pressure Raised
Walter said "and her issue" — to the children — unprompted, kindly, in a private context. Not in a legal document, not in a formal statement: in conversation, to the people whose inheritance he has stolen. How many times has he said these words, in how many rooms, since Josiah told him in 1924?

---

## What Compounds

- **Door (i) — the date asymmetry:** Tightened further. The misquotation is now shown to be habitual: not only written (R4 in Ch 11) but spoken in private, unprompted, in a domestic context, using his own natural phrasing. Walter does not say "and her issue" because he is lying; he says it because it is the only version he knows. This is what the discovery will need: not a forger's error but a genuine misremembering that happened to go into the document.

- **Prior chapters advanced:** Ch 11 — R4's written misquotation (June 1925) is joined by this spoken instance (spring 1927), in a different context, using the same words; the pattern is established across time and context.

- **Days to hearing:** 155 days. Noted in passing mid-chapter.

---

## Continuity Notes

- Walter Eccleston visited Bank Parade and told Nora and George what their mother was to have had. He said "and her issue" (in Nora's reporting of his words). He was kind; he seemed genuinely fond of their late mother.
- This is Misquotation 3 on the page — in Nora's reported speech, reaching the record through period-true channel: a witness recounting what was said in her presence.
- Nora's character: clear-eyed, direct, not given to sentiment about money. Fond of her mother. Not a cause.
- George: sixteen; asking direct questions; harder hit than he shows.
- 155 days to hearing.
- The narration must NOT remark on the "and her issue" usage. Nora says it; the narration records it; the prose moves on.
- Do NOT have Prescott connect R4's phrasing (Ch 11) with what Nora has just reported. He cannot yet — the connection will be made in Ch 17.
- The displacement function: Prescott does not name what this visit does to him; but it settles something.

# Chapter 14 — The Commission

**One-line summary:** The application to examine Edward Hargreaves in Canada is refused on the ground that his address is unknown and no mechanism of service exists; the calendar moves against Prescott; the witness door is permanently closed.

---

## POV and Tense
Arthur Prescott — third person limited, past tense.

## Setting / Time
Garside & Prescott, Winckley Square, Preston. May 1927. A Tuesday morning; the letter from London counsel arrives with the court's response.

## Chapter Shape
**Correspondence chapter.** A letter received; its consequences worked through; a telephone call or further letter to London counsel; an immediate recalibration of the case plan. One location; the action concentrated in the morning.

## Ending Mode
**Turn.** The refused commission is the one moment in the book where the calendar moves against Prescott rather than with him. Days are lost to the application; the expected witness avenue is definitively closed. This is the structural setback of Movement II.

---

## Goal, Obstacle, Action Beats

**Prescott's goal:** Receive the court's response on the commission application and determine the consequences for the case.

**Obstacle:** The commission is refused. The witness is untraceable; without a fixed address in Canada, there is no mechanism of service and no commission can be executed. The English court will not issue a commission when it cannot be delivered. The application consumed weeks; the hearing date is now 140 days away; the time spent on the application is gone.

**Beats:**

1. **The letter arrives:** Counsel in London writes: the court has declined to issue the commission to examine Hargreaves. The ground: the applicant has been unable to supply a fixed address in Canada at which the commission could be served; without a traceable address, a commission cannot be executed and the application cannot succeed. The court's decision is not appealable on these facts; a fresh application would require a verified address.

2. **Prescott's reaction (controlled):** He reads the letter twice. He sets it on the desk. He walks to the window. He does not say what he feels. What he thinks: the witness avenue is gone. He knew the odds; he submitted anyway because he was obliged to try. The outcome is what it is.

3. **The calendar cost:** The application was submitted in April; it is now May. Eight weeks lost in the commission thread — weeks that cannot be recovered. Hearing date: 140 days. He has 140 days, not the 172 he had when the application was filed. The lost time is real.

4. **What the closure means for the case:** Without the gardener's evidence, the attestation cannot be examined by any testimony. The carter is dead; the gardener is gone. The codicil's due execution story is unbreakable by witness evidence. Which means: the attestation, considered alone, is not a route. The text must do everything.

5. **The compensating clarity:** There is, Prescott notes, a kind of negative argument available. The witnesses were chosen — the carter who died in September, the gardener who sailed in October — chosen at a moment when no living person could have known they would both be unavailable. Unless the second codicil was prepared AFTER both men were unavailable — after October 1926 — but was deliberately dated to August. The despatch-box stood at the mill for six days in late October. Walter was the only one with access in those six days. The timing of the forgery, including the witness selection, fits exactly the period when both men were newly unavailable. But this is argument, not evidence, and Prescott notes it as such.

6. **A letter to London counsel:** Prescott writes to counsel: the commission has failed; the case must be made on typewriter evidence and text; please confirm we are proceeding on that footing. He also notes the calendar: 140 days; the brief must be complete in eight weeks at the outside.

7. **Close:** The refused commission letter goes into the file. The file grows. 140 days to the hearing. Prescott takes out the next matter to be addressed; the work continues, as it must. The setback is in the file; it is not named as a setback.

---

## Outcome / Turn
The commission is refused; the witness door is closed permanently. Calendar cost: eight weeks. Days remaining: 140. The attestation cannot be attacked by testimony; the text must carry the entire weight of the case. This is the case's crisis point — not a loss, but a constraint that defines everything that follows.

## New Question or Pressure Raised
The text must do it. Can a recital's error — one word wrong in a formal instrument — convict a man? What else does the text say, and what does the rest of the record say about who could have composed it that way?

---

## What Compounds

- **Door (c) — the witnesses:** Closes. The witnesses are permanently beyond examination. Carter dead; gardener untraceable in Canada; commission refused for want of an address. The attestation cannot be challenged or confirmed by any testimony now or at the hearing. This is, from the defence's perspective, an unassailable point — but it is equally unassailable from Prescott's: the silence of the witnesses, once authorship is shown, becomes part of the design.

- **Prior chapters advanced:** Ch 12 — the commission application was submitted in the witnesses chapter; this chapter ends it; the witness thread is exhausted.

- **Days to hearing:** **140 days** — and the calendar has moved against Prescott (from 172 at Ch 12 to 140 now, a loss of 32 days to the commission application rather than the proportionate reduction). The eight weeks lost to the commission are a real cost. This is the one occasion in the book where the calendar moves the wrong way.

---

## Continuity Notes

- Commission to examine Hargreaves in Canada: refused by the court for want of traceable address.
- The refusal is final; no fresh application is possible without a verified address for Hargreaves in Canada.
- Calendar cost: eight weeks consumed by the commission application; 140 days to hearing (down from 172).
- This is the calendar-against-Prescott beat: the one time in the book where the countdown shortens by more than the natural passage of time.
- The witness avenue is closed permanently. This must not be re-opened in later chapters.
- 140 days to hearing: noted explicitly.

# Chapter 16 — The Date

**One-line summary:** Preparing the hearing brief, Prescott re-examines R5 as an exhibit: the firm's November 2 letter gave Walter the first codicil's date in writing — and nothing else; the letter-book carbon corroborates; the asymmetry is now a formal record item.

---

## POV and Tense
Arthur Prescott — third person limited, past tense.

## Setting / Time
Garside & Prescott, Winckley Square, Preston. July 1927. A working week in final preparation; the hearing brief being assembled document by document.

## Chapter Shape
**Single scene — document examination.** Prescott assembles the brief; R5 is examined as an exhibit in the context of the date question. One location; methodical. The chapter is about the architecture of what Walter could and could not have known.

## Ending Mode
**Declarative-close.** The chapter closes on a plain statement of the asymmetry as a record fact: Walter had the date; he did not have the text; R5 explains why. The prose states it cleanly and stops.

---

## Goal, Obstacle, Action Beats

**Prescott's goal:** Establish precisely, as an exhibit, how Walter could have known the correct date of the first codicil to put in the second codicil's recital — and confirm that no route exists by which he could have obtained the correct text.

**Obstacle:** The date looks like it could simply be known by recollection — Walter was present at the September reading. But the precise date ("the fifteenth day of March 1924") in the recital, while it matches R5 exactly, could also have been remembered from hearing Garside read the instrument. The argument from the date alone is not as clean as the argument from the word. Prescott must set up the asymmetry precisely: both halves of it.

**Beats:**

1. **The hearing brief assembled:** Prescott is working through the exhibits in sequence, preparing the brief for counsel. He reaches R5 — the firm's notice letter of 2 November 1926. He examines it as an exhibit, formally.

2. **R5 re-examined:** [R5 referenced by name and key phrase — not quoted in full again; the date ("the 15th March 1924") is extracted as the material element.] Prescott traces the documentary chain: R5 was sent to Thurston & Marsh on 2 November 1926. Walter's solicitors received it; Walter would have seen it. The letter contains the date of the first codicil precisely as it appears in the second codicil's recital: "the fifteenth day of March 1924."

3. **The letter-book carbon as corroboration:** The letter-book carbon of R5 confirms the transmission — dated, addressed, filed. The date was in writing to Thurston & Marsh from 2 November 1926. Before that date — including in the six days the despatch-box stood at the mill — Walter did not have the date in writing. R5 gave it to him.

4. **The timeline of the forgery:** The despatch-box stood at the mill from approximately mid-October 1926 (when Hargreaves sailed to Canada — one of the two newly-unavailable witnesses) to when Walter produced the codicil. R5 was sent on 2 November. The forgery must have been made between 2 November 1926 (when Walter received the date in writing) and the day he produced it to his solicitors. The forger dated the instrument 14 August to predate his access to the box.

5. **The asymmetry stated:** Prescott writes the working note: "The recital of the second codicil is exact as to date ('the fifteenth day of March 1924') and wrong as to the operative words ('and her issue' for 'or her issue'). The date was in Walter Eccleston's hands in writing from 2 November 1926, by transmission of R5. The text of the first codicil was never transmitted in writing from this firm or from any other source, as established by the letter-book record (Ch 6 finding) and the profession canvass (Ch 8 finding). The recital reproduces the date that was available in writing; it does not reproduce the text that was not."

6. **What this proves:** Prescott sets down what this establishes and what it does not. It establishes that the source of the date in the recital was R5 and not the executed text. Combined with the executed text's different word — and Walter's habitual misquotation (documented in R4, Ch 11, and in Ch 13's attendance note) — it establishes that the recital was composed from memory and from R5, not from the executed document. This is not, by itself, conclusive of authorship. But it is conclusive that the recital was not composed by someone who had access to the executed text.

7. **Close:** 90 days to the hearing. Prescott files the working note. The asymmetry is now in the record. The discovery — seeing the variance itself — has not yet been made. He has been working around it for months. He has not yet looked at the two texts side by side.

---

## Outcome / Turn
The date asymmetry is a formal record item: Walter had the date from R5; he did not have the text; the recital exhibits both halves of this. The argument is assembled. The discovery remains to be made.

## New Question or Pressure Raised
The asymmetry is established: date right, text wrong. But Prescott has been assembling this argument about the date without yet making the one comparison that would show the variance directly — R3's recital against R2's text. He has been around the codicils in circles. He has not yet read one against the other.

---

## What Compounds

- **Door (i) — the date asymmetry:** Advances to its penultimate step. The documentary source of the date (R5) is established as a record item; the absence of any text source is confirmed; the working note states the asymmetry's two halves. What remains is the direct comparison of R2 and R3 — which will come in the next chapter.

- **Prior chapters advanced:** Ch 6 — the letter-book finding (no text transmitted) is now cited in the working note; Ch 11 — R4's written misquotation ("and her issue," June 1925) is now part of the asymmetry's logic; Ch 13 — the spoken misquotation reported by Nora further documents the habitual version.

- **Days to hearing:** 90 days. Noted at the close.

---

## Continuity Notes

- R5 is referenced by key phrase and date; it is NOT quoted in full again (it was already quoted in full in Ch 6).
- The working note: "The recital is exact as to date; wrong as to the operative words. The date was transmitted in writing; the text was not."
- The date R5 was sent: 2 November 1926. Walter had the date from that point. He did not have the date before that point.
- The forgery was made between 2 November 1926 (when R5 gave Walter the date) and the day he produced the codicil to his solicitors. The instrument was backdated to 14 August.
- 90 days to hearing.
- Prescott has NOT yet placed R2 and R3 side by side and compared the operative words. This comparison is the discovery in Ch 17. The drafter must ensure this chapter does not pre-empt the discovery.

# Chapter 17 — The Ninth Word

**One-line summary:** Late and alone, doing a final file-discipline check before the brief goes to London, Prescott reads the propounded second codicil against the strong-room original of the first — and sees, in the ninth word of the recital, the difference between "and" and "or."

---

## POV and Tense
Arthur Prescott — third person limited, past tense.

## Setting / Time
Garside & Prescott, Winckley Square, Preston. A July evening, perhaps 9 or 10 p.m. The office empty except for Prescott; the strong-room open; both documents on the table.

## Chapter Shape
**Bottle — interiority-light, document-anchored.** One location; one act; near real-time. The chapter is almost entirely Prescott reading two documents. What happens is small and enormous.

## Ending Mode
**Turn.** The discovery is the structural pivot of the entire novel. Everything that follows is consequence; everything before it was preparation. The chapter ends with the variance seen and R4 pulled from the file — the three pieces in Prescott's hands, and nowhere left to go but forward.

---

## Goal, Obstacle, Action Beats

**Prescott's goal:** Complete the final file-discipline check before dispatching the brief to London counsel — compare the propounded copy of the second codicil against the firm's own records to confirm that every citation in the brief is exact.

**Obstacle:** He is tired; the office is late; the check is routine. He does not know what he is about to find. The obstacle is the ordinariness of the act: this is a clerk's check, not a detective's eureka moment.

**Beats:**

1. **The setting:** Late evening; the office empty. Mr. Booth has gone home. The brief for London is nearly complete. Prescott, before he sends it, does what Garside always did and what he has done himself since: he reads everything against the original, once, from the start.

2. **The strong-room:** He goes down to the strong-room and retrieves the Eccleston deed-box. He opens it and takes out the first codicil — the executed original, in the strong-room since March 1924. He brings it upstairs.

3. **The propounded copy:** He has the second codicil — the propounded instrument produced by Thurston & Marsh — from the action files. He places both documents on the desk.

4. **The comparison begins:** He reads the second codicil's recital to compare it with the first codicil's text. He is checking for citation accuracy in the brief. He reads the recital: "WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely—"

5. **The first codicil:** He reads the first codicil's operative clause: "...unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely..."

6. **The ninth word:** He stops. He goes back to the recital. He counts: "Margaret Fairhurst" — one, two — "and" — the ninth word. He looks at the first codicil: "or." He looks again at the recital: "and." He sits still for a moment. The ninth word of the recital is wrong.

7. **What Prescott understands:** He does not say it aloud; there is no one to say it to. He understands what the difference means, and what it proves, and what it does not prove, in the space of perhaps twenty seconds. The recital quotes the first codicil — any careful codicil quotes the instrument it revokes — and it quotes it wrong. Not on the date (the date is exact). On the operative word. The one word that would survive in a man's memory incorrectly if he had only ever heard the clause described, not read it. The one word that Walter Eccleston has been getting wrong since 1924.

8. **R4 pulled from the file:** Prescott goes to the exhibit file and finds R4 — Walter's bank letter of 11 June 1925 (filed in Ch 11 as a financial exhibit). He reads it: "in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst and her issue." He notes: fourteen months before the second codicil's date, in Walter's own hand, the same wrong word. The document is not new; it has been in the file for months. He is reading it as if for the first time.

9. **The proof chain assembled (privately):** The recital says "and." The executed text says "or." Walter's bank letter — in his hand, fourteen months before the codicil's date — says "and." No copy of the first codicil ever left the firm; the text was never transmitted to anyone. Walter was present at the September reading but never had the text before his eyes. Walter has said "and" since Josiah told him in March 1924, in Josiah's own spoken words. The recital was not taken from the document; it was taken from a memory that was wrong in exactly the way Walter's memory was wrong, on exactly the word that a spoken account would blur.

10. **Not triumph:** Prescott puts both documents down and the bank letter with them. He does not feel triumph. He feels the weight of what the record has produced — slowly, exactly, without drama. He notes the time. He notes the date. He writes a single sentence in the working file: "The recital of the second codicil cites the first codicil as giving the residue 'unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely.' The executed instrument (R2) says 'or her issue.' The variance is between R2 and R3's recital."

11. **Close:** He replaces both documents. He sits at the desk for a while; the office around him; the strong-room register, Garside's hand, on the shelf below. Then he takes out a fresh sheet of paper and begins to write the addition to the brief.

---

## Outcome / Turn
The variance is found. The ninth word of the recital says "and" where the executed first codicil says "or." R4 says "and" in Walter's hand, fourteen months earlier. The discovery is not a guess; it is a file check. Nothing new has entered the record; the three pieces (R2, R3, R4) were all already there.

## New Question or Pressure Raised
The variance is found. Now it must be proved — not just that the recital is wrong, but that Walter is the only candidate who could have made it wrong in exactly this way, with the date exactly right. The brief must be rewritten to lead with the variance. 88 days.

---

## What Compounds

- **Door (i) — the date asymmetry:** Closes. The direct comparison of R2 and R3 reveals the variance; R4 (from Ch 11) ties the misquotation to Walter's habitual version. The asymmetry is now complete: the date (right, from R5) and the word (wrong, from Walter's memory). Walter is the only candidate who satisfies both conditions.

- **Prior chapters advanced:** Ch 1 — R2 was introduced entire in the first chapter; Ch 2 — R3 was introduced entire in the second chapter; Ch 11 — R4 entered the file as a financial exhibit; the discovery is a re-reading of what all three chapters have already put before the reader.

- **Days to hearing:** 88 days. The brief must be complete. The discovery has come nearly too late.

---

## Continuity Notes

- [R2 quoted again in key operative clause — drafter must call `read_record` before quoting]: "...unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston **or her issue** absolutely..."
- [R3 recital quoted again — drafter must call `read_record` before quoting]: "...I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst **and her issue** absolutely..."
- [R4 quoted in key phrase — drafter must call `read_record`]: "in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst **and her issue**..."
- The variance: ninth word of the recital; "and" in R3; "or" in R2.
- R4 was entered as a financial exhibit in Ch 11; its significance is only now perceived. It is not new to the file; it is new to Prescott's understanding of the file.
- The discovery is file discipline, not intuition. Prescott is checking citations in the brief. He is not inspired; he is thorough.
- The chapter ends with Prescott writing the brief addition, not with any dramatised realisation. The weight is in the plain sentence; the gloss must be absent.
- 88 days to hearing.
- Nothing material enters this chapter that has not been on the page before. R2 (Ch 1), R3 (Ch 2), R4 (Ch 11) are all already in the reader's record.
- Do NOT have Prescott name his grief, his admiration for Garside, or any feeling. The only permitted emotion is the notation: "He sits at the desk for a while." Then he works.

# Chapter 6 — The Letter-Book

**One-line summary:** Prescott works through the firm's complete outgoing correspondence on the Eccleston estate and confirms that no request for the first codicil's text — or for so much as its date — was ever received from anyone before R5.

---

## POV and Tense
Arthur Prescott — third person limited, past tense.

## Setting / Time
Garside & Prescott, Winckley Square, Preston. January 1927. A working morning; the letter-book open on the desk; the Eccleston correspondence file assembled beside it.

## Chapter Shape
**Single scene — document examination.** Prescott reviews the firm's outgoing letter-book and the corresponding incoming letters for the Eccleston matter, start to finish. One location; methodical.

## Ending Mode
**Resolved-beat.** The chapter closes with a fact fixed: no one ever asked for the text of the first codicil, or for its date, through any channel. Only R5 went out — giving the date, not the text. This is established as a record item; it cannot be revisited.

---

## Goal, Obstacle, Action Beats

**Prescott's goal:** Establish whether anyone — Thurston & Marsh, Walter, any third party — ever obtained the text of the first codicil or its date from Garside & Prescott by any channel, before or after Josiah's death.

**Obstacle:** The answer, if it is "no," proves only a negative. A negative is not nothing — but it is the beginning of an argument about how the second codicil's recital was composed, not the end of it.

**Beats:**

1. **Opening:** Prescott begins with the letter-book for 1924, the year the first codicil was made. He knows what he is looking for: any outgoing letter that quotes, reproduces, or paraphrases the text of the first codicil; any acknowledgment of an incoming request for the same. He works forward.

2. **The 1924 correspondence:** The execution of the first codicil: Garside's covering letter to Josiah enclosing the instrument for execution; a brief acknowledgment from Josiah; the carbon of the letter to Edgar Fairhurst notifying him of the new provision. None of these quote the operative clause; none go to Walter or Thurston & Marsh. The letter to Edgar says only that Mr. Eccleston has made "a testamentary provision" for Mrs. Fairhurst and her family and that the firm holds the instrument.

3. **1925 and 1926 correspondence:** The mortgage renewal (March 1925); Josiah's routine correspondence; a brief exchange about the Hall's insurance. Nothing from or to Thurston & Marsh about the first codicil's text. Nothing from Walter. Nothing from anyone.

4. **R5 examined in full (first full appearance):** In November 1926, the firm's notice letter to Thurston & Marsh. [R5 quoted in full as a set-off passage.] It gives the date of the first codicil — "a codicil thereto dated the 15th March 1924" — but nothing of the text. It says the codicil "materially affects the disposition of the residue" and nothing further. This is the only occasion the first codicil's date was transmitted by the firm to any external party. Prescott reads it again and notes: the letter gives the date; it gives nothing else. Thurston & Marsh, and through them Walter, had the date in writing from 2 November 1926. They had nothing of the text.

5. **The letter-book carbon:** The letter-book entry for R5 — the carbon of the outgoing letter — sits in the firm's own record. It is its own corroborating exhibit: dated, addressed, the firm's reference. It confirms the transmission of the date and the absence of any text.

6. **The conclusion stated in the working note:** Prescott writes a note for the file: "No request for the text of the 1924 codicil, or its full terms, was ever received from Thurston & Marsh or from Mr. Walter Eccleston or from any other party. R5 (November 1926) transmitted the date of the instrument only." He dates it. The working note becomes a file item; it will be in the brief to counsel.

7. **Prescott's private observation:** Looking at the letter-book entries, he sees again the precision of Garside's practice — every outgoing letter complete, every enclosure noted, every reference carried. The letter-book is as exact as the register. For a forger who never asked for the text, there is nothing here that would have helped him get it right.

---

## Outcome / Turn
Door (e) is closed. No one asked for the first codicil's text. Only the date was transmitted — from R5, on 2 November 1926, to Thurston & Marsh. Any recital of the first codicil's terms in any document produced after that date must have its source somewhere other than the firm.

## New Question or Pressure Raised
If the text of the first codicil never left the firm, how did the second codicil's recital know the date so precisely — and get the text wrong? Where did the date come from (answer: R5), and where did the text come from (not the document — but from somewhere)?

---

## What Compounds

- **Door (e) — the firm:** Closes. The letter-book confirms no request for the codicil's text reached the firm from anyone. The only transmission was R5 (the date alone) on 2 November 1926. The text was never given out.

- **Prior chapters advanced:** Ch 2 — R5 was sent; this chapter examines the letter-book carbon that confirms it; the absence of any prior request is now a file item. Ch 5 — Garside's precision in the register is mirrored in the letter-book; the firmness of both records is confirmed.

- **Days to hearing:** 265 days. Stated mid-chapter, not at the close.

---

## Continuity Notes

- **R5 quoted in full** (first and only full appearance; after this point, references by name or key phrase only — never quoted in full again).
- The letter-book carbon of R5 is now explicitly in the Prescott file as a corroborating exhibit.
- No request for the text of the first codicil was ever received by the firm from anyone.
- R5 gave Walter (through Thurston & Marsh) the date of the first codicil: "the 15th March 1924." It gave nothing of the text.
- This negative fact is established as a record item; it cannot be revisited.
- Garside displacement: the precision of the letter-book as a further instance of Garside's habit.
- The letter to Edgar Fairhurst from March 1924 said only that a "testamentary provision" had been made — it did not quote the operative clause.

# Threads — The Probate of Eccleston

Six braided threads run through the twenty chapters. The spine — *can Prescott prove the second
codicil is a forgery?* — is not listed here; it is the scaffold the threads hang on. Each thread
below is a question that can be named, tracked across multiple chapters, and that places pressure
on the spine from a distinct angle.

---

## Thread 1: The Firm's Own Risk

- **Question:** Can Garside & Prescott — a small two-man firm now reduced to one — afford,
  financially and institutionally, to carry this action to the end?

- **Enters:** Ch 2 ("The Second Codicil") — when Prescott commits to caveating and carrying the
  action at the firm's own risk; costs are recoverable only if the action succeeds, and there is
  no client with funds.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 5 — Garside's death makes Prescott the sole partner; the full financial exposure is now
    his alone.
  - Chs 6–10 — every chapter of the record-building movement incurs unbilled cost; each door
    closed is also money spent.
  - Ch 11 — Walter's financial desperation (documented through R4 and the sale contract) mirrors
    the firm's own position from the other side.
  - Ch 14 — the refused commission is the one moment the calendar moves *against* Prescott; the
    days lost are also costs sunk and irrecoverable.
  - Ch 18 — the brief dispatched to London; all costs now fully committed before the outcome is
    known.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 20 ("The Estate") — costs are recovered; the firm is solvent; it will
  continue. The recovery does not make it wealthy; it makes it able to go on.

- **What it's about underneath:** Without this thread, the investigation is a professional
  obligation. With it, every stage of the record-building is also a wager — the firm is
  gambling itself on the file being sufficient. This is why the compounding mechanism matters
  beyond plot: each door closed is a door the firm needs closed to survive. The stakes are
  not only two children's futures; they are Garside's life's work — the office on Winckley
  Square, Mr. Booth at his desk, the register on the shelf. The thread answers the question
  the brief poses about Prescott's character: he is not a man who takes risks lightly, and
  he is taking this one anyway, because the file tells him what the file tells him.

---

## Thread 2: Garside in the File

- **Question:** Will Prescott find his way through grief for Garside — and will Garside's
  exactitude, built into forty years of file discipline, prove sufficient to win the case
  Garside never lived to finish?

- **Enters:** Ch 5 ("The Hinge") — Garside dies at his desk; the file, the register, the action,
  and the grief all pass to Prescott at once. The strong-room register is read in Garside's hand;
  the September entry is more precise than the occasion required; Prescott does not name what he
  feels. The clock starts: 290 days.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 7 — the File chapter: the forty-year record built with more care than the occasion required;
    the first full displacement beat; Prescott finds Garside in procedure.
  - Ch 9 — at Vale Mill: the estate's prior documents (Garside's work) are visible in the mill
    records Prescott examines.
  - Ch 15 — the Hall depositions are built on instruments Garside drew and custodied; the record
    that constrains the servants' testimony was Garside's record.
  - Ch 17 — the discovery turns on the strong-room register entry in Garside's hand; the precise
    notation of the September reading — instrument read entire, date included, who was present —
    is the thing that makes the chain complete.
  - Ch 18 — the brief is assembled from what Garside built; Prescott is writing a case Garside
    prepared for without knowing it.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 20 ("The Estate") — Prescott returns the file to the strong-room and opens
  the register to note the matter's completion. He reads back up the page: the September 1926
  entry in Garside's hand. *"More precise than the occasion required. He made the record for
  exactly this. He could not have known it; he made it anyway, because that was his habit."* The
  old man is everywhere in the record, and the record is what won.

- **What it's about underneath:** This is the book's internal thread — the only one that is a
  character question rather than a plot question. Prescott cannot grieve directly; the register
  of this man and this book does not permit it. What the thread asks is whether the method
  Garside taught — the unremarkable professional habit of building the file better than the
  occasion required — will prove equal to the case it never anticipated. The answer is yes, and
  that yes is grief converted to procedure and back again. The discovery in Ch 17 is not a
  detective's triumph; it is a clerk's reflex, a check Garside would have run, done late at night
  because that is what Garside always did. The resolution is not catharsis; it is the plain
  sentence that carries disproportionate weight because everything before it has been controlled.

---

## Thread 3: The Children

- **Question:** Will Nora and George Fairhurst remain *people* — with their own grief, their own
  weight, their own futures — rather than an abstract cause Prescott is fighting on behalf of?

- **Enters:** Ch 4 ("Bank Parade") — the first visit; Edgar Fairhurst, Nora (nineteen), and George
  (sixteen) as people not yet reduced to legal positions; the stake made human.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 13 ("The Fairhursts") — the second Bank Parade visit; Nora reports that Walter told the
    children what their mother was to have had, using the wrong word, with misplaced generosity.
    The third fair-play misquotation lands here, through Nora's voice — period-true channel,
    a witness in the room, not a document.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 19/20 — the estate passes; the last Bank Parade visit; Nora is "quieter
  than Prescott expected — not exultant, not aggrieved, the way people are when something
  long-awaited arrives and proves to be not quite what was imagined." George asks what happens
  to the mill. They receive what the law gives them.

- **What it's about underneath:** The brief flags this concern explicitly: "the children must
  remain people rather than a cause." Without this thread the book is pure procedure; two
  documents, two calendars, nine doors. With it, the machine is also the story of what two
  dead people (Josiah, Margaret) set in motion for two living ones. The thread is deliberately
  thin — only three chapters — because that is the correct weight: enough to keep the stake
  human, not so much that the children become protagonists in a book that belongs to Prescott.
  Nora's understatement at the last Bank Parade visit is the cost the book refuses to conceal.

---

## Thread 4: Walter's Logic

- **Question:** Is Walter Eccleston a villain — or a man who convinced himself, by compounding
  logic over three years, that he was correcting a late injustice rather than committing a felony?

- **Enters:** Ch 2 ("The Second Codicil") — Walter calls at the office with his cover story and his
  first misquotation; he is plausible; his account of Josiah is not performed; his grief for his
  uncle reads as genuine. The reader (but not yet Prescott) has already seen "or her issue" in Ch 1.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 3 — the forty-year habit of the firm, and Josiah's trust in it, establishes the context of
    Walter's expectation — fifteen years managing the mill, Josiah's confidence in him, the
    codicil as an aberration Walter expected Josiah to correct.
  - Ch 9 — the mill visit: working short time, forty men where it once ran eighty; Walter's men
    like him; the mill is his life's work. The book lets him be competent.
  - Ch 11 — R4 as financial exhibit: Walter's letter to his bank in June 1925, borrowing against
    an expectancy he genuinely believed he had, before he knew Josiah would die without correcting
    the codicil. The compounding logic of the debt is on the page.
  - Ch 13 — Walter, kindly, to Nora and George: telling the children what their mother was to have
    had. He gets the word wrong, mid-generosity. The gesture is not performed cruelty; it is
    the cruelty of a man who does not know he is wrong.
  - Ch 16 — the date Walter had from R5 (in writing), and the text he never had from anyone.
    The asymmetry of his knowledge is established; the trap is set.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 19 ("Solemn Form") — Walter is handed the strong-room original of the first
  codicil and reads the word *or* for the first time in his life. He learns that the thing he
  forged around was a word he had never seen. Prescott's register at that moment is procedural
  and almost apologetic. Walter's counsel takes instructions; the action is abandoned. The
  criminal consequence follows. He was not a monster. He was a man who persuaded himself he was
  correcting an error. Both propositions remain true. He still goes down.

- **What it's about underneath:** The book requires the reader to hold two things at once: that
  Walter's logic is internally coherent (fifteen years, an expectancy, Josiah's own assurance,
  a debt that compounded while he waited), and that coherent logic does not make the action
  right. The thread works by building Walter slowly — plausible in Ch 2, humanised in Ch 9,
  sympathetic in his financial desperation in Ch 11, even generous in Ch 13 — and then allowing
  the exposure in Ch 19 to land on a man the reader has had reason to understand, if not excuse.
  The hurt of the exposure is calibrated by how much the thread has done. Walter is
  undone not by a trap but by a word he was never in a room with.

---

## Thread 5: The Witness Trap

- **Question:** Does the fact that neither attesting witness to the second codicil can ever
  testify — one dead, one untraceable in Canada — doom Prescott's case?

- **Enters:** Ch 2 ("The Second Codicil") — both witnesses identified as beyond examination; the
  defense's case on due execution looks unbreakable by testimony; Prescott has no witness to
  cross-examine.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 12 ("The Witnesses") — the carter's death confirmed; his genuine signatures collected;
    the commission application submitted for the gardener in Canada.
  - Ch 14 ("The Commission") — the commission is refused for want of a traceable address; the
    calendar moves *against* Prescott; the case cannot be won on testimony; the witnesses will
    never speak.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 17 and Ch 19 — *Deliberately*: the witnesses never testify, and this
  becomes part of the design rather than a defeat. Walter chose them because neither could be
  asked; the very precision of the choice (two men beyond reach, selected from genuine witnesses
  on earlier estate papers) is itself mappable to a forger who knew the estate's history. The
  text carries the whole weight, without a single living witness to due execution, and carries it.

- **What it's about underneath:** This thread closes off the "obvious" path and forces the case
  onto the text alone. The conventional resolution — break the attestation through witness
  testimony — is denied permanently in Ch 14, and the book neither rescues itself through
  forensics (the handwriting experts split) nor contrives a late witness. What remains is the
  record: exact, complete, and sufficient without human testimony. This is the themes chapter
  ("the record against memory") enacted as a structural thread: the witnesses never speak
  because they cannot, and the record — which cannot be made to forget — does not need them.
  The refusal of the witness-testimony path is the book's most deliberate formal commitment.

---

## Thread 6: The One-Word Variance

- **Question:** Is the proof of the forgery hiding in plain sight — in the difference between
  "or her issue" and "and her issue" — visible to any reader of the documents who looks carefully
  *before Prescott sees it*?

- **Enters:** Ch 1 ("The Strong-Room") — R2 quoted in full: *"unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of
  Bank Parade Preston **or** her issue absolutely."* The word is on the page. The reader sees it
  first. No remark is made.

- **Advanced in:**
  - Ch 2 — R3 quoted in full; its recital reads *"unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst **and** her
    issue absolutely."* Both forms are now on the page, in consecutive chapters; the narration is
    silent. Walter says "and her issue" to Prescott, mid-sentence, unremarked.
  - Ch 11 — R4 enters as a financial exhibit; Walter's bank letter of June 1925: *"in favour of my
    late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst **and** her issue."* In his hand, dated, in the file. No annotation
    from the narration.
  - Ch 13 — Nora reports Walter's words to the children: "and her issue," from Walter's mouth to
    the people it most concerned, delivered with kindness. Third plant; still unremarked.

- **Resolves in:** Ch 17 ("The Ninth Word") — Prescott sees it; the proof is assembled; the brief
  is rewritten. Whether the reader has already seen it is the one question the book cannot answer
  for them — and deliberately does not try.

- **What it's about underneath:** This is the reader's thread — the one where the book trusts
  the reader to be a detective. The three plants are placed at intervals, never in consecutive
  chapters, never signalled, and the narration never underlines the variance. Prescott does not
  discover something the book has hidden; he discovers something the book displayed. The fair-play
  contract means the discovery chapter is either a confirmation or a revelation, depending solely
  on whether the reader was paying attention. The book leaves that open *deliberately*, not as a
  failure to resolve but as the structural enactment of its own argument: the record is exact;
  perception is not. The one licensed irresolution of the whole novel (beyond the handwriting
  experts' split) is whether the reader, at Ch 1, saw "or."

---

## Notes on resolution pattern

- **Threads 1, 2, 3, 4** all resolve in the final movement (Chs 17–20), as intended by the brief's
  "settling of every account."
- **Thread 5** resolves as a deliberate *refusal* — the witnesses never testify, and this is
  formally correct, not a drafting failure. The refused commission in Ch 14 is the permanent close
  of the testimony path; the text carries everything.
- **Thread 6** resolves at Ch 17 for Prescott; whether it has already resolved for the reader is
  the one question the book cannot answer — and the one question it is not required to answer. This
  is the book's single operative irresolution, complementing (but distinct from) the handwriting
  experts' split, which the brief designates as the "one licensed irresolution."
- **Thread 2** is the book's sole fully internal thread (a character question, not a plot question).

The deed box was already on the table.

Prescott had come in through Winckley Square at half past nine to find it sitting in the centre of the examining table, the Eccleston label in Garside's hand, the lock unchecked. He set down his briefcase and stood for a moment looking at it. The fire had been made up; Mr. Booth had taken his coat. Nothing in the room required comment.

Garside had heard the news the previous evening — Josiah Eccleston, eighty-one years old, cotton spinner and magistrate of this county, dead at Eccleston Hall on the morning of the seventeenth. Every instrument for thirty years had come through this office. There were not many clients of thirty years' standing, and this was not a morning to count what remained of them.

He opened the lid.

The instruments lay in order: the will first, in its deed paper, tied with green tape; the first codicil behind it, similarly dressed; the firm's letter-book carbon of the acknowledgement after execution. Beneath all of it lay the attendance notes, the correspondence, the working file of a man's dispositions across seven years. The custody had been Garside's from the beginning. In the strong-room register the entries ran in Garside's careful hand from 1919: the will deposited, the will verified, the codicil added in March of twenty-four. The last entry was September of this year, the date in the margin column, the purpose set down in the body of the entry in a hand that had by then begun to run thin at the descenders. Garside had noted the occasion fully — the instrument fetched, the family assembled at the Hall, the names of those present recorded in the margin alongside the date.

Prescott's own name was among them.

He had been in this room long enough to know that a file built with more care than occasion required was not an accident. Garside built files the way he argued cases: on the assumption that everything might someday need to be produced. Two decades had made the assumption Prescott's own. He lifted the will from its wrapper, untied the tape, and smoothed the document flat.

The date was the third day of June, nineteen hundred and nineteen.

"We should read it properly," Garside said from the door.

Prescott did not look up. "Yes," he said. "We should."

# Chapter 1 — The Strong-Room

The deed box was on the table when Prescott arrived: black painted steel, "ECCLESTON" lettered in white on the lid, the label in Garside's copper-plate facing up across the room. Garside was at the far end of the table with his hat still on, which meant he had not been in from the strong-room long.

"Dead yesterday evening," Garside said. "The Hall sent a telegram."

Josiah Eccleston had been a client of the firm since before Prescott came into articles. Cotton spinner, magistrate, owner of the Hall at Ribchester and the Vale Mill above the village — a man whose every instrument from will to conveyance had come through this office in the thirty years since Garside first took his instructions. Prescott had known him first as a name in the ledger, and later, from the will itself onwards, as a man who shook hands as though a contract were meant by it. He had been eighty-one years old. He had died, as far as anyone knew without disorder, on a Tuesday evening in October, at the Hall.

The coal fire was going. Outside on the square the October light was doing what it did.

Garside set his hat down and opened the deed box.

The will was first: folded twice on cream paper, "WILL — J. ECCLESTON — 3 JUNE 1919" on the outside. Garside opened it, turned to the fourth clause, and read:

> I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my nephew Walter Eccleston of Vale Mill House Ribchester absolutely and I appoint the said Walter Eccleston sole executor of this my will.

Prescott noted the date and the name and set his pen down.

Garside folded the will and reached into the box. The codicil was underneath: same cream paper, "CODICIL — J. ECCLESTON — 15 MARCH 1924" on the outside fold, shorter by half. He opened it.

"After the reconciliation," he said, more to himself than to Prescott. He read:

> I REVOKE clause 4 of my said will and IN PLACE THEREOF I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely AND IN ALL OTHER RESPECTS I confirm my said will.

The coal shifted behind the grate. Prescott wrote down the date — fifteen March nineteen-twenty-four — and the name and address, and waited.

"Clause four revoked entire," Garside said. "Gift and executorship both — he intended a complete revision. There is, at present, no executor." He set the codicil alongside the will. "Section thirty-three of the Wills Act does nothing for a niece against lapse. She is collateral, not a descendant. He used the substitutional form accordingly."

Margaret Fairhurst. Prescott had known her name from the codicil's making two years before, and had noted the memorandum in the file when she died: May 1925, a year and a half before Josiah. Her issue were her two children — Nora, nineteen, and George, sixteen — living with their father at the Bank Parade address named in the instrument. Edgar Fairhurst. A schoolmaster.

"Both children are minors," Prescott said. "Majority is twenty-one."

"Letters of administration with the will annexed," Garside said. "To the father as guardian, if the instruments stand."

Walter Eccleston had managed the mill for fifteen years on the expectation of this estate. Prescott knew the mill was mortgaged — the kind of information that accumulated in a solicitor's knowledge without being entered in any single place. What Walter would make of the codicil's terms was a question for the next letter.

He took up the strong-room register from beside the box.

The register was a cloth-bound ledger: date column on the left, document described in the centre, clerk's signature at the right margin. Garside had maintained it in his own hand since 1906; Prescott had added entries as occasion required, in his own narrower hand, the two scripts sharing the same columns for two decades. He opened to the current year and ran down the September entries.

September the nineteenth. The entry was Garside's:

*First codicil, J. Eccleston — fetched from strong-room. Reading at Eccleston Hall at testator's request. Present: H.G., A.P., W. Eccleston, two members of the household. Instrument read entire. Returned same day. H.G.*

Prescott had been at that reading. He had carried the deed-box into the drawing room at the Hall and stood there while Garside read the codicil from first word to last — date and all — to Josiah, who was in his chair and had been failing since August. Walter had been there, and the two women from the household, and Josiah's man beside the door. Josiah had wanted no surprises. The register confirmed it in Garside's hand: instrument read entire, returned same day.

Walter Eccleston had stood beside the fireplace with his arms at his sides, listening.

Prescott turned to the working correspondence at the back of the file. The papers from the previous week were loosely arranged: the telegram from the Hall, a draft letter of condolence, and behind them his own attendance note from the despatch-box inventory.

He had made the note at the Hall table on the afternoon of the inventory, while Walter stood by. The box had been opened on the dining-room table and Prescott had listed each item as it was removed: three insurance policies, title deeds to the Hall, unsigned drafts of two rental agreements, a letter from the bank dated 1923, three letters tied in blue ribbon, an unsigned copy of the will.

No codicil.

He read through the list a second time and found the same. He clipped the note to the front of the file.

Garside restored the will and the codicil to the deed box and carried it back to the strong-room himself — he always carried the Eccleston box himself — and Prescott heard the iron door of the vault close below, and the latch engage. A minute later Garside came back up without the box and stood in the doorway.

"Two instruments," Prescott said. "The will and the first codicil. The estate belongs to the Fairhurst children if the instruments stand. There is no executor, and there was no second codicil in the despatch-box." He looked at his notes. "I should write to Thurston and Marsh today, about proving the will in proper form. And we must write to Bank Parade."

"Yes," Garside said. He sat down and took up his pen.

The file was in order: the will of the third of June nineteen-nineteen, the codicil of the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four, the strong-room register exact about both. What Walter Eccleston would make of those terms was a question the record had not yet been required to answer.

input.content:
# Chapter 2 — The Second Codicil

Prescott was halfway through the Bank Parade letter when Mr. Booth appeared in the doorway with the morning post.

The Thurston & Marsh envelope was on top. It was thicker than a simple acknowledgment — thick enough for an enclosure.

The covering note was on their good paper. Their client, it advised, had lately found among his late uncle's personal papers a codicil to the will, dated the fourteenth day of August nineteen-twenty-six, which he believed had been made privately by the testator in the final months of his life. A copy was enclosed. In these circumstances, they trusted that the will might now be proved in common form in the ordinary way; they would be glad to hear how their client might proceed.

Garside read it at his desk, held out his hand for the enclosure, read that too, and set it face-down on the blotter.

"The letter-book," he said.

Prescott took the letter-book from the cupboard. The carbon of the firm's notice letter was two pages in — dated the second of November, the typing clean.

> Dear Sirs, — We act in the estate of the late Mr. Josiah Eccleston of Eccleston Hall. We hold his will dated the 3rd June 1919 and a codicil thereto dated the 15th March 1924 which materially affects the disposition of the residue. We shall be glad to receive your client's proposals for proving the will in proper form. — Yours faithfully, GARSIDE & PRESCOTT

He closed the letter-book and set it on the table.

Garside turned the enclosure over and read it aloud:

> WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.

Outside the window Winckley Square lay quiet in the November light.

"Dated the fourteenth of August," Prescott said.

"Yes."

The despatch-box had been inventoried in the last week of October, three weeks after the funeral, with Prescott recording each item as it came out and Walter present beside the table. No codicil among them — his attendance note was in the file. After the inventory, the box had stood at the mill, in Walter's keeping, for six days. The codicil had been produced after the box was returned to the Hall.

"The firm received no instruction to draw this," Prescott said. "No request for the text of the first codicil. No inquiry as to its terms."

"We gave them the date in the notice." Garside's forefinger rested on the letter-book. "I thought it proper. That is all we sent."

Prescott took the copy to the window. The paper was good foolscap, typed on a machine he could not immediately place as belonging to the firm or to any office associated with it. The signature — *Josiah Eccleston*, in dark ink — was in a formed hand of the right general character; it offered nothing that announced itself as certainly genuine or certainly not. Below the signature, an attestation clause: *Thomas Birch*, carrier, of a Ribchester address; *Frederick Hallett*, gardener, of a lane near Salesbury.

"Neither of them at their given addresses, I should think," he said.

"That remains to be determined." Garside was reaching for his overcoat; he had a meeting elsewhere. "Write to Bank Parade this afternoon. Mr. Fairhurst must enter a caveat before any other step is taken, and he must do it promptly. The instrument has two witnesses and a date and a signature that will not be settled quickly." He had his hat. "Nothing to Thurston and Marsh beyond acknowledgment. Nothing at all."

---

Walter Eccleston called at the office that same afternoon.

No appointment had been made. Mr. Booth brought his card in without comment, and Prescott arrived in the front room a moment later to find Walter already settled in the chair opposite Garside's desk, coat and hat set aside, with the ease of a man who had spent twenty years at home in other people's offices. He greeted Garside and Prescott both. He said he had come himself because it seemed the right thing to do, given the long connection.

He was fifty or thereabouts — broad in the shoulder, a dark wool coat, the considered quiet that came from managing men through a long stretch of difficult years. He had known Josiah Eccleston all his working life and had known this firm almost as long. He was polite, and he was thoroughly certain about all of it.

His account was orderly. He had gone through his uncle's insurance papers in the despatch-box in the days following the inventory. He was, he said, very conscious of having been present at that inventory and of the codicil not being there then; his best understanding was that Josiah must have kept it separately and it had simply been overlooked, or added to the box on a later occasion. Josiah had been up at the mill three or four times in the spring, before the illness; the mill office had a typewriter, and it would have been nothing for him to sit down and draft something out. He had always transacted his correspondence at the mill rather than at the Hall. It was entirely in his character.

"He always said the arrangement for Margaret and her issue wouldn't stand as he'd left it," Walter said, in a tone that was not argumentative, only explanatory. "That he'd made it in a soft mood and always meant to put it right. He said so more than once, and to more than one person." He looked briefly at his hands. "I would very much rather there were no solemn-form action about this. These are Margaret's children. I have no wish to be in dispute with Margaret's children."

Garside said that the firm must advise its clients and take instructions in the ordinary way, and that nothing further could be said at this stage. Walter accepted this with a brief nod — the nod of a man accustomed to solicitors' answers. He stood, and shook Garside's hand, and then Prescott's, and left without further remark.

Prescott wrote the attendance note in full: Walter's account of finding the codicil, his description of Josiah's correspondence habits at the mill, the timing of the despatch-box as Walter understood it, his stated wish to avoid proceedings. All of it dated and initialled and clipped to the file.

Then he went back to the letter-book and read the November second carbon a second time. The firm's notice letter had given Walter's solicitors the date of the first codicil in writing: the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four. Nothing beyond it. No text; no terms; no word of the instrument except that it bore that date and materially affected the residue. The letter-book confirmed it: that was all that had gone out.

---

Edgar Fairhurst entered the caveat at the Probate Registry on the eighth of November. The notice arrived at Winckley Square three days later — a printed card, the date stamped in violet ink — and Prescott noted it in the file and clipped it to the caveat cover.

The file now held the will, the first codicil, the despatch-box inventory attendance note, the firm's notice letter carbon, Walter's attendance note, and the copy of the second codicil. A second codicil the firm had never been asked to draw, in an estate it had administered for thirty years without a privately-made instrument of any kind.

He set the file on Mr. Booth's tray. Outside Winckley Square the light was already gone.

# Chapter 3 — The Habit

The Eccleston index ran to three pages.

Prescott spread them flat on the table beside the window. Pale November light lay on the paper from the square. The list was in Garside's hand from the first entry to the last: a matter number at the left margin, a brief description in the centre column, a date at the right. It had begun in 1884. He set his pen down and read from the beginning.

The first entry: *Eccleston, J. — conv. of mill premises, Ribchester, March 1884.* Below it, in close sequence, a second conveyance, then a deed of covenant over the mill machinery, then a first will — made in 1891, superseded. Garside's hand had been somewhat looser in those early years; by 1900 the columns were fully regular and the descriptions exact. The entries continued without break or interruption for forty years. They ended with a codicil executed in March 1924.

Prescott pulled the older cabinets first.

The conveyance of 1884 was in its original envelope, folded square, on rag paper without tear or stain. A young man buying his first mill premises had come to a solicitor recently qualified, and both men had since become, in their respective trades, what they were. The purchase of Eccleston Hall in 1898 occupied two drawers of deeds and a correspondence packet. The mortgage of 1921 — Blackburn bank — carried a note in Garside's hand on the inside cover of the instrument: *Prepared on client's instructions, 17 March 1921. Terms agreed with lender.* The precision was characteristic.

Below the mortgage, the Hall title deeds ran to three separate bundles, each tied and labelled, all correctly lodged.

He found the earlier wills in the bottom drawer. Two, both superseded: 1891 and 1904. Each had been drawn by Garside & Prescott, executed on the firm's premises, held in the strong-room until replaced. The 1919 will — the standing instrument, now in the strong-room — had replaced the second of these. The will of 1904 bore the same Winckley Square address as the present firm; the will of 1891 bore Garside's name alone.

There was nothing here to suggest that Josiah Eccleston had ever made a legal instrument privately, before a stranger solicitor, or in any way outside this firm.

Prescott turned to the correspondence.

Josiah's letters to the firm ran to two packets, sorted by year. They were brief and direct, written in a plain hand that had grown slightly uneven in the final years — the hand of a man who had not found correspondence convenient and had nonetheless kept it orderly. He wrote when Garside wrote to him; he confirmed, instructed, accepted. His replies ran to a paragraph or two: the matter agreed, the instruction given, the arrangement understood. In forty years of correspondence there was not a single letter that did not have a legal purpose.

Prescott read through the letters of 1924 and 1925. Then the letters of 1926, which ran only to June. In none of them, from the day the first codicil was executed in March 1924 to the last letter Josiah had written before his illness, was there any mention of a changed mind. No dissatisfaction with the arrangement for Mrs. Fairhurst's children. No instruction — or shadow of an instruction — to reconsider what had been settled in that March. The letters were the record of a man who had said what he had said about his estate and had not revisited it.

The attendance note for the fifteenth of March 1924 was in the file behind the first codicil copy.

---

> 15 March 1924. Instructions from Mr. Josiah Eccleston at the office. Client has renewed relations with his niece Mrs. Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston and desires to revoke clause 4 of his will of the 3rd June 1919. Codicil revokes clause 4 entire and gives the residue to Mrs. Margaret Fairhurst or her issue absolutely; all other provisions confirmed. Settled, executed, and attested in due form. Instrument to strong-room. *Or her issue*: collateral; substitutional form required. — H.G.

---

The note had been written with more care than a brief attendance record required. Prescott made a note on the working file cover — *corroborating exhibit: attend. note 15 March 1924, H.G.* — and set the original back.

Two pages further in the packet was a letter Josiah had written in late April 1924, six weeks after the codicil was made. It thanked Garside for his attendance in March and said, briefly, that the arrangement had been the right thing to do. Three lines on the matter and nothing equivocal. Garside had filed it inside a small folded card rather than flat in the packet as the rest lay — not the ordinary practice; the card kept the letter clean and flat. Prescott read it and set it face-down.

The file was well kept.

He returned to the index and worked through the remaining entries. A mortgage correspondence note, 1922. A tenancy agreement, that year. A bank letter, 1923. An attendance note on the mortgage terms, 1924 — in it, a record of what Josiah had said about the mill's near-term prospects, cautious but not defeatist. Then nothing in the index until the codicil entry, the last on the third page.

He was writing the finding in the working note when Garside came through the room.

"What have you found?"

"Nothing outside the firm," Prescott said. "Every instrument from the first conveyance in 1884. Two superseded wills, both drawn here. No exception in forty years. His correspondence from March 1924 to June 1926 contains nothing to suggest any wish to change the first codicil."

Garside had his coat and was going somewhere. He paused in the doorway.

"Josiah was not a man who did things unofficially," he said, in the tone of a fact about a person rather than a finding about a case. He moved on.

Prescott wrote it in the working note. He dated the note, set it at the front of the file, and returned the Eccleston papers to their drawers as the afternoon light failed at the windows.

The index lay at the top of the file, three pages in Garside's hand from 1884 to 1924, the last entry in the same hand as the first.

There was nothing in forty years of this client's business to suggest that he had ever made a legal instrument outside this firm, or without a solicitor present to see it made.

The working note said that. The file would say it. Prescott set them together on Mr. Booth's tray and went to compose the afternoon post.
