# Chapter 1 — The Strong-Room

The deed box was on the table when Prescott arrived: black painted steel, "ECCLESTON" lettered in white on the lid, the label in Garside's copper-plate facing up across the room. Garside was at the far end of the table with his hat still on, which meant he had not been in from the strong-room long.

"Dead yesterday evening," Garside said. "The Hall sent a telegram."

Josiah Eccleston had been a client of the firm since before Prescott came into articles. Cotton spinner, magistrate, owner of the Hall at Ribchester and the Vale Mill above the village — a man whose every instrument from will to conveyance had come through this office in the forty years since Garside first took his instructions. Prescott had known him first as a name in the ledger, and later, from the will itself onwards, as a man who shook hands as though a contract were meant by it. He had been eighty-one years old. He had died, as far as anyone knew without disorder, on a Tuesday evening in October, at the Hall.

The coal fire was going. Outside on the square the October light was doing what it did.

Garside set his hat down and opened the deed box.

The will was first: folded twice on cream paper, "WILL — J. ECCLESTON — 3 JUNE 1919" on the outside. Garside opened it, turned to the fourth clause, and read:

> I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my nephew Walter Eccleston of Vale Mill House Ribchester absolutely and I appoint the said Walter Eccleston sole executor of this my will.

Prescott noted the date and the name and set his pen down.

Garside folded the will and reached into the box. The codicil was underneath: same cream paper, "CODICIL — J. ECCLESTON — 15 MARCH 1924" on the outside fold, shorter by half. He opened it.

"After the reconciliation," he said, more to himself than to Prescott. He read:

> I REVOKE clause 4 of my said will and IN PLACE THEREOF I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely AND IN ALL OTHER RESPECTS I confirm my said will.

The coal shifted behind the grate. Prescott wrote down the date — fifteen March nineteen-twenty-four — and the name and address, and waited.

"Clause four revoked entire," Garside said. "Gift and executorship both — he intended a complete revision. There is, at present, no executor." He set the codicil alongside the will. "Section thirty-three of the Wills Act does nothing for a niece against lapse. She is collateral, not a descendant. He used the substitutional form accordingly."

Margaret Fairhurst. Prescott had known her name from the codicil's making two years before, and had noted the memorandum in the file when she died: May 1925, a year and a half before Josiah. Her issue were her two children — Nora, nineteen, and George, sixteen — living with their father at the Bank Parade address named in the instrument. Edgar Fairhurst. A schoolmaster.

"Both children are minors," Prescott said. "Majority is twenty-one."

"Letters of administration with the will annexed," Garside said. "To the father as guardian, if the instruments stand."

Walter Eccleston had managed the mill for fifteen years on the expectation of this estate. Prescott knew the mill was mortgaged — the kind of information that accumulated in a solicitor's knowledge without being entered in any single place. What Walter would make of the codicil's terms was a question for the next letter.

He took up the strong-room register from beside the box.

The register was a cloth-bound ledger: date column on the left, document described in the centre, clerk's signature at the right margin. Garside had maintained it in his own hand since 1906; Prescott had added entries as occasion required, in his own narrower hand, the two scripts sharing the same columns for two decades. He opened to the current year and ran down the September entries.

September the nineteenth. The entry was Garside's:

*First codicil, J. Eccleston — fetched from strong-room. Reading at Eccleston Hall at testator's request. Present: H.G., A.P., W. Eccleston, two members of the household. Instrument read entire. Returned same day. H.G.*

Prescott had been at that reading. He had carried the deed-box into the drawing room at the Hall and stood there while Garside read the codicil from first word to last — date and all — to Josiah, who was in his chair and had been failing since August. Walter had been there, and the two women from the household, and Josiah's man beside the door. Josiah had wanted no surprises. The register confirmed it in Garside's hand: instrument read entire, returned same day.

Walter Eccleston had stood beside the fireplace with his arms at his sides, listening.

Prescott turned to the working correspondence at the back of the file. The papers from the previous week were loosely arranged: the telegram from the Hall, a draft letter of condolence, and behind them his own attendance note from the despatch-box inventory.

He had made the note at the Hall table on the afternoon of the inventory, while Walter stood by. The box had been opened on the dining-room table and Prescott had listed each item as it was removed: three insurance policies, title deeds to the Hall, unsigned drafts of two rental agreements, a letter from the bank dated 1923, three letters tied in blue ribbon, an unsigned copy of the will.

No codicil.

He read through the list a second time and found the same. He clipped the note to the front of the file.

Garside restored the will and the codicil to the deed box and carried it back to the strong-room himself — he always carried the Eccleston box himself — and Prescott heard the iron door of the vault close below, and the latch engage. A minute later Garside came back up without the box and stood in the doorway.

"Two instruments," Prescott said. "The will and the first codicil. The estate belongs to the Fairhurst children if the instruments stand. There is no executor, and there was no second codicil in the despatch-box." He looked at his notes. "I should write to Thurston and Marsh today, about proving the will in proper form. And we must write to Bank Parade."

"Yes," Garside said. He sat down and took up his pen.

The file was in order: the will of the third of June nineteen-nineteen, the codicil of the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four, the strong-room register exact about both. What Walter Eccleston would make of those terms was a question the record had not yet been required to answer.

# Chapter 2 — The Second Codicil

Prescott was halfway through the Bank Parade letter when Mr. Booth appeared in the doorway with the morning post.

The Thurston & Marsh envelope was on top. It was thicker than a simple acknowledgment — thick enough for an enclosure.

The covering note was on their good paper. Their client, it advised, had lately found among his late uncle's personal papers a codicil to the will, dated the fourteenth day of August nineteen-twenty-six, which he believed had been made privately by the testator in the final months of his life. A copy was enclosed. In these circumstances, they trusted that the will might now be proved in common form in the ordinary way; they would be glad to hear how their client might proceed.

Garside read it at his desk, held out his hand for the enclosure, read that too, and set it face-down on the blotter.

"The letter-book," he said.

Prescott took the letter-book from the cupboard. The carbon of the firm's notice letter was two pages in — dated the second of November, the typing clean.

> Dear Sirs, — We act in the estate of the late Mr. Josiah Eccleston of Eccleston Hall. We hold his will dated the 3rd June 1919 and a codicil thereto dated the 15th March 1924 which materially affects the disposition of the residue. We shall be glad to receive your client's proposals for proving the will in proper form. — Yours faithfully, GARSIDE & PRESCOTT

He closed the letter-book and set it on the table.

Garside turned the enclosure over and read it aloud:

> WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.

Outside the window Winckley Square lay quiet in the November light.

"Dated the fourteenth of August," Prescott said.

"Yes."

The despatch-box had been inventoried in the last week of October, a week after the death, with Prescott recording each item as it came out and Walter present beside the table. No codicil among them — his attendance note was in the file. After the inventory, the box had stood at the mill, in Walter's keeping, for six days. The codicil had been produced after the box was returned to the Hall.

"The firm received no instruction to draw this," Prescott said. "No request for the text of the first codicil. No inquiry as to its terms."

"We gave them the date in the notice." Garside's forefinger rested on the letter-book. "I thought it proper. That is all we sent."

Prescott took the copy to the window. The paper was good foolscap, typed on a machine he could not immediately place as belonging to the firm or to any office associated with it. The signature — *Josiah Eccleston*, in dark ink — was in a formed hand of the right general character; it offered nothing that announced itself as certainly genuine or certainly not. Below the signature, an attestation clause: *Thomas Birch*, carrier, of a Ribchester address; *Frederick Hallett*, gardener, of a lane near Salesbury.

"Neither of them at their given addresses, I should think," he said.

"That remains to be determined." Garside was reaching for his overcoat; he had a meeting elsewhere. "Write to Bank Parade this afternoon. Mr. Fairhurst must enter a caveat before any other step is taken, and he must do it promptly. The instrument has two witnesses and a date and a signature that will not be settled quickly." He had his hat. "Nothing to Thurston and Marsh beyond acknowledgment. Nothing at all."

---

Walter Eccleston called at the office that same afternoon.

No appointment had been made. Mr. Booth brought his card in without comment, and Prescott arrived in the front room a moment later to find Walter already settled in the chair opposite Garside's desk, coat and hat set aside, with the ease of a man who had spent twenty years at home in other people's offices. He greeted Garside and Prescott both. He said he had come himself because it seemed the right thing to do, given the long connection.

He was fifty or thereabouts — broad in the shoulder, a dark wool coat, the considered quiet that came from managing men through a long stretch of difficult years. He had known Josiah Eccleston all his working life and had known this firm almost as long. He was polite, and he was thoroughly certain about all of it.

His account was orderly. He had gone through his uncle's insurance papers in the despatch-box in the days following the inventory. He was, he said, very conscious of having been present at that inventory and of the codicil not being there then; his best understanding was that Josiah must have kept it separately and it had simply been overlooked, or added to the box on a later occasion. Josiah had been up at the mill three or four times in the spring, before the illness; the mill office had a typewriter, and it would have been nothing for him to sit down and draft something out. He had always transacted his correspondence at the mill rather than at the Hall. It was entirely in his character.

"He always said the arrangement for Margaret and her issue wouldn't stand as he'd left it," Walter said, in a tone that was not argumentative, only explanatory. "That he'd made it in a soft mood and always meant to put it right. He said so more than once, and to more than one person." He looked briefly at his hands. "I would very much rather there were no solemn-form action about this. These are Margaret's children. I have no wish to be in dispute with Margaret's children."

Garside said that the firm must advise its clients and take instructions in the ordinary way, and that nothing further could be said at this stage. Walter accepted this with a brief nod — the nod of a man accustomed to solicitors' answers. He stood, and shook Garside's hand, and then Prescott's, and left without further remark.

Prescott wrote the attendance note in full: Walter's account of finding the codicil, his description of Josiah's correspondence habits at the mill, the timing of the despatch-box as Walter understood it, his stated wish to avoid proceedings. All of it dated and initialled and clipped to the file.

Then he went back to the letter-book and read the November second carbon a second time. The firm's notice letter had given Walter's solicitors the date of the first codicil in writing: the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four. Nothing beyond it. No text; no terms; no word of the instrument except that it bore that date and materially affected the residue. The letter-book confirmed it: that was all that had gone out.

---

Edgar Fairhurst entered the caveat at the Probate Registry on the eighth of November. The notice arrived at Winckley Square three days later — a printed card, the date stamped in violet ink — and Prescott noted it in the file and clipped it to the caveat cover.

The file now held the will, the first codicil, the despatch-box inventory attendance note, the firm's notice letter carbon, Walter's attendance note, and the copy of the second codicil. A second codicil the firm had never been asked to draw, in an estate it had administered for forty years without a privately-made instrument of any kind.

He set the file on Mr. Booth's tray. Outside Winckley Square the light was already gone.

# Chapter Five — The Hinge

The court had risen early. Prescott came back through Winckley Square at ten minutes past eleven, briefcase in hand, and found the outer door unlocked.

Mr. Booth was standing in the passage.

In sixteen years Prescott had never seen Mr. Booth standing in the passage. The managing clerk occupied either his desk in the front room or the corridor between the deed-room and the letterpress; he did not stand in the passage as though waiting to be told where to go next.

He said: "Mr. Garside, sir. About half past nine. He was at his desk when it happened — the notes are open."

They were. Garside had been annotating the margin of a client letter: the pen lay on the page, still uncapped, the ink dried in the nib before anyone had thought to close it. The annotation was three words and not finished. Dr. Ainsworth came at ten o'clock and confirmed what was evident before he arrived.

The arrangements took the rest of the morning. The doctor's certificate; a brief attendance from the coroner's office, who found nothing requiring them further; a message to Garside's chambers contact in Manchester; a telegram to Garside's sister in Harrogate, who was his only surviving family. Mr. Booth handled most of it with the quiet efficiency of twenty years' managing. Prescott signed one letter at Garside's desk that could not wait and returned to his own. The chair had not yet been vacated; but it would have to be used.

He was thirty-eight. He had worked beside this man for sixteen years.

By the afternoon the office was working again, because it had to. There were three matters due before the week's end.

---

The days that followed had a shape that became recognisable only in retrospect: a week of considerable effort with little to show for it. The clients were written to, each file noted with the date and the name of the partner now handling it. Two long-running matters were referred to larger firms better placed to carry them. The other matters remained.

Mr. Booth's habits did not change. He put the post on Prescott's desk each morning and collected the outgoing letters at noon and at four, and continued to treat the telephone as an instrument of occasional and controlled utility. The firm was Prescott and Booth now. Neither of them used those words; there was no occasion that required it.

The Eccleston file sat on the corner of Prescott's desk through those first days: the caveat entered, the administrator pendente lite still to be applied for, the action assigned to the Probate Division and waiting for a date. Prescott attended to more urgent matters first. On the fourth evening, when the office was quiet and the street outside had gone dark, he put everything else aside and opened the file from the beginning.

---

It was not that he expected to find anything new. He read the file because it was what Garside would have done before proceeding: a thorough read, everything together, to know exactly what one had and what one did not. He went through the will, the first codicil, the covering correspondence, the register index sheet, the attendance notes, the letter-book carbon, Josiah's letter to Margaret Fairhurst, the working note Prescott had written in November recording forty years of instruments and the silence of the correspondence thereafter. He read each item and set it face-down to the right of the blotter. The coal in the grate had burned low; he put three pieces on before sitting down again with the strong-room register.

He had consulted the register in October — glanced at the September entry to confirm what he and Garside had both been present to witness. He read the page now in full.

The register was a tall narrow ledger, twenty years of entries in two hands: Garside's copper-plate filling the greater part of it, with Prescott's narrower script appearing in the same columns for the matters he had handled in the latter years. The overall character of the book was Garside's, and what it expressed above all was a standard — the level of detail required of each entry, whether the occasion was large or small: instrument named in full, date given, purpose of withdrawal stated, persons present listed, time out and time in recorded, condition on return noted, initials given. No practice requirement compelled this. It was simply what the register was.

He found the September entry.

---

*19 September 1926. Document: First Codicil, J. Eccleston, dated 15 March 1924. Purpose: Read to assembled family at testator's request; testator's health declining; testator wished there to be no surprises. Persons present: H. Garside; A. Prescott; W. Eccleston; Mr. E. Beckett (steward); one other of the household. Instrument read entire, including date. Time out: 9.45 a.m. Time returned: 3.20 p.m. Document in good order on return. H.G.*

---

He sat with this for some time.

The entry was consistent with every other entry in the book: the same instrument named in full, the same purpose given, the same persons noted, the same times. It had not been written for this moment. It had been written on the afternoon of the nineteenth of September in the ordinary course of what the register required — which is to say, considerably more than what practice required. *Instrument read entire, including date.* That phrase was not in any requirement of law or practice. It was Garside's.

He turned back through the pages. The same character for twenty years. A box of deeds fetched for a completion in 1918. The will read to Josiah at the Hall in 1919. The mortgage papers in 1921. Every entry at the same level — not the level a register strictly required, but the level of a man who did not distinguish between what required a record and what deserved one.

He closed the register and set it back on its shelf. He sat with the open file for a few minutes longer. The coal was nearly spent.

---

The letter from the Principal Probate Registry had come that morning; he had set it aside for the afternoon and not reached it. He opened it now.

The action had been set down for hearing in the Probate Division. The date fixed: the sixth of October 1927.

He counted forward. He was in December; it was the twentieth. He counted to October.

Two hundred and ninety days.

He banked the fire, locked the strong-room, and put on his coat. He walked home through Winckley Square in the cold of December. Two hundred and ninety days.

# The File

The papers from the Hall came by registered post on the twenty-second, packed in a cardboard box with the administrator's covering note on top: one pocket diary, 1926; one bundle of correspondence, inward and outward, January to October; one set of household accounts. Prescott had not requested the accounts.

It was two hundred and fifty-seven days to the hearing.

He lifted the diary out first. Small, leather-covered, a brass clasp stiff from disuse — the kind sold in any stationer's, a shilling and sixpence, renewed each year without much deliberation. Josiah Eccleston's name was written inside the front cover in a hand that was still his own but smaller, and somewhat less firm, than the hand in the instruments in the strong-room.

He opened it to the first of January and began.

The entries were sparse from the start. January: a mill appointment on the eighth — the subject noted (looms on short time; questions about the dye-house roof), Walter's name not in it. February: another mill appointment; a doctor's visit on the nineteenth — Dr. Cullis, two words only, suggesting something routine; and a letter acknowledged from a cousin in Harrogate. March: a note from the magistrates' clerk, one of Josiah's cases forwarded to a colleague in Clitheroe. The entry had the air of a letter that had not been unexpected, and had not been unwelcome.

The mill appointments grew fewer in spring. The last was on the fourteenth of May: *W.E. — mill — morning.* Four words. After that, nothing about the mill.

The entries became sparser and more domestic. Beckett here and there — the steward, the same name as in the strong-room register. A note about the south field. The insurance broker. Josiah's world, in the pages of his diary, had contracted steadily through the summer, away from the mill and toward the house and the land around it.

Prescott turned to August.

The fourteenth was a Saturday. The entry read: *Hot again. Beckett here this afternoon — the south field question — resolved.* And below, in a slightly smaller hand: *Neck troubling me this morning.*

That was the last entry. After it: blank pages, clean, through September and October and the remainder of the year.

Prescott read the entry a second time. It was the record of an ordinary day: no appointment beyond Beckett, no instrument made or directed, no reference to any testamentary act. A diary did not prove a negative. But it was a record, and the record said nothing.

---

He set the diary aside and lifted the correspondence bundle.

The administrator had divided it — formal on the left, household on the right. Prescott worked through the formal side first. Three letters to and from Garside & Prescott, all already in the firm's letter-book and accounted for there. A letter from a Ribchester solicitor on a tenancy matter. Two from the estate's insurance brokers. Nothing to or from Thurston & Marsh; nothing from any other firm on any question touching the will or the codicil; nothing that had not already been known from the letter-book side.

The household side he read more quickly. Family correspondence; replies to local matters; the magistrates' clerk again. He came, near the bottom of the right-hand bundle, to a letter in Josiah's hand — but a different hand from the instruments: softer, unguarded, the hand of a man writing to someone he was glad to write to. Addressed to Miss Nora Fairhurst, Bank Parade, Preston. Dated the third of April, 1926.

He read it carefully. Not long — three-quarters of a page, a correction in the second paragraph, a postscript about a book he had promised to send. It said nothing about the estate's disposition, nothing about instruments or codicils. But near the end Josiah had written:

*I am very glad we have the matter settled between us, and I mean it to stay settled. Your mother knew it. You know it. That is what I wished.*

He read those three sentences again. Then he made a note of the letter and set it to one side for the exhibits bundle.

---

He had read the instrument register in full in December, and knew what it contained. He took it from the strong-room now for the same reason he had written the letter-book note the previous week: to fix the finding as a record item. He ran his eye down the Eccleston column from 1884 to the end.

The original lease of Vale Mill, 1884. A mortgage, 1889, discharged 1892. The deed of gift of the Ribchester farmland, 1903. The lease extension of 1908. The will, third of June 1919. And, in Garside's invariable hand, the last entry in the column: *First Codicil — J. Eccleston dec. — 15 March 1924.*

Nothing after it. Forty years of instruments for one estate, and then a line. He closed the register and returned it to the strong-room.

---

When he came back to the table, there was one more item in the bundle — flat at the bottom, below the register extracts and the attending notes, easy to miss. A letter in Garside's hand, on plain notepaper rather than the firm's standard paper. Dated the fourteenth of March, 1924.

He sat down and read it.

Three sentences. The codicil was enclosed, properly engrossed and ready for execution; Mr. Eccleston would need to sign it in the presence of two witnesses, both present together at the same time, neither of whom took any benefit under the instrument; Garside would attend at the Hall if preferred, or if Mr. Eccleston wished to arrange the witnesses himself, the office would be glad to receive the executed original at his convenience.

Three sentences, and each one exact. The witness requirement stated in full for a man who had been signing instruments since 1884 and had not required instruction in forty years. The note about the executed original — not a request but an offer, *the office would be glad to receive it*, as if Garside had thought about the document's custody before the letter left his desk.

It had been written for the record. Not for Josiah.

Prescott held it a moment, then set it with the exhibits.

The whole file had that quality. Each letter a fraction more precise than the matter strictly required; each attendance note kept at the same level whether the occasion was routine or not; the register built to a standard that had no source in any statute or practice requirement, but had its source entirely in the man who had built it. The file was the work of a man who had never distinguished between what required a record and what deserved one.

And the file was going to prove a forgery.

---

He wrote the working note in the hand he used for formal file items, and read it back once before he dated it.

*No private record or correspondence contains any reference to any intention to revoke or alter the first codicil after its execution in March 1924. No instrument in the firm's register was made in the name of Josiah Eccleston after that date. The survey of instruments is complete: every instrument made by Josiah Eccleston for a period of forty years was made through the firm of Garside & Prescott, and the last was the first codicil.*

He dated it the twenty-seventh of January, 1927, and placed it at the front of the working file.

---

The strong-room smelled as it always did: clean paper, iron shelves, the dry compound of ink aged past sharpness into something denser and quieter. He set the register in its place, checked the order of the cabinet, and closed the door. The lock turned with its usual certainty.

He turned off the lamp and went out into Winckley Square, and home.

# The Witnesses

> SIGNED by the said JOSIAH ECCLESTON as and for his last codicil in the presence of us both
> present at the same time who at his request in his presence and in the presence of each other
> have hereunto subscribed our names as witnesses:
>
> THOMAS BIRCH, Carrier, of Ribchester in the County of Lancaster.
>
> FREDERICK HALLETT, Gardener, of near Salesbury in the County of Lancaster.

Both men were in the instrument index.

The index was a bound ledger, red boards worn soft at the corners, in Garside's hand from its first
entry in 1906 to the last he had made before the autumn. It recorded witness by name, trade, address,
instrument number, and date — so that finding any given specimen was a question of reading a column
and walking to a shelf. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester: four entries, the earliest in 1912, the
latest in March 1921. Frederick Hallett, gardener, near Salesbury: one entry, the same March 1921
instrument.

Prescott noted the instrument numbers and wrote to the Ribchester registrar that afternoon. He
instructed Booth to pull both instruments from the file.

---

The registrar's reply arrived four days later. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester, had died on the
twenty-eighth of September 1926. The cause given was influenza. Prescott wrote by return for a
certified copy of the death certificate, and it came within the week.

He opened his attendance book and wrote the date.

The instruments Booth had found carried Birch's signature on both: the deed of cottage tenancy from
November 1914 and the property schedule from March 1921. The 1914 hand was angular and firm at the
ascenders; by 1921 it had settled, the loop of the g broader, the B somewhat taller. Consistent with
itself across seven years. Prescott had been present at the 1921 signing. He packaged both originals
with a covering note and posted them to Croft in Manchester, together with a photographic copy of the
attestation page of the propounded codicil.

The March 1921 property schedule bore one further signature as witness, below Birch's: Hallett's hand,
shorter in body, the letters more angled, a single specimen. He sent it to Croft under a second cover.

---

He had written to Atkinson at Ribchester on the same day as the registrar — Atkinson whose practice
was agricultural conveyancing and the kind of local inquiry that required knowing the farms east of
Langridge Moor. The address *near Salesbury* was the sort of description that needed someone who knew
the road.

Atkinson's reply took nine days and ran to two pages. Hallett had worked the previous spring and
summer for a farmer named Ogden on the Salesbury road — kitchen garden and light farmwork. In the
first days of October 1926, Hallett had given notice. He had left no address with Ogden, none with
any neighbour Atkinson could find, none with the post office, which had handled one redirected letter
and could not say where it had gone. Atkinson had then made inquiry at the shipping offices in Preston,
which was the obvious next step, and had found that in the second week of October 1926 a Frederick
Hallett of Ribchester had taken an assisted passage from Liverpool to Quebec aboard the *SS Aurania*.

No fixed address in Canada.

Prescott added the departure date to his attendance book below the first entry. Then the next two:
the last week of October, Josiah's death; the first days of November, the despatch-box opened with
Prescott present, no codicil in it. Six days at the mill. The four dates made a column and described
a shape, and the shape described a thing, and he drew his pen through the space where that thing
would have been written, because the brief was not a place for what was not evidence.

---

Croft's two reports arrived in the same cover, their dates of composition ten days apart. They were
written in the same form.

> *In the matter of the Estate of Josiah Eccleston, deceased. I have examined the attestation
> signature attributed to THOMAS BIRCH on a photographic copy of the propounded codicil and
> compared it with the two authenticated specimens submitted: the cottage tenancy deed of November
> 1914 and the property schedule of March 1921, both originals. The signature on the propounded
> instrument is consistent with both specimens in general formation, pen pressure, and the
> development that seven years' interval between specimens would naturally produce. Given that my
> comparison rests upon a photographic copy of the propounded instrument rather than the original,
> and that two authenticated specimens only are available, I am not in a position to offer a
> positive identification. I cannot exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction executed from
> comparison material of comparable quality to that submitted to me. — H. Croft, Document
> Examiner.*

The second report came in the same register.

> *In the matter of the Estate of Josiah Eccleston, deceased. I have examined the attestation
> signature attributed to FREDERICK HALLETT on a photographic copy of the propounded codicil and
> compared it with the single authenticated specimen submitted: the property schedule of March 1921,
> original. The signature is consistent with the specimen in its general formation and character.
> A single specimen does not establish the full range of a hand, and I am unable to form a view
> on natural variation or development across the intervening period. I am not in a position to
> offer a positive identification. I cannot exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction.
> — H. Croft, Document Examiner.*

One witness was dead. The other was in Canada without a fixed address. Neither signature, on the
evidence before him, could be distinguished from a skilled copy of the genuine article.

He put both reports in the file.

---

There was a practical consequence to Hallett being alive rather than dead, which was that a commission
might be applied for. If the Probate Division granted it, a judicial officer in Canada would take
Hallett's evidence on the question of due execution — if Hallett could be located. Prescott wrote to
Mitchell in London with the full position: the witness's identity; his last confirmed employment;
his departure from Ribchester in the first days of October 1926 and his assisted passage aboard the
*Aurania*; Atkinson's inquiries and their result; the confirmed absence of any traceable address.
Mitchell's reply came within the week. The power to issue a commission existed; the difficulty was
personal service, which required an address, which was not available; the commission, if granted,
would take time the calendar did not have. Nevertheless Mitchell recommended applying, disclosing
the difficulty in full. To decline to apply was to abandon the question before it was put.

Prescott agreed, and Mitchell filed the application in the last week of April.

One hundred and seventy-two days to the hearing. The draft of the application was in the file —
the instrument, the witness's identity and last known whereabouts, the absence of a fixed address
in Canada, the submission that his evidence on due execution could not otherwise be obtained. It
was a well-drawn piece of work. Whether the court would look past the address difficulty was a
question whose answer was not yet available.

He noted the date of filing in the margin of his attendance book and placed the file on Booth's
tray for the shelf.

# The Commission

The letter from Mitchell came by the first post on Tuesday. Booth brought it up from the letter-rack and set it on the desk above the Hadfield figures Prescott had been working through — London postmark, Mitchell's own hand on the envelope — and Prescott opened it with the small bronze knife he kept for correspondence, which had been Garside's.

The refusal was in the first paragraph.

---

*The court has declined to issue the commission to examine Mr. Frederick Hallett. The ground stated is that the applicant has been unable to supply a fixed address in Canada at which the commission could be served, and the court will not issue a commission that cannot be executed. A fresh application would require a verified address. The decision is not appealable on these facts.*

---

He read it a second time. He set it on the desk.

He rose and walked to the window. The square below was fully in leaf — the lime trees in front of the courthouse had come on considerably in the past fortnight — and a postman was working along the opposite pavement at a pace that did not suggest urgency. A woman was crossing below with a basket, looking at nothing in particular. None of this was of any interest to him. He stood at the window and allowed the thing to settle.

The witnesses were done. Both of them, from both directions: Birch was dead, and his death was in the registrar's certificate; Hallett had gone to Canada without an address, and the court could not reach him there on the available materials. Mitchell had submitted the application with the address difficulty disclosed in full — there had been no other way to proceed with credit — and the court had done what courts did when the mechanism of service did not exist. Four weeks had passed from the application in the last week of April to this Tuesday in May: four weeks that could not be recovered. There had been a hundred and seventy-two days on the clock when Mitchell had filed; there were a hundred and forty now. The difference was the commission application, entirely.

A man who sat down immediately had not quite finished admitting the thing to himself. He stood a while longer at the window and admitted it.

The attestation was permanently closed, from every direction that involved a living witness. Neither man could now be examined, whether to break the second codicil's due execution or to support it. The defence's case rested on the silence of the witnesses: unassailable, because nobody living could speak to what had or had not happened in August 1926 in the presence of two men who were, respectively, dead and somewhere in Canada. Prescott's side was in the same position, on the other face of the same coin — neither attestation could be confirmed or broken, because neither attester could be reached. It was not a defeat in any sense the brief could name; it was a closed door, and the brief had not been built on this door. But there was a difference between choosing not to lean on a route and having it closed behind you, and Prescott was precise about differences of this kind.

There was a shape to the situation, however, that he had noted before and put aside.

Six weeks ago, after entering the four-date column in the attendance book — Birch dead on the twenty-eighth of September, Hallett gone in the second week of October, Josiah dead in the third week, the despatch-box inventoried in early November — he had drawn his pen through the space where the inference would have gone. He returned to that space now. The two witnesses named on the second codicil had been chosen from among the men who had genuinely witnessed Josiah's instruments in years past: men in Garside's index, men whose authentic signatures were therefore on file, men against whose known hands Croft could take a fair comparison. Both had become unavailable in the same autumn, within days of each other. Both had been newly unavailable — one dead, one gone — in the weeks before the despatch-box stood six days at the mill in October.

A document executed in August, before the influenza had run its course, before the passage to Quebec, would have named them without foreknowledge that either would be gone.

Unless someone had composed it afterward, and dated it to August.

He did not write this in the attendance book. He had already drawn a pen through it once, and that had been right: a thought crossed out does not become evidence by revival. What it might become — with authorship established on independent grounds and each innocent explanation foreclosed by document rather than argument — was something counsel could set before the court in the proper order. Not today. In due course.

He returned to the desk and drew a sheet of paper from the drawer.

He wrote to Mitchell. The commission had failed; the witness avenue was definitively closed; they were to proceed on the footing that the case must be made on the typewriter evidence and the text. He asked Mitchell to confirm his understanding of the position and to advise on what form the text argument should take in the brief — what it would be required to establish, and in what sequence it would need to be put. He noted the calendar: a hundred and forty days to the hearing; the brief must be complete within eight weeks at the outside.

He read the letter through and made one correction: *are proceeding* to *must proceed*, which was the honest form. He sealed it and carried it through to Booth's tray.

"Midday post," he said.

Booth looked up from the letter-book. "Right," he said, and returned to it.

The commission letter went into the file in its correct position: behind the application, ahead of Mitchell's April note. Prescott clipped the folder and squared it to the left of the desk. The file grew in the way files grew when a proceeding was properly kept — one document at a time, each in its right place, the record of everything attempted and everything concluded, the corridor of closed doors. A solicitor who left an avenue unexamined in solemn form proceedings could not afterward explain himself, which was why the application had been made, and why the commission letter was now in the file; both reasons remained sound. The avenue had been examined. The result was in the record.

What remained was the text.

A hundred and forty days. He wrote the figure in the margin of Mitchell's letter before filing it. What the brief must establish, in eight weeks, was what the second codicil's recital could and could not have been drawn from: that the executed first codicil had never left the strong-room; that no copy of any kind had existed outside this office; that no one anywhere in the county had been furnished with its language; and that whatever the recital had been composed from, it was not the instrument. The machine evidence placed the typing at the mill office. The text would establish what the recital had and had not seen. Together they told a story that the record had been building toward since November, and the text was what had to carry it — not as a fallback, but as what it had always been.

He took the Hadfield figures from the desk and settled back to the columns he had been working through when the post came in.

# The Hall

The track to Eccleston Hall branched from the Ribchester road above the mill, taking the hillside at a steeper gradient so that the Hall gate stood at an elevation where the mill below was foreshortened and the valley opened wide to the west. Prescott hired a motor at Ribchester station — the second week of June, clear weather, the Ribble low and clean below — and the driver brought him up a raked gravel approach that curved before the south front of the house.

He stepped down and looked at it.

Two storeys, late Georgian stone, good proportions: not a great estate, but a house built with some idea of its own character. The grounds were maintained — lawns cut, kitchen garden occupied — but with fewer hands than the place had evidently required; the coach-house stood open and empty, and there was one figure visible in the walled garden and no one else. The administrator pendente lite met the minimum domestic expenses, and the minimum showed. Josiah had managed the Hall and the mill below it for sixty years and had died in its east bedroom in October; now the estate sat without instructions, and the house was kept until someone told it what to do next.

Elias Beckett met him at the front door and took him through to the library.

Beckett had been steward at the Hall for fourteen years. He was in his late fifties, deliberate in manner, and he arrived in the library with a clothbound household journal set before him on the table and already open. Prescott had brought a clerk from the Preston office; the deposition was to be taken formally, sworn, and filed.

"From about the middle of May last year," Prescott said, once the clerk had recorded the preliminary matter, "was Mr. Eccleston in the habit of going out?"

"No." Beckett placed one hand on the open diary without turning the page. "His last outing was the fourteenth of May. He went to the mill — Simms took him in the motor, as he always did — and he came home by four. I have it here." He turned the journal and showed the entry.

*Mr E. to the mill, with Simms. Home by four.*

It was the last such entry for many pages. What followed was domestic — deliveries, the doctor's visits beginning in June, household receipts.

"The doctor's visits increased from June?"

"Weekly by June. Twice a week by August."

"In your judgment," Prescott said, "could Mr. Eccleston have made a journey to the mill in August? Twelve miles?"

Beckett did not answer at once. He was not a man who answered before he had arrived at the answer. "He could not," he said. "He could not have done it without Simms and the motor, and I should have known — nothing leaves this house without my being aware of it. In any case, by August the journey itself was beyond him. He had his wits, right to the end — I would not have you think otherwise — but the road to the mill and back would not have been possible for him. Not in August."

"You would have known if any such journey had taken place?"

"Nothing went out in August," Beckett said.

Prescott asked next about the September visit.

"The nineteenth," Beckett said, and turned without searching to the correct page of the journal. "Mr. Garside came, and another gentleman from Preston — yourself, I take it. Half past ten. They went into the drawing room with Mr. Eccleston and the family. The deed-box; the papers inside; about an hour. They left before midday. Mr. Eccleston was in the drawing room the whole time. He could not have left the house that day without my knowledge."

He showed Prescott the page.

*Sep. 19 — Mr. Garside and another from Preston, half past ten. Drawing room. Instruments. Family. Gone by noon.*

Prescott read it and returned the journal.

The strong-room register, in Garside's hand, carried the same event on the same date: the first codicil fetched, read entire in the presence of the testator and the assembled family, returned the same afternoon. The Hall's household diary and the strong-room register in Preston confirmed the same hour from opposite ends of twelve miles — one record kept in a solicitor's basement, one in a household journal on the valley road. Garside had noted the September visit with more precision than a courtesy call required. He could not have known, on the nineteenth of September, what that precision would need to do.

The remaining questions were thorough and took some time. Between May and October: had Mr. Eccleston ever left the Hall unaccompanied; had the motor ever gone out for his use without Beckett's knowledge; had any visitor arrived who had removed him from the premises. The answers were consistent and did not require repeating. Beckett signed the deposition and the clerk witnessed it.

Mrs. Hargreaves, the cook — nine years at the Hall — was brought in next. She had been on the premises throughout August and had left it only twice, on half-days she could specify. Mr. Eccleston had not gone out; she was certain of it; nothing of that kind had happened. She signed where the clerk indicated and returned to the kitchen without further remark. Ellen Bradshaw, the housemaid, two years in her position, required less time still: Mr. Eccleston had not left the house in August; she had no uncertainty on the point.

Prescott took the afternoon train back to Preston with the three depositions in the briefcase.

Dr. Hartley's response was waiting, forwarded that morning by the administrator: certified extracts from the medical notes for August 1926, covering four visits to the Hall, the fifth of the month through the twenty-seventh. Shortness of breath on exertion, restricted movement, prescription adjusted twice. No outing or journey mentioned at any visit. The doctor had added a line in his own hand:

---

*In my professional opinion, Mr. Josiah Eccleston was not capable of making a journey of twelve miles in August 1926. Such a journey would have been medically inadvisable in the strongest terms. I am satisfied on the evidence of my own clinical observations that he did not make one.*

---

Prescott placed the certified notes and the doctor's letter behind the three depositions and sat down with a sheet of paper.

---

*Door (b) — Josiah's presence at the mill on the date of the second codicil — CLOSED.*

*Depositions from Mr. E. Beckett (steward, fourteen years' service), Mrs. E. Hargreaves (cook, nine years), and Miss E. Bradshaw (housemaid, two years), all of Eccleston Hall, Ribchester, each sworn before a commissioned clerk; corroborated by certified medical notes of Dr. T. Hartley, M.B., of Ribchester: the late Mr. Josiah Eccleston did not leave Eccleston Hall for any external destination after 14 May 1926. He was physically incapable of travel to Vale Mill, Ribchester — approximately twelve miles from the Hall — from June 1926 onward. The second codicil is dated 14 August 1926. On that date Mr. Eccleston was confined to the Hall, in failing health, and the journey was not possible for him. The second codicil cannot represent a visit by the testator to the mill office on the date it bears.*

---

He made one amendment — *in failing health, not capable of such a journey* to *in failing health, and the journey was not possible for him* — and initialled it.

One hundred and twenty-five days.

# The Date

The hearing brief had been growing for three days. Mr. Booth had laid the exhibits in numbered order on the long table in the outer office — each document confirmed against the schedule, the index number pencilled in the upper right corner, the relevance notation entered in the right-hand column — and Prescott had been working through them in sequence, transferring the verified bundles to the briefcase that would travel to London at the end of the month. It was the second week of July; the square outside was light until nine, and the office without its winter coal fire felt opened out, the iron grate cleaned and cold.

He had accounted for twenty-two exhibits. The twenty-third was the firm's notice letter of the second of November 1926 to Thurston & Marsh of Church Street.

He laid it on the desk and read it as a document rather than as something he had written.

The letter gave notice of the will and of the first codicil, the codicil described as *dated the 15th March 1924 which materially affects the disposition of the residue.* Those were the words: a date, and a bare statement of material effect. No text of the codicil; no identification of the beneficiary; no operative language. It was what solicitors wrote to other solicitors at the outset of an estate matter, when what was required was notice rather than disclosure.

The letter-book carbon confirmed the transmission. The copy was in its correct position in the letter-book, dated and addressed, sequenced between the first of November and the fourth. Garside had established the letter-book system the year Prescott had come into the office as an articled clerk, and nothing about it had varied since. The letter of the second of November had been sent; its contents had reached Thurston & Marsh on or about the third; from shortly after that date the date of the first codicil — *the 15th March 1924* — had been in their client's hands in writing.

Before the second of November, what had been available?

The September reading. On the nineteenth of September 1926, Garside had fetched the first codicil from the strong-room and driven to Eccleston Hall; the strong-room register recorded the fetch and the same-day return in Garside's hand. In the drawing room at the Hall, Garside had read the instrument entire to the assembled family: the gift, the date, the form of words, the revocation of clause 4. Prescott had been in the room, carrying the deed-box. Walter Eccleston had been in the room. The date of the first codicil had been spoken in that room: *the fifteenth of March 1924.* Walter had heard it once, in September, amid a great deal else.

Memory might have preserved the date, or might not. Five weeks later, in the days before R5 arrived — in the days the despatch-box stood at the mill — memory of a single occasion was the only source. After the second of November, memory was supplemented by writing.

Prescott drew the second codicil from exhibit envelope two and read the recital.

---

WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.

---

The date in the recital was *the fifteenth day of March 1924.* The date in the firm's notice letter was *the 15th March 1924.* The same figures in two conventions: the abbreviated form a notice letter would use, and the written-out style a drafter would set into the recital of an executed instrument. The correspondence was exact.

The operative words in the recital were *unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely.*

The firm's notice letter had not given operative words. It had given the date and the bare fact of material effect. The letter-book record showed that no text of the operative clause of the first codicil had been transmitted from this firm in writing; the profession canvass of the previous August had established that no solicitor in the county had been asked to advise on the codicil's terms. If the operative words in the recital had reached the drafter from any written source, that source was not in evidence and was not in the record.

The operative words of the executed first codicil were *unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely.* The recital's version — *and her issue* — was not those words. It was the version that appeared in exhibits already filed: in Walter Eccleston's letter to his bank manager on the eleventh of June 1925, in Walter's own hand, fourteen months before the codicil's stated date; and in the attendance note recording Nora Fairhurst's account of what Walter had told the children in early May. Three instances of the same version across three years. The version was consistent; it did not vary; it was Walter's version.

Prescott set the notice letter and the second codicil side by side and took up a fresh sheet.

The working note occupied two pages.

---

*Working note — exhibit 23 (R5, notice letter, 2 Nov. 1926) — 16 July 1927*

*The firm's notice letter to Thurston & Marsh of 2 November 1926 (R5, exhibit 23) gave the date of the first codicil as "the 15th March 1924." It gave no operative text of the codicil. The letter-book carbon (exhibit 7) confirms transmission on 2 November 1926. The date of the first codicil was not in writing from this firm or from any other established source before that date.*

*The recital of the second codicil (R3, exhibit 2) recites the first codicil as "dated the fifteenth day of March 1924" and as giving the residue "unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely." The date in the recital ("the fifteenth day of March 1924") corresponds exactly to the date in R5. The operative words in the recital ("and her issue") do not correspond to the operative words of the executed first codicil ("or her issue" — R2, exhibit 1). They correspond to the version documented in the hand of Walter Eccleston as at 11 June 1925 (R4, exhibit 14) and in the attendance note of 13 May 1927 (exhibit 21).*

*The recital reproduces the element of the first codicil that was supplied in writing by this firm's correspondence (the date). It does not reproduce the element that was not so supplied (the operative text); it reproduces instead a version of the operative words documented as Walter Eccleston's own, derived from a spoken account and not from the executed instrument.*

*Taken alone, this does not establish authorship. Combined with the foreclosures established by exhibits 1–22 — the machine, the presence, the witnesses, the profession, the firm's own record, the habit, the despatch-box, the September reading — it establishes that the recital was composed by a person who had the date from R5, had the operative words from memory of a spoken account, and had no access to the executed first codicil at any point.*

*A.P., 16.vii.27*

---

He filed the working note behind exhibit twenty-three. He returned the second codicil to its envelope and set it back in its position. Twenty-four was the extract from the strong-room register.

Ninety days to the hearing. The asymmetry was in the record: the date had been in writing; the text had not.

# The Ninth Word

The last of the evening light had gone from the square by half past eight, and the gas lamps had come on. Mr. Booth had been home since six. The coal fire was out — it had not been lit since March — and Prescott had opened the window against the July heat; the sounds of the square came in through it, the cobbles and the pigeons settling, and the faint warm smell of a summer evening in a northern town.

He had the brief spread across the desk in three sections: the narrative, the exhibit schedule, and the amended affidavit of due execution still wanting Mitchell's countersignature from London. Counsel would have everything by the first of August if Prescott kept to the timetable. He was going to keep to the timetable.

Before anything left the office, he did what Garside had always done and what Prescott had done himself since Garside's desk became his: he read every citation in the narrative against the original document from which it was drawn. The brief cited the first codicil at exhibit one. Exhibit one was in the strong-room. He took the key from its hook.

---

The strong-room was in the basement: stone floor, iron shelves, the registered documents of thirty years in bundles and deed-boxes at their marked positions. The Eccleston deed-box was on the second shelf — black painted steel, *ECCLESTON* stencilled in white on the lid — and he had been down for it often enough in the past eight months that the shelf knew his hand by now.

The strong-room register sat above, in its place. Garside's hand went back twenty years in that ledger. He did not open it. He knew what was in it; he had known since December.

He lifted the deed-box and carried it upstairs.

---

He opened the box on the desk. The first codicil — the executed original, on good rag paper, in the strong-room since the day of its execution in March 1924 — was in its wrapper at the top. He set it to the left of the desk.

From the action file he drew the propounded second codicil, the instrument produced by Thurston & Marsh. He set it to the right.

He picked up the second codicil and read from the recital.

---

*WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.*

---

He put it down and took up the first codicil. He read the operative gift.

---

*...unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely...*

---

He put the first codicil down.

He read the recital again from the gift clause forward, slowly. He stopped at the ninth word.

The recital said *and*. The executed instrument said *or*.

He sat with both documents in front of him and said nothing, because there was no one in the room.

---

Any careful codicil, revoking an earlier instrument, recited that instrument — and took the wording of the recital from somewhere. The recital before him had the date right: *the fifteenth day of March 1924*, word for word, the date the firm had given to Thurston & Marsh in the notice letter of the second of November. The firm had given them nothing else. Not the address of the legatee. Not the operative clause. Nothing beyond the date.

The recital did not have the operative word from the executed text. It had the word a man would carry who had been told about the codicil, once, in speech, and had never read the instrument itself. The spoken sentence and the signed paper were not the same; they had not been the same since March 1924. The recital was not composed from the document.

He got up and went to the exhibit cabinet.

---

Exhibit fourteen was Walter Eccleston's letter to Mr. Holt, his bank manager, dated the eleventh of June 1925. He had filed it himself, three months ago, as part of the financial evidence. He had not read it since.

He read it now.

---

*Dear Mr. Holt, — You ask what further security I can offer beyond the mortgage. My uncle has made a codicil, as I told you, in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst and her issue, but I am assured the arrangement will not stand; he made it in a soft mood and has spoken since of putting it right. My expectations are otherwise what they have always been. — Yours faithfully, WALTER ECCLESTON*

---

The eleventh of June 1925. Fourteen months before the date of the instrument found in the despatch-box.

He returned to the desk and laid all three documents in a row: the executed first codicil, the propounded second codicil, exhibit fourteen. The recital said *and*. The executed text said *or*. The letter — in Walter Eccleston's hand, in the file, written in June of 1925 — said *and*.

He stood for a moment, looking at the three documents.

---

He gathered the exhibit, replaced the first codicil in its wrapper, and returned the deed-box to the second shelf. Then he came back upstairs and sat at the desk.

He drew a sheet from the writing pad.

---

*The recital of the second codicil (R3, exhibit 2) cites the first codicil as giving the residue 'unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely.' The executed instrument (R2, exhibit 1) says 'or her issue.' The variance is between R2 and R3's recital. A.P., 18.vii.27.*

---

He set the sheet in the working file. He noted the date. The eighteenth of July. Eighty-eight days.

He sat at the desk for a while: the square outside; the office around him; somewhere below, the strong-room register in Garside's hand on its shelf.

Then he took out a fresh sheet of paper and began to write the addition to the brief.

# Solemn Form

He had the deed-box under his arm by nine. He had been awake at half past three, had read through the authorship section of the brief by the bedside lamp, found no errors in it, and put it face-down on the desk. He did not sleep again until after five. The walk from the hotel to the Royal Courts of Justice was twenty minutes along the Strand, and the October morning was cold enough that he was glad of it — the room had been warm and small, and he had done everything in it that could be done.

The Royal Courts of Justice stood at the eastern end of the Strand — the particular Victorian Gothic of the State announcing its intentions in stone and pinnacles — and it was the third time Prescott had been inside it on Garside & Prescott business, the first two being a chambers meeting and a matter that had settled before argument and been no business of the court at all. The building had not diminished in the interval. He crossed the forecourt with the deed-box and found the corridor for the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division, which already held the morning's population of barristers in gowns, their solicitors at their elbows, each pair apart from the next with the composed patience of people who do this regularly and have learned that patience is part of the work. The smell of the place was distinctive — old stone, varnished wood, coal smoke from the court fires working behind closed doors — the smell of a building that has held the same proceedings for fifty years and taken the character of them into its walls.

Their counsel found him before ten. Keane was a tall man of about forty-five, considered in manner, who had acknowledged the brief in August with a letter of three sentences and who had since written twice with questions about the exclusion section. He had the unhurried confidence of a man who has read the brief and finds it sufficient. He shook Prescott's hand and asked whether the originals were in the deed-box.

Prescott confirmed they were.

They stood together in the corridor while it filled further. The courtroom doors had not yet opened; through the gap where a latch had not quite caught, Prescott could see the brass rail of the witness box and the bench above it, both empty.

---

Counsel for the defendant came across to them at ten minutes to ten. His name was Ardern, and Prescott knew from the action papers that he had been at the bar for twenty-five years. He was a shorter man, compact, who moved through the corridor with the ease of long practice.

The request was framed correctly. Whether the plaintiff's solicitor might permit the defendant a few minutes to examine the executed original of the first codicil, before the judge took his seat — purely for the purposes of instruction, Ardern said, and Prescott's side would retain custody throughout. It was said without the tone of a man asking a favour, and without the tone of a man who expected to be refused.

Keane looked at Prescott, briefly, because it was Prescott's deed-box.

Prescott set it on the bench beside him and opened the lid. The Eccleston papers were arranged as he had laid them in Preston the week before: the custody list on top, the originals beneath in exhibit order. He lifted the custody list, and beneath it, in a folded envelope marked in his own hand — *R2. First Codicil (executed original)* — was the instrument that had been in the strong-room since the fifteenth of March 1924.

He handed the envelope to Ardern without speaking.

---

Walter Eccleston was standing eight or ten feet away, beside a young man from Thurston & Marsh that Prescott did not recognise. He had come into the building while Prescott and Keane were talking; Prescott had noted his arrival at the edge of his attention without looking at him directly. He looked at him now. Walter was watching Ardern cross the corridor with the envelope.

Ardern held the envelope out. Walter took it. He opened it carefully — he was a careful man — and drew out the codicil. Rag paper, folded twice, typewritten, a single page. He unfolded it and began to read.

He read it the way a man reads a document he expects to confirm what he knows: quickly, his eyes moving across the type.

And then he slowed.

He went back a line, read it again; went back further; came to rest at a particular point in the instrument and stayed. He read it again from that point, deliberately, his head very slightly inclined. Then he read it a third time and was quite still.

He was fifty or thereabouts, broad-shouldered, a man whose presence had always been larger than his physical size. He was not large now. He held the instrument and stood without moving, and something in the set of his shoulders was different from a moment before, though Prescott could not have named precisely what.

---

Prescott watched and did not speak. He did not need to read the instrument alongside Walter to know which words he had reached.

Walter had held the clause in the wrong form since March 1924 — *and*, where the executed text said *or* — because Josiah had told him what the codicil provided in his own words, and Walter had taken Josiah's words and made them his own. He had put them in writing to his bank manager in June 1925. He had put them into the instrument he had typed in the six days the despatch-box was at the mill. He had repeated them, with some generosity, to two children in a parlour on Bank Parade. He had never been in a room with the executed text before this moment. He had been wrong since March 1924 and had not known it.

Prescott kept his face composed and his hands at his sides. There was nothing to say.

After some moments, Walter spoke briefly to Ardern — low, inaudible at the distance. Ardern put a hand once on Walter's arm, professional and brief, and withdrew with him down the corridor. Two men, twenty feet away, a conference too quiet to follow.

Keane stood beside Prescott and did not speak, which was correct.

A barrister passed between them on his way to another court, acknowledged Keane with a nod, and moved on.

Three minutes, or a little more.

When Ardern returned, his manner was composed in the way of a man who has instructions he does not enjoy executing but who will execute them precisely.

"My client is not in a position to proceed," he said. "I am instructed to apply for a withdrawal of the claim."

---

The matter came before the judge at a quarter past ten: the application to withdraw; Keane's assent on behalf of the plaintiff in solemn form; the brief exchange of counsel establishing the disposition of the instruments and the question of costs. The judge was a spare man of about sixty with a dry manner and a habit of precise speech who had clearly had the brief — his questions were exact — and who received the application without visible surprise.

The second codicil had not been proved; accordingly it was not to be admitted to probate. The instruments of 1919 and 1924 stood. Letters of administration with the will annexed would be sought in due course through the Principal Registry.

The handwriting evidence: two opinions, directly irreconcilable — one finding the signature genuine, one finding it not. The judge noted that the decision had not rested on either. He added one observation, speaking to the courtroom at large rather than to either set of counsel: that in cases of this kind the most reliable witnesses were frequently the most ordinary — a letter-book entry, a register note, a word in a recital — because ordinary documents do not accommodate themselves to what comes after. He said it in the same flat tone he had used throughout, and moved to the costs.

The costs were to be paid by the defendant. Garside & Prescott, which had carried the action at its own risk from the caveat onward, would recover them in full.

---

By eleven the corridor was nearly empty. The matter had gone quickly — as matters go quickly, Prescott knew, once the decision has been made before it reaches the court.

Keane gave him his hand and said that it had been well conducted. That was the right amount to say. Prescott thanked him, and they parted.

He opened the deed-box and replaced the first codicil, in its envelope, in its place in the exhibit order. He noted the custody on the list: *R2. Returned from use. RCJ, 14 Oct. 1927. A.P.* He closed the lid.

He would telephone Mr. Booth from the hotel before midday. He would write to Edgar Fairhurst this afternoon.

He picked up the deed-box and walked toward the entrance.

# Chapter 1 — The Strong-Room

The deed box was on the table when Prescott arrived: black painted steel, "ECCLESTON" lettered in white on the lid, the label in Garside's copper-plate facing up across the room. Garside was at the far end of the table with his hat still on, which meant he had not been in from the strong-room long.

"Dead yesterday evening," Garside said. "The Hall sent a telegram."

Josiah Eccleston had been a client of the firm since before Prescott came into articles. Cotton spinner, magistrate, owner of the Hall at Ribchester and the Vale Mill above the village — a man whose every instrument from will to conveyance had come through this office in the forty years since Garside first took his instructions. Prescott had known him first as a name in the ledger, and later, from the will itself onwards, as a man who shook hands as though a contract were meant by it. He had been eighty-one years old. He had died, as far as anyone knew without disorder, on a Tuesday evening in October, at the Hall.

The coal fire was going. Outside on the square the October light was doing what it did.

Garside set his hat down and opened the deed box.

The will was first: folded twice on cream paper, "WILL — J. ECCLESTON — 3 JUNE 1919" on the outside. Garside opened it, turned to the fourth clause, and read:

> I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my nephew Walter Eccleston of Vale Mill House Ribchester absolutely and I appoint the said Walter Eccleston sole executor of this my will.

Prescott noted the date and the name and set his pen down.

Garside folded the will and reached into the box. The codicil was underneath: same cream paper, "CODICIL — J. ECCLESTON — 15 MARCH 1924" on the outside fold, shorter by half. He opened it.

"After the reconciliation," he said, more to himself than to Prescott. He read:

> I REVOKE clause 4 of my said will and IN PLACE THEREOF I GIVE DEVISE AND BEQUEATH all the residue of my estate both real and personal whatsoever and wheresoever unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely AND IN ALL OTHER RESPECTS I confirm my said will.

The coal shifted behind the grate. Prescott wrote down the date — fifteen March nineteen-twenty-four — and the name and address, and waited.

"Clause four revoked entire," Garside said. "Gift and executorship both — he intended a complete revision. There is, at present, no executor." He set the codicil alongside the will. "Section thirty-three of the Wills Act does nothing for a niece against lapse. She is collateral, not a descendant. He used the substitutional form accordingly."

Margaret Fairhurst. Prescott had known her name from the codicil's making two years before, and had noted the memorandum in the file when she died: May 1925, a year and a half before Josiah. Her issue were her two children — Nora, nineteen, and George, sixteen — living with their father at the Bank Parade address named in the instrument. Edgar Fairhurst. A schoolmaster.

"Both children are minors," Prescott said. "Majority is twenty-one."

"Letters of administration with the will annexed," Garside said. "To the father as guardian, if the instruments stand."

Walter Eccleston had managed the mill for fifteen years on the expectation of this estate. Prescott knew the mill was mortgaged — the kind of information that accumulated in a solicitor's knowledge without being entered in any single place.

He took up the strong-room register from beside the box.

The register was a cloth-bound ledger: date column on the left, document described in the centre, clerk's signature at the right margin. Garside had maintained it in his own hand since 1906; Prescott had added entries as occasion required, in his own narrower hand, the two scripts sharing the same columns for two decades. He opened to the current year and ran down the September entries.

September the nineteenth. The entry was Garside's:

*First codicil, J. Eccleston — fetched from strong-room. Reading at Eccleston Hall at testator's request. Present: H.G., A.P., W. Eccleston, two members of the household. Instrument read entire. Returned same day. H.G.*

Prescott had been at that reading. He had carried the deed-box into the drawing room at the Hall and stood there while Garside read the codicil from first word to last — date and all — to Josiah, who was in his chair and had been failing since August. Walter had been there, and the two women from the household, and Josiah's man beside the door. Josiah had wanted no surprises.

Walter Eccleston had stood beside the fireplace with his arms at his sides, listening.

Prescott turned to the working correspondence at the back of the file. The papers from the previous week were loosely arranged: the telegram from the Hall, a draft letter of condolence, and behind them his own attendance note from the despatch-box inventory.

He had made the note at the Hall table on the afternoon of the inventory, while Walter stood by. The box had been opened on the dining-room table and Prescott had listed each item as it was removed: three insurance policies, title deeds to the Hall, unsigned drafts of two rental agreements, a letter from the bank dated 1923, three letters tied in blue ribbon, an unsigned copy of the will.

No codicil.

He read through the list a second time and found the same. He clipped the note to the front of the file.

Garside restored the will and the codicil to the deed box and carried it back to the strong-room himself — he always carried the Eccleston box himself — and Prescott heard the iron door of the vault close below, and the latch engage. A minute later Garside came back up without the box and stood in the doorway.

"Two instruments," Prescott said. "The will and the first codicil. The estate belongs to the Fairhurst children if the instruments stand. There is no executor, and there was no second codicil in the despatch-box." He looked at his notes. "I should write to Thurston and Marsh today, about proving the will in proper form. And we must write to Bank Parade."

"Yes," Garside said. He sat down and took up his pen.

The file was in order: the will of the third of June nineteen-nineteen, the codicil of the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four, the strong-room register exact about both. What Walter Eccleston would make of those terms was a question the record had not yet been required to answer.
