# The File

The papers from the Hall came by registered post on the twenty-second, packed in a cardboard box with the administrator's covering note on top: one pocket diary, 1926; one bundle of correspondence, inward and outward, January to October; one set of household accounts. Prescott had not requested the accounts.

It was two hundred and fifty-seven days to the hearing.

He lifted the diary out first. Small, leather-covered, a brass clasp stiff from disuse — the kind sold in any stationer's, a shilling and sixpence, renewed each year without much deliberation. Josiah Eccleston's name was written inside the front cover in a hand that was still his own but smaller, and somewhat less firm, than the hand in the instruments in the strong-room.

He opened it to the first of January and began.

The entries were sparse from the start. January: a mill appointment on the eighth — the subject noted (looms on short time; questions about the dye-house roof), Walter's name not in it. February: another mill appointment; a doctor's visit on the nineteenth — Dr. Cullis, two words only, suggesting something routine; and a letter acknowledged from a cousin in Harrogate. March: a note from the magistrates' clerk, one of Josiah's cases forwarded to a colleague in Clitheroe. The entry had the air of a letter that had not been unexpected, and had not been unwelcome.

The mill appointments grew fewer in spring. The last was on the fourteenth of May: *W.E. — mill — morning.* Four words. After that, nothing about the mill.

The entries became sparser and more domestic. Beckett here and there — the steward, the same name as in the strong-room register. A note about the south field. The insurance broker.

Prescott turned to August.

The fourteenth was a Saturday. The entry read: *Hot again. Beckett here this afternoon — the south field question — resolved.* And below, in a slightly smaller hand: *Neck troubling me this morning.*

That was the last entry. After it: blank pages, clean, through September and October and the remainder of the year.

Prescott read the entry a second time. It was the record of an ordinary day: no appointment beyond Beckett, no instrument made or directed, no reference to any testamentary act. A diary did not prove a negative. But it was a record, and the record said nothing.

---

He set the diary aside and lifted the correspondence bundle.

The administrator had divided it — formal on the left, household on the right. Prescott worked through the formal side first. Three letters to and from Garside & Prescott, all already in the firm's letter-book and accounted for there. A letter from a Ribchester solicitor on a tenancy matter. Two from the estate's insurance brokers. Nothing to or from Thurston & Marsh; nothing from any other firm on any question touching the will or the codicil; nothing that had not already been known from the letter-book side.

The household side he read more quickly. Family correspondence; replies to local matters; the magistrates' clerk again. He came, near the bottom of the right-hand bundle, to a letter in Josiah's hand — but a different hand from the instruments: softer, unguarded, the hand of a man writing to someone he was glad to write to. Addressed to Miss Nora Fairhurst, Bank Parade, Preston. Dated the third of April, 1926.

He read it carefully. Not long — three-quarters of a page, a correction in the second paragraph, a postscript about a book he had promised to send. It said nothing about the estate's disposition, nothing about instruments or codicils. But near the end Josiah had written:

*I am very glad we have the matter settled between us, and I mean it to stay settled. Your mother knew it. You know it. That is what I wished.*

He made a note of the letter and set it to one side for the exhibits bundle.

---

He had read the instrument register in full in December, and knew what it contained. He took it from the strong-room now for the same reason he had written the letter-book note the previous week: to fix the finding as a record item. He ran his eye down the Eccleston column from 1884 to the end.

The original lease of Vale Mill, 1884. A mortgage, 1889, discharged 1892. The deed of gift of the Ribchester farmland, 1903. The lease extension of 1908. The will, third of June 1919. And, in Garside's invariable hand, the last entry in the column: *First Codicil — J. Eccleston dec. — 15 March 1924.*

Nothing after it. Forty years of instruments for one estate, and then a line. He closed the register and returned it to the strong-room.

---

When he came back to the table, there was one more item in the bundle — flat at the bottom, below the register extracts and the attending notes, easy to miss. A letter in Garside's hand, on plain notepaper rather than the firm's standard paper. Dated the fourteenth of March, 1924.

He sat down and read it.

Three sentences. The codicil was enclosed, properly engrossed and ready for execution; Mr. Eccleston would need to sign it in the presence of two witnesses, both present together at the same time, neither of whom took any benefit under the instrument; Garside would attend at the Hall if preferred, or if Mr. Eccleston wished to arrange the witnesses himself, the office would be glad to receive the executed original at his convenience.

Three sentences, and each one exact. The witness requirement stated in full for a man who had been signing instruments since 1884 and had not required instruction in forty years. The note about the executed original — not a request but an offer, *the office would be glad to receive it*, as if Garside had thought about the document's custody before the letter left his desk.

It had been written for the record. Not for Josiah.

Prescott held it a moment, then set it with the exhibits.

The whole file had that quality. Each letter a fraction more precise than the matter strictly required; each attendance note kept at the same level whether the occasion was routine or not; the register built to a standard that had no source in any statute or practice requirement, but had its source entirely in the man who had built it. The file was the work of a man who had never distinguished between what required a record and what deserved one.

And the file was going to prove a forgery.

---

He wrote the working note in the hand he used for formal file items, and read it back once before he dated it.

*No private record or correspondence contains any reference to any intention to revoke or alter the first codicil after its execution in March 1924. No instrument in the firm's register was made in the name of Josiah Eccleston after that date. The survey of instruments is complete: every instrument made by Josiah Eccleston for a period of forty years was made through the firm of Garside & Prescott, and the last was the first codicil.*

He dated it the twenty-seventh of January, 1927, and placed it at the front of the working file.

---

The strong-room smelled as it always did: clean paper, iron shelves, the dry compound of ink aged past sharpness into something denser and quieter. He set the register in its place, checked the order of the cabinet, and closed the door. The lock turned with its usual certainty.

He turned off the lamp and went out into Winckley Square, and home.

# The Gazette

Mr. Booth had the list on Prescott's desk by nine o'clock on Monday morning: forty-three firms in the county, alphabetical, addresses verified against the current Law Society directory. Two columns on the right — one for the date the letter went, one for the date of reply.

"I've left out the two Clitheroe firms," Booth said. "They're not in the main directory, but they practise. And Rawlinson and Peel have a Garstang office that acts for several valley estates."

"Add them."

"That brings it to forty-six."

Prescott had been working on the notice since the previous week. The difficulty was scope — narrow it too much and a firm might read itself out of the question on a technicality; broaden it too much and the replies would come back freighted with qualifications that required letters in return. The final text, as Booth read it back, was:

*Any solicitor who has acted for, or received instructions from, the late Josiah Eccleston of Eccleston Hall, Ribchester, in connection with any testamentary instrument, codicil, or revocation of any testamentary instrument, at any time after March 1924, is invited to communicate with Garside & Prescott, Solicitors, Winckley Square, Preston.*

Booth suggested removing the comma after the second *instrument*. Prescott agreed. The notice went to the Gazette offices by the afternoon post.

The circular letters went out on Thursday, the third of February: forty-six letters on the firm's headed paper, each signed by Prescott. He had added a last paragraph asking each firm to reply even if its answer was entirely negative, so that the record of the canvass would be complete on every name.

---

The first replies arrived the following week. Most were brief to the point of curtness: *We have no file for the name Eccleston and have received no instructions from any person of that name in connection with any testamentary matter.* Four in the first post; six on Thursday; five more by the end of the week. Booth ticked them off the list.

By the end of the second week there were eighteen replies. One of them required a note. A Lancaster office had a 1919 file — a conveyance on which they had acted for the other party, in a matter entirely unrelated to the estate and that would have been immaterial even if it had concerned Josiah Eccleston directly. Prescott wrote the explanation in the margin and set it with the irrelevants.

He was looking, throughout, for the exception: the firm that answered with care, saying it had a file and that the matter was not without complication, and that its senior partner would be glad to speak with Prescott at his convenience. None of them was the exception.

Booth managed the list from his own desk — ticking each name, noting the date, setting aside those that required a letter in reply. He did not need to be told what to do with any of them. By the third week, thirty-one had replied; the rate of replies eased. Two in a post, then one, then a gap of a day.

---

By mid-February, thirty-one firms had replied and fifteen had not.

Two hundred and thirty-five days to the hearing.

The remaining fifteen would answer in their own time.

---

The Gazette produced nothing.

By the time the last circular reply had come in, the advertisement had been running for three weeks and no response had appeared in its column. Prescott had not expected one. A solicitor who had taken testamentary instructions from a man of Josiah Eccleston's standing, and had subsequently seen his name in the circular letter — the address, the dates, the explicit request for a reply even if negative — would not have waited for the Gazette to prompt him. He would have answered the letter. Prescott made a note of the date and the absence and placed it in the file.

---

The last expected reply arrived on the twenty-fourth of February.

A Blackburn firm Prescott did not know by name — not in any county matter he could place, not in the principal directories he consulted — confirmed in two sentences that they held no file for Josiah Eccleston and had received no instructions from him in connection with any testamentary question. The letter was in the proper form.

He took Booth's list from the desk. Forty-six names; forty-six ticks in the reply column.

"That's the last," he said.

Booth looked across from his side of the room. "I held back the second Clitheroe firm for two or three days," he said. "Their reply came in on Friday. I thought you should see the Blackburn letter first, in case there was anything in it."

The second Clitheroe firm's reply was on Booth's desk — two sentences, no file, no instructions — and Prescott read it and set it with the others.

He pulled the file toward him and began to write.

---

*The London Gazette advertisement, placed the week of the 3rd February 1927, produced no response of any kind. Circular letters were addressed to every firm of solicitors known to practise in the county of Lancaster — forty-six firms in all, including three valley offices not listed in the principal directory — and every firm has now replied. The substance of the replies, taken together, is as follows: no firm in the county was instructed by the late Mr. Josiah Eccleston, or by any person acting or purporting to act on his behalf, to draw any testamentary instrument, codicil, or revocation of any testamentary instrument at any time after the execution of the first codicil dated the 15th March 1924. No firm received any communication from Mr. Eccleston touching his testamentary affairs after that date. The canvass is complete; the result is negative in every case.*

He dated it the twenty-fourth of February, 1927, and placed it at the front of the file.

---

Forty-six firms, and every one of them kept its files. Most of them kept their files to the level that the matter required; some kept them to a level somewhat above it — the standard Prescott had grown up in, which supposed that you could not always know, at the time you were building the record, exactly what the record would later be required to show. On the question of Josiah Eccleston's testamentary affairs after March 1924, all forty-six were agreed: nothing. No instruction received, no instrument drawn, no file opened.

The cover story required a solicitor who had taken instructions for a codicil in the summer of 1926, drawn the instrument, overseen its execution, and subsequently vanished from the professional record of the county without a file entry, a letter-book carbon, a bill rendered or paid, or a reply to the circular letter when the whole county had been invited to write. There was no such solicitor.

The profession had not done this. The door was locked.

# The Sale Contract

Booth had left the administrator's second parcel on the side of the desk — not quite at the centre and not at the edge, as he always placed things he considered likely to be unwelcome, as if the middle distance were the appropriate location for something he had no wish to be asked about. The brown paper was addressed to Prescott in Hadfield's careful hand, the knot tied in the practised way of a man who had been managing documents for thirty years and tied them the same way every time.

Prescott opened it after Booth had gone upstairs to the copying room. Four items: the mortgage instrument, the conditional sale contract, a bundle of banking correspondence bound in red tape, and the administrator's monthly account for March. He set them in order of origin — mortgage oldest, monthly account most recent — and began at the beginning.

---

The mortgage had been Garside's matter from the first. The instrument number at the head of the page was in his hand — the clean, deliberate numerals he had used for every instrument through this office since the year he established the register, each digit made the same way across three decades of files — and the attestation clause below the covenants was set in the form Garside had preferred, the signature block indented a full measure from the covenant text and the witness clause arranged above it in a single clean sentence. Eight thousand five hundred pounds secured on the mill's plant and machinery and its goodwill, held by the County Bank in Blackburn at four and a half per cent, with the interest payable at each of the quarter-days in the year. The mortgage was made in the spring of 1921, when the mill had needed capital for plant renewal and Josiah had put up the security against the estate's credit rather than draw from his own reserves. The principal obligation was the estate's, not Walter's in his personal capacity, which was a distinction that mattered for the title but not for the question of who had depended on the estate's solvency to hold his position together.

Hadfield's February letter, already in the file, had confirmed that the most recent two quarter-days' interest had been met from the estate's liquid capital rather than from the mill's operating income. The mill's operating income had been insufficient to service the debt. The principal sat where it had sat since 1921: untouched, the whole sum outstanding, waiting on the sale. Under the conditional contract, the purchaser was taking the estate subject to the mortgage, with discharge from the proceeds of completion forming part of the closing transaction. If the sale completed.

---

The sale contract was a Manchester firm's work, commercial property men, and they had drafted it with the methodical confidence of solicitors who expected no difficulty with the condition they were inserting. Prescott read it through again from the recitals, which described the vendor's title by reference to a grant of representation that had not yet issued and that would not issue until the action was resolved. The condition was in clause twenty-four.

*Completion of this Agreement is in all respects conditional upon the vendor producing a grant of representation establishing his title to the said estate and hereditaments.*

Two memoranda of extension were clipped behind the contract: the first had been agreed in January, granting eight further weeks; the second was dated the fifteenth of March and granted eight more. A note from Thurston & Marsh to the purchaser's solicitors accompanied the second memorandum, advising that a further extension was not anticipated. The purchaser had been generous twice. Whatever patience had been available appeared to have been used.

Without the grant, the contract could not complete. Without the action being resolved — in one direction or the other — the grant could not issue. The administrator could collect the estate's income and pay its debts, but could not distribute or convey. The mill sat in this position as it sat in every other: the same short-time working, the same wage bill, the same mortgage interest being drawn from capital that was not being replenished. The purchaser's patience ran in one direction. The estate's capital ran in the other. The action ran between them.

---

The bundle of banking correspondence was nine letters from Walter Eccleston to his bank manager, Mr. Holt, running from the spring of 1924 through to January 1927. Five replies from Holt were tucked into the appropriate envelopes; four letters had no reply, or none that had been preserved. Prescott untied the red tape and set the letters in sequence.

The picture was consistent across three years — a record of how a man had explained his position to himself and to others under increasing pressure. The early letters explained. The codicil was a temporary arrangement, made in a soft mood by an old man who had spoken since of putting the matter right. The mill was carrying a mortgage, but mills carried mortgages; that was not peculiar to this mill. Walter's expectations were what they had always been, which was to say that he expected Josiah to do what Josiah had assured him he intended to do. The arrangement would not stand; it had not stood in any practical sense; the inheritance would come through as it had always been understood that it would.

Holt's replies grew shorter. By early 1926 he had begun asking questions about security. By the end of 1926 his replies were two lines where they had once been half a page, and they asked for answers Walter had already given once and could only give again. Walter gave them again, in longer versions of the same assurance: the estate would come through, the grant would follow, the bank should be patient.

Among the nine letters was one dated the eleventh of June 1925, written after Holt had put the security question to him directly. Prescott placed it on the desk.

---

*Dear Mr. Holt, — You ask what further security I can offer beyond the mortgage. My uncle has made a codicil, as I told you, in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst and her issue, but I am assured the arrangement will not stand; he made it in a soft mood and has spoken since of putting it right. My expectations are otherwise what they have always been. — Yours faithfully, WALTER ECCLESTON*

---

He clipped it in sequence with the rest of the letters and opened Hadfield's March account.

---

The March figures were not an improvement on February's. Gross income from the mill was down sixteen pounds on the previous month; the wage bill was met; the March quarter-day on the mortgage interest had been paid from the estate's capital rather than its earnings, the same as the two quarter-days before it. The net loss against projected income was a little over three hundred pounds, and Hadfield's estimate of reserves — calculated on his February assumptions and not revised — showed approximately three months of liquidity remaining at the current rate of depletion. He noted this without recommendation. What happened after the estate's capital was exhausted was not a question he was authorised to answer from his position, and Prescott had no mechanism to answer it from his.

---

Prescott assembled the exhibits. The mortgage instrument first — the earliest document, the foundation of the financial position. The sale contract, with the two extension memoranda clipped behind it and the Thurston & Marsh note behind those. The nine letters from Walter to Holt, in date order, with Holt's five replies where they belonged. Hadfield's monthly account at the back, the most recent piece of the record.

He clipped the bundle and noted the reference on the cover sheet. One hundred and eighty-five days to the hearing; he had written the figure that morning, and it sat in the margin of his working notes where he had put it, the same way the earlier figures sat in earlier margins, each one smaller than the one before it.

Context was not proof. Motive explained the forgery; it did not establish that the forgery had been made, or by whom, or how. The proof was in the text of the second codicil and in the text it recited, and the argument that would be built from those two texts had not yet been assembled into the brief. It was the most work still remaining.

He stacked the financial exhibits and set the brief to one side.

# The Witnesses

> SIGNED by the said JOSIAH ECCLESTON as and for his last codicil in the presence of us both
> present at the same time who at his request in his presence and in the presence of each other
> have hereunto subscribed our names as witnesses:
>
> THOMAS BIRCH, Carrier, of Ribchester in the County of Lancaster.
>
> FREDERICK HALLETT, Gardener, of near Salesbury in the County of Lancaster.

Both men were in the instrument index.

The index was a bound ledger, red boards worn soft at the corners, in Garside's hand from its first
entry in 1906 to the last he had made before the autumn. It recorded witness by name, trade, address,
instrument number, and date — so that finding any given specimen was a question of reading a column
and walking to a shelf. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester: four entries, the earliest in 1912, the
latest in March 1921. Frederick Hallett, gardener, near Salesbury: one entry, the same March 1921
instrument.

Prescott noted the instrument numbers and wrote to the Ribchester registrar that afternoon. He
instructed Booth to pull both instruments from the file.

---

The registrar's reply arrived four days later. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester, had died on the
twenty-eighth of September 1926. The cause given was influenza. Prescott wrote by return for a
certified copy of the death certificate, and it came within the week.

He opened his attendance book and wrote the date.

The instruments Booth had found carried Birch's signature on both: the deed of cottage tenancy from
November 1914 and the property schedule from March 1921. The 1914 hand was angular and firm at the
ascenders; by 1921 it had settled, the loop of the g broader, the B somewhat taller. Consistent with
itself across seven years. Prescott had been present at the 1921 signing. He packaged both originals
with a covering note and posted them to Croft in Manchester, together with a photographic copy of the
attestation page of the propounded codicil.

The March 1921 property schedule bore one further signature as witness, below Birch's: Hallett's hand,
shorter in body, the letters more angled, a single specimen. He sent it to Croft under a second cover.

---

He had written to Atkinson at Ribchester on the same day as the registrar — Atkinson whose practice
was agricultural conveyancing and the kind of local inquiry that required knowing the farms east of
Langridge Moor.

Atkinson's reply took nine days and ran to two pages. Hallett had worked the previous spring and
summer for a farmer named Ogden on the Salesbury road — kitchen garden and light farmwork. In the
first days of October 1926, Hallett had given notice. He had left no address with Ogden, none with
any neighbour Atkinson could find, none with the post office, which had handled one redirected letter
and could not say where it had gone. Atkinson had then made inquiry at the shipping offices in Preston
and had found that in the second week of October 1926 a Frederick Hallett of Ribchester had taken
an assisted passage from Liverpool to Quebec aboard the *SS Aurania*.

No fixed address in Canada.

Prescott added the departure date to his attendance book below the first entry. Then the next two:
the last week of October, Josiah's death; the first days of November, the despatch-box opened with
Prescott present, no codicil in it. Six days at the mill. The four dates made a column and described
a shape, and the shape described a thing, and he drew his pen through the space where that thing
would have been written, because the brief was not a place for what was not evidence.

---

Croft's two reports arrived in the same cover, their dates of composition ten days apart. They were
written in the same form.

> *In the matter of the Estate of Josiah Eccleston, deceased. I have examined the attestation
> signature attributed to THOMAS BIRCH on a photographic copy of the propounded codicil and
> compared it with the two authenticated specimens submitted: the cottage tenancy deed of November
> 1914 and the property schedule of March 1921, both originals. The signature on the propounded
> instrument is consistent with both specimens in general formation, pen pressure, and the
> development that seven years' interval between specimens would naturally produce. Given that my
> comparison rests upon a photographic copy of the propounded instrument rather than the original,
> and that two authenticated specimens only are available, I am not in a position to offer a
> positive identification. I cannot exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction executed from
> comparison material of comparable quality to that submitted to me. — H. Croft, Document
> Examiner.*

The second report came in the same register. The Hallett attestation, compared against the single
1921 specimen, was consistent in general formation and character; a single specimen did not establish
the full range of a hand; Croft was unable to form a view on natural variation or development across
the intervening period; he was not in a position to offer a positive identification and could not
exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction.

He put both reports in the file.

---

There was a practical consequence to Hallett being alive rather than dead, which was that a commission
might be applied for. If the Probate Division granted it, a judicial officer in Canada would take
Hallett's evidence on the question of due execution — if Hallett could be located. Prescott wrote to
Mitchell in London with the full position: the witness's identity; his last confirmed employment;
his departure from Ribchester in the first days of October 1926 and his assisted passage aboard the
*Aurania*; Atkinson's inquiries and their result; the confirmed absence of any traceable address.
Mitchell's reply came within the week. The power to issue a commission existed; the difficulty was
personal service, which required an address, which was not available; the commission, if granted,
would take time the calendar did not have. Nevertheless Mitchell recommended applying, disclosing
the difficulty in full.

Prescott agreed, and Mitchell filed the application in the last week of April.

One hundred and seventy-two days to the hearing. The draft of the application was in the file —
the instrument, the witness's identity and last known whereabouts, the absence of a fixed address
in Canada, the submission that his evidence on due execution could not otherwise be obtained. It
was a well-drawn piece of work.

He noted the date of filing in the margin of his attendance book and placed the file on Booth's
tray for the shelf.

# The Commission

The letter from Mitchell came by the first post on Tuesday. Booth brought it up from the letter-rack and set it on the desk above the Hadfield figures Prescott had been working through — London postmark, Mitchell's own hand on the envelope — and Prescott opened it with the small bronze knife he kept for correspondence, which had been Garside's.

The refusal was in the first paragraph.

---

*The court has declined to issue the commission to examine Mr. Frederick Hallett. The ground stated is that the applicant has been unable to supply a fixed address in Canada at which the commission could be served, and the court will not issue a commission that cannot be executed. A fresh application would require a verified address. The decision is not appealable on these facts.*

---

He read it a second time. He set it on the desk.

He rose and walked to the window. The square below was fully in leaf — the lime trees in front of the courthouse had come on considerably in the past fortnight — and a postman was working along the opposite pavement at a pace that did not suggest urgency. A woman was crossing below with a basket, looking at nothing in particular. He stood at the window and allowed the thing to settle.

The witnesses were done. Both of them, from both directions: Birch was dead, and his death was in the registrar's certificate; Hallett had gone to Canada without an address, and the court could not reach him there on the available materials. Mitchell had submitted the application with the address difficulty disclosed in full — there had been no other way to proceed with credit — and the court had done what courts did when the mechanism of service did not exist. Four weeks had passed from the application in the last week of April to this Tuesday in May: four weeks that could not be recovered. There had been a hundred and seventy-two days on the clock when Mitchell had filed; there were a hundred and forty now. The difference was the commission application, entirely.

A man who sat down immediately had not quite finished admitting the thing to himself. He stood a while longer at the window and admitted it.

The attestation was permanently closed, from every direction that involved a living witness. Neither man could now be examined, whether to break the second codicil's due execution or to support it. The defence's case rested on the silence of the witnesses: unassailable, because nobody living could speak to what had or had not happened in August 1926 in the presence of two men who were, respectively, dead and somewhere in Canada. Prescott's side was in the same position, on the other face of the same coin — neither attestation could be confirmed or broken, because neither attester could be reached. It was not a defeat in any sense the brief could name; it was a closed door, and the brief had not been built on this door. But there was a difference between choosing not to lean on a route and having it closed behind you.

There was a shape to the situation, however.

Six weeks ago, after entering the four-date column in the attendance book — Birch dead on the twenty-eighth of September, Hallett gone in the second week of October, Josiah dead in the third week, the despatch-box inventoried in early November — he had drawn his pen through the space where the inference would have gone. He returned to that space now. The two witnesses named on the second codicil had been chosen from among the men who had genuinely witnessed Josiah's instruments in years past: men in Garside's index, men whose authentic signatures were therefore on file, men against whose known hands Croft could take a fair comparison. Both had become unavailable in the same autumn, within days of each other. Both had been newly unavailable — one dead, one gone — in the weeks before the despatch-box stood six days at the mill in October.

A document executed in August, before the influenza had run its course, before the passage to Quebec, would have named them without foreknowledge that either would be gone.

Unless someone had composed it afterward, and dated it to August.

He did not write this in the attendance book. He had already drawn a pen through it once, and that had been right: a thought crossed out does not become evidence by revival. What it might become — with authorship established on independent grounds and each innocent explanation foreclosed by document rather than argument — was something counsel could set before the court in the proper order. Not today. In due course.

He returned to the desk and drew a sheet of paper from the drawer.

He wrote to Mitchell. The commission had failed; the witness avenue was definitively closed; they were to proceed on the footing that the case must be made on the typewriter evidence and the text. He asked Mitchell to confirm his understanding of the position and to advise on what form the text argument should take in the brief — what it would be required to establish, and in what sequence it would need to be put. He noted the calendar: a hundred and forty days to the hearing; the brief must be complete within eight weeks at the outside.

He read the letter through and made one correction: *are proceeding* to *must proceed*. He sealed it and carried it through to Booth's tray.

"Midday post," he said.

Booth looked up from the letter-book. "Right," he said, and returned to it.

The commission letter went into the file in its correct position: behind the application, ahead of Mitchell's April note. Prescott clipped the folder and squared it to the left of the desk. The file grew in the way files grew when a proceeding was properly kept — one document at a time, each in its right place, the record of everything attempted and everything concluded, the corridor of closed doors. A solicitor who left an avenue unexamined in solemn form proceedings could not afterward explain himself, which was why the application had been made, and why the commission letter was now in the file; both reasons remained sound. The avenue had been examined. The result was in the record.

What remained was the text.

A hundred and forty days. He wrote the figure in the margin of Mitchell's letter before filing it.

He took the Hadfield figures from the desk and settled back to the columns he had been working through when the post came in.

# Solemn Form

He had the deed-box under his arm by nine. He had been awake at half past three, had read through the authorship section of the brief by the bedside lamp, found no errors in it, and put it face-down on the desk. He did not sleep again until after five. The walk from the hotel to the Royal Courts of Justice was twenty minutes along the Strand, and the October morning was cold enough that he was glad of it — the room had been warm and small, and he had done everything in it that could be done.

The Royal Courts of Justice stood at the eastern end of the Strand — the particular Victorian Gothic of the State announcing its intentions in stone and pinnacles — and it was the third time Prescott had been inside it on Garside & Prescott business, the first two being a chambers meeting and a matter that had settled before argument and been no business of the court at all. The building had not diminished in the interval. He crossed the forecourt with the deed-box and found the corridor for the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division, which already held the morning's population of barristers in gowns, their solicitors at their elbows, each pair apart from the next with the composed patience of people who do this regularly and have learned that patience is part of the work. The smell of the place was distinctive — old stone, varnished wood, coal smoke from the court fires working behind closed doors — the smell of a building that has held the same proceedings for fifty years and taken the character of them into its walls.

Their counsel found him before ten. Keane was a tall man of about forty-five, considered in manner, who had acknowledged the brief in August with a letter of three sentences and who had since written twice with questions about the exclusion section. He had the unhurried confidence of a man who has read the brief and finds it sufficient. He shook Prescott's hand and asked whether the originals were in the deed-box.

Prescott confirmed they were.

They stood together in the corridor while it filled further. The courtroom doors had not yet opened; through the gap where a latch had not quite caught, Prescott could see the brass rail of the witness box and the bench above it, both empty.

---

Counsel for the defendant came across to them at ten minutes to ten. His name was Ardern, and Prescott knew from the action papers that he had been at the bar for twenty-five years. He was a shorter man, compact, who moved through the corridor with the ease of long practice.

The request was framed correctly. Whether the plaintiff's solicitor might permit the defendant a few minutes to examine the executed original of the first codicil, before the judge took his seat — purely for the purposes of instruction, Ardern said, and Prescott's side would retain custody throughout. It was said without the tone of a man asking a favour, and without the tone of a man who expected to be refused.

Keane looked at Prescott, briefly, because it was Prescott's deed-box.

Prescott set it on the bench beside him and opened the lid. The Eccleston papers were arranged as he had laid them in Preston the week before: the custody list on top, the originals beneath in exhibit order. He lifted the custody list, and beneath it, in a folded envelope marked in his own hand — *R2. First Codicil (executed original)* — was the instrument that had been in the strong-room since the fifteenth of March 1924.

He handed the envelope to Ardern without speaking.

---

Walter Eccleston was standing eight or ten feet away, beside a young man from Thurston & Marsh that Prescott did not recognise. He had come into the building while Prescott and Keane were talking; Prescott had noted his arrival at the edge of his attention without looking at him directly. He looked at him now. Walter was watching Ardern cross the corridor with the envelope.

Ardern held the envelope out. Walter took it. He opened it carefully — he was a careful man — and drew out the codicil. Rag paper, folded twice, typewritten, a single page. He unfolded it and began to read.

He read it the way a man reads a document he expects to confirm what he knows: quickly, his eyes moving across the type.

And then he slowed.

He went back a line, read it again; went back further; came to rest at a particular point in the instrument and stayed. He read it again from that point, deliberately, his head very slightly inclined. Then he read it a third time and was quite still.

He was fifty or thereabouts, broad-shouldered, a man whose presence had always been larger than his physical size. He was not large now. He held the instrument and stood without moving, and something in the set of his shoulders was different from a moment before, though Prescott could not have named precisely what.

---

Prescott watched and did not speak.

He had never been in a room with the executed text before this moment. He had been wrong since March 1924 and had not known it.

Prescott kept his face composed and his hands at his sides. There was nothing to say.

After some moments, Walter spoke briefly to Ardern — low, inaudible at the distance. Ardern put a hand once on Walter's arm, professional and brief, and withdrew with him down the corridor. Two men, twenty feet away, a conference too quiet to follow.

Keane stood beside Prescott and did not speak, which was correct.

A barrister passed between them on his way to another court, acknowledged Keane with a nod, and moved on.

Three minutes, or a little more.

When Ardern returned, his manner was composed in the way of a man who has instructions he does not enjoy executing but who will execute them precisely.

"My client is not in a position to proceed," he said. "I am instructed to apply for a withdrawal of the claim."

---

The matter came before the judge at a quarter past ten: the application to withdraw; Keane's assent on behalf of the plaintiff in solemn form; the brief exchange of counsel establishing the disposition of the instruments and the question of costs. The judge was a spare man of about sixty with a dry manner and a habit of precise speech who had clearly had the brief — his questions were exact — and who received the application without visible surprise.

The second codicil had not been proved; accordingly it was not to be admitted to probate. The instruments of 1919 and 1924 stood. Letters of administration with the will annexed would be sought in due course through the Principal Registry.

The handwriting evidence: two opinions, directly irreconcilable — one finding the signature genuine, one finding it not. The judge noted that the decision had not rested on either. He added one observation, speaking to the courtroom at large rather than to either set of counsel: that in cases of this kind the most reliable witnesses were frequently the most ordinary — a letter-book entry, a register note, a word in a recital — because ordinary documents do not accommodate themselves to what comes after. He said it in the same flat tone he had used throughout, and moved to the costs.

The costs were to be paid by the defendant. Garside & Prescott, which had carried the action at its own risk from the caveat onward, would recover them in full.

---

By eleven the corridor was nearly empty. The matter had gone quickly — as matters go quickly, Prescott knew, once the decision has been made before it reaches the court.

Keane gave him his hand and said that it had been well conducted. That was the right amount to say. Prescott thanked him, and they parted.

He opened the deed-box and replaced the first codicil, in its envelope, in its place in the exhibit order. He noted the custody on the list: *R2. Returned from use. RCJ, 14 Oct. 1927. A.P.* He closed the lid.

He would telephone Mr. Booth from the hotel before midday. He would write to Edgar Fairhurst this afternoon.

He picked up the deed-box and walked toward the entrance.

# Chapter 2 — The Second Codicil

Prescott was halfway through the Bank Parade letter when Mr. Booth appeared in the doorway with the morning post.

The Thurston & Marsh envelope was on top. It was thicker than a simple acknowledgment — thick enough for an enclosure.

The covering note was on their good paper. Their client, it advised, had lately found among his late uncle's personal papers a codicil to the will, dated the fourteenth day of August nineteen-twenty-six, which he believed had been made privately by the testator in the final months of his life. A copy was enclosed. In these circumstances, they trusted that the will might now be proved in common form in the ordinary way; they would be glad to hear how their client might proceed.

Garside read it at his desk, held out his hand for the enclosure, read that too, and set it face-down on the blotter.

"The letter-book," he said.

Prescott took the letter-book from the cupboard. The carbon of the firm's notice letter was two pages in — dated the second of November, the typing clean.

> Dear Sirs, — We act in the estate of the late Mr. Josiah Eccleston of Eccleston Hall. We hold his will dated the 3rd June 1919 and a codicil thereto dated the 15th March 1924 which materially affects the disposition of the residue. We shall be glad to receive your client's proposals for proving the will in proper form. — Yours faithfully, GARSIDE & PRESCOTT

He closed the letter-book and set it on the table.

Garside turned the enclosure over and read it aloud:

> WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.

Outside the window Winckley Square lay quiet in the November light.

"Dated the fourteenth of August," Prescott said.

"Yes."

The despatch-box had been inventoried in the last week of October, a week after the death, with Prescott recording each item as it came out and Walter present beside the table. No codicil among them — his attendance note was in the file. After the inventory, the box had stood at the mill, in Walter's keeping, for six days. The codicil had been produced after the box was returned to the Hall.

"The firm received no instruction to draw this," Prescott said. "No request for the text of the first codicil. No inquiry as to its terms."

"We gave them the date in the notice." Garside's forefinger rested on the letter-book. "I thought it proper. That is all we sent."

Prescott took the copy to the window. The paper was good foolscap, typed on a machine he could not immediately place as belonging to the firm or to any office associated with it. The signature — *Josiah Eccleston*, in dark ink — was in a formed hand of the right general character; it offered nothing that announced itself as certainly genuine or certainly not. Below the signature, an attestation clause: *Thomas Birch*, carrier, of a Ribchester address; *Frederick Hallett*, gardener, of a lane near Salesbury.

"Neither of them at their given addresses, I should think," he said.

"That remains to be determined." Garside was reaching for his overcoat; he had a meeting elsewhere. "Write to Bank Parade this afternoon. Mr. Fairhurst must enter a caveat before any other step is taken, and he must do it promptly. The instrument has two witnesses and a date and a signature that will not be settled quickly." He had his hat. "Nothing to Thurston and Marsh beyond acknowledgment. Nothing at all."

---

Walter Eccleston called at the office that same afternoon.

No appointment had been made. Mr. Booth brought his card in without comment, and Prescott arrived in the front room a moment later to find Walter already settled in the chair opposite Garside's desk, coat and hat set aside. He had the ease of a man who had spent twenty years at home in other people's offices. He greeted Garside and Prescott both. He said he had come himself because it seemed the right thing to do, given the long connection.

He was fifty or thereabouts — broad in the shoulder, a dark wool coat, the considered quiet that came from managing men through a long stretch of difficult years. He had known Josiah Eccleston all his working life and had known this firm almost as long.

His account was orderly. He had gone through his uncle's insurance papers in the despatch-box in the days following the inventory. He was, he said, very conscious of having been present at that inventory and of the codicil not being there then. His best understanding was that Josiah must have kept it separately and it had simply been overlooked, or added to the box on a later occasion. Josiah had been up at the mill three or four times in the spring, before the illness; the mill office had a typewriter, and it would have been nothing for him to sit down and draft something out. He had always transacted his correspondence at the mill rather than at the Hall.

"He always said the arrangement for Margaret and her issue wouldn't stand as he'd left it," Walter said, in a tone that was not argumentative, only explanatory. "That he'd made it in a soft mood and always meant to put it right. He said so more than once, and to more than one person." He looked briefly at his hands. "I would very much rather there were no solemn-form action about this. These are Margaret's children. I have no wish to be in dispute with Margaret's children."

Garside said that the firm must advise its clients and take instructions in the ordinary way, and that nothing further could be said at this stage. Walter accepted this with a brief nod — the nod of a man accustomed to solicitors' answers. He stood, and shook Garside's hand, and then Prescott's, and left without further remark.

Prescott wrote the attendance note in full: Walter's account of finding the codicil, his description of Josiah's correspondence habits at the mill, the timing of the despatch-box as Walter understood it, his stated wish to avoid proceedings. All of it dated and initialled and clipped to the file.

Then he went back to the letter-book and read the November second carbon a second time. The firm's notice letter had given Walter's solicitors the date of the first codicil in writing: the fifteenth of March nineteen-twenty-four. Nothing beyond it. No text; no terms; no word of the instrument except that it bore that date and materially affected the residue.

---

Edgar Fairhurst entered the caveat at the Probate Registry on the eighth of November. The notice arrived at Winckley Square three days later — a printed card, the date stamped in violet ink — and Prescott noted it in the file and clipped it to the caveat cover.

The file now held the will, the first codicil, the despatch-box inventory attendance note, the firm's notice letter carbon, Walter's attendance note, and the copy of the second codicil. A second codicil the firm had never been asked to draw, in an estate it had administered for forty years without a privately-made instrument of any kind.

He set the file on Mr. Booth's tray. Outside Winckley Square the light was already gone.

# Chapter 3 — The Habit

The Eccleston index ran to three pages.

Prescott spread them flat on the table beside the window. Pale November light lay on the paper from the square. The list was in Garside's hand from the first entry to the last: a matter number at the left margin, a brief description in the centre column, a date at the right. It had begun in 1884. He set his pen down and read from the beginning.

The first entry: *Eccleston, J. — conv. of mill premises, Ribchester, March 1884.* Below it, in close sequence, a second conveyance, then a deed of covenant over the mill machinery, then a first will — made in 1891, superseded. Garside's hand had been somewhat looser in those early years; by 1900 the columns were fully regular and the descriptions exact. The entries continued without break or interruption for forty years. They ended with a codicil executed in March 1924.

Prescott pulled the older cabinets first.

The conveyance of 1884 was in its original envelope, folded square, on rag paper without tear or stain. A young man buying his first mill premises had come to a solicitor recently qualified, and both men had since become, in their respective trades, what they were. The purchase of Eccleston Hall in 1898 occupied two drawers of deeds and a correspondence packet. The mortgage of 1921 — Blackburn bank — carried a note in Garside's hand on the inside cover of the instrument: *Prepared on client's instructions, 17 March 1921. Terms agreed with lender.*

Below the mortgage, the Hall title deeds ran to three separate bundles, each tied and labelled, all correctly lodged.

He found the earlier wills in the bottom drawer. Two, both superseded: 1891 and 1904. Each had been drawn by Garside & Prescott, executed on the firm's premises, held in the strong-room until replaced. The 1919 will — the standing instrument, now in the strong-room — had replaced the second of these. The will of 1904 bore the same Winckley Square address as the present firm; the will of 1891 bore Garside's name alone.

Prescott turned to the correspondence.

Josiah's letters to the firm ran to two packets, sorted by year. They were brief and direct, written in a plain hand that had grown slightly uneven in the final years — the hand of a man who had not found correspondence convenient and had nonetheless kept it orderly. He wrote when Garside wrote to him; he confirmed, instructed, accepted. His replies ran to a paragraph or two: the matter agreed, the instruction given, the arrangement understood. In forty years of correspondence there was not a single letter that did not have a legal purpose.

Prescott read through the letters of 1924 and 1925. Then the letters of 1926, which ran only to June. In none of them, from the day the first codicil was executed in March 1924 to the last letter Josiah had written before his illness, was there any mention of a changed mind. No dissatisfaction with the arrangement for Mrs. Fairhurst's children. No instruction — or shadow of an instruction — to reconsider what had been settled in that March.

The attendance note for the fifteenth of March 1924 was in the file behind the first codicil copy.

---

> 15 March 1924. Instructions from Mr. Josiah Eccleston at the office. Client has renewed relations with his niece Mrs. Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston and desires to revoke clause 4 of his will of the 3rd June 1919. Codicil revokes clause 4 entire and gives the residue to Mrs. Margaret Fairhurst or her issue absolutely; all other provisions confirmed. Settled, executed, and attested in due form. Instrument to strong-room. *Or her issue*: collateral; substitutional form required. — H.G.

---

Prescott made a note on the working file cover — *corroborating exhibit: attend. note 15 March 1924, H.G.* — and set the original back.

Two pages further in the packet was a letter Josiah had written in late April 1924, six weeks after the codicil was made. It thanked Garside for his attendance in March and said, briefly, that the arrangement had been the right thing to do. Three lines on the matter and nothing equivocal. Garside had filed it inside a small folded card rather than flat in the packet as the rest lay — not the ordinary practice; the card kept the letter clean and flat. Prescott read it and set it face-down.

The file was well kept.

He was writing the finding in the working note when Garside came through the room.

"What have you found?"

"Nothing outside the firm," Prescott said. "Every instrument from the first conveyance in 1884. Two superseded wills, both drawn here. No exception in forty years. His correspondence from March 1924 to June 1926 contains nothing to suggest any wish to change the first codicil."

Garside had his coat and was going somewhere. He paused in the doorway.

"Josiah was not a man who did things unofficially," he said. He moved on.

Prescott wrote it in the working note. He dated the note, set it at the front of the file, and returned the Eccleston papers to their drawers as the afternoon light failed at the windows.

The index lay at the top of the file, three pages in Garside's hand from 1884 to 1924, the last entry in the same hand as the first.

There was nothing in forty years of this client's business to suggest that he had ever made a legal instrument outside this firm, or without a solicitor present to see it made.

The working note said that. The file would say it. Prescott set them together on Mr. Booth's tray and went to compose the afternoon post.

# Chapter Five — The Hinge

The court had risen early. Prescott came back through Winckley Square at ten minutes past eleven, briefcase in hand, and found the outer door unlocked.

Mr. Booth was standing in the passage.

In sixteen years Prescott had never seen Mr. Booth standing in the passage. The managing clerk occupied either his desk in the front room or the corridor between the deed-room and the letterpress.

He said: "Mr. Garside, sir. About half past nine. He was at his desk when it happened — the notes are open."

They were. Garside had been annotating the margin of a client letter: the pen lay on the page, still uncapped, the ink dried in the nib before anyone had thought to close it. The annotation was three words and not finished. Dr. Ainsworth came at ten o'clock and confirmed what was evident before he arrived.

The arrangements took the rest of the morning. The doctor's certificate; a brief attendance from the coroner's office, who found nothing requiring them further; a message to Garside's chambers contact in Manchester; a telegram to Garside's sister in Harrogate, who was his only surviving family. Mr. Booth handled most of it with the quiet efficiency of twenty years' managing. Prescott signed one letter at Garside's desk that could not wait and returned to his own. The chair had not yet been vacated; but it would have to be used.

He was thirty-eight. He had worked beside this man for sixteen years.

By the afternoon the office was working again, because it had to. There were three matters due before the week's end.

---

The clients were written to, each file noted with the date and the name of the partner now handling it. Two long-running matters were referred to larger firms better placed to carry them. The other matters remained.

Mr. Booth's habits did not change. He put the post on Prescott's desk each morning and collected the outgoing letters at noon and at four, and continued to treat the telephone as an instrument of occasional and controlled utility. The firm was Prescott and Booth now. Neither of them used those words.

The Eccleston file sat on the corner of Prescott's desk through those first days: the caveat entered, the administrator pendente lite still to be applied for, the action assigned to the Probate Division and waiting for a date. Prescott attended to more urgent matters first. On the fourth evening, when the office was quiet and the street outside had gone dark, he put everything else aside and opened the file from the beginning.

---

He went through the will, the first codicil, the covering correspondence, the register index sheet, the attendance notes, the letter-book carbon, Josiah's letter to Margaret Fairhurst, the working note Prescott had written in November recording forty years of instruments and the silence of the correspondence thereafter. He read each item and set it face-down to the right of the blotter. The coal in the grate had burned low; he put three pieces on before sitting down again with the strong-room register.

He had consulted the register in October — glanced at the September entry to confirm what he and Garside had both been present to witness. He read the page now in full.

The register was a tall narrow ledger, twenty years of entries in two hands: Garside's copper-plate filling the greater part of it, with Prescott's narrower script appearing in the same columns for the matters he had handled in the latter years. The overall character of the book was Garside's.

He found the September entry.

---

*19 September 1926. Document: First Codicil, J. Eccleston, dated 15 March 1924. Purpose: Read to assembled family at testator's request; testator's health declining; testator wished there to be no surprises. Persons present: H. Garside; A. Prescott; W. Eccleston; Mr. E. Beckett (steward); one other of the household. Instrument read entire, including date. Time out: 9.45 a.m. Time returned: 3.20 p.m. Document in good order on return. H.G.*

---

He did not move for some time.

The entry was consistent with every other entry in the book: the same instrument named in full, the same purpose given, the same persons noted, the same times. *Instrument read entire, including date.* That phrase was not in any requirement of law or practice. It was Garside's.

He turned back through the pages. The same character for twenty years. A box of deeds fetched for a completion in 1918. The will read to Josiah at the Hall in 1919. The mortgage papers in 1921. Every entry at the same level — not the level a register strictly required, but the level of a man who did not distinguish between what required a record and what deserved one.

He closed the register and set it back on its shelf. He sat with the open file for a few minutes longer. The coal was nearly spent.

---

The letter from the Principal Probate Registry had come that morning; he had set it aside for the afternoon and not reached it. He opened it now.

The action had been set down for hearing in the Probate Division. The date fixed: the sixth of October 1927.

He counted forward. He was in December; it was the twentieth. He counted to October.

Two hundred and ninety days.

He banked the fire, locked the strong-room, and put on his coat. He walked home through Winckley Square in the cold of December. Two hundred and ninety days.

# The File

The papers from the Hall came by registered post on the twenty-second, packed in a cardboard box with the administrator's covering note on top: one pocket diary, 1926; one bundle of correspondence, inward and outward, January to October; one set of household accounts. Prescott had not requested the accounts.

It was two hundred and fifty-seven days to the hearing.

He lifted the diary out first. Small, leather-covered, a brass clasp stiff from disuse — the kind sold in any stationer's, a shilling and sixpence, renewed each year without much deliberation. Josiah Eccleston's name was written inside the front cover in a hand that was still his own but smaller, and somewhat less firm, than the hand in the instruments in the strong-room.

He opened it to the first of January and began.

The entries were sparse from the start. January: a mill appointment on the eighth — the subject noted (looms on short time; questions about the dye-house roof), Walter's name not in it. February: another mill appointment; a doctor's visit on the nineteenth — Dr. Cullis, two words only, suggesting something routine; and a letter acknowledged from a cousin in Harrogate. March: a note from the magistrates' clerk, one of Josiah's cases forwarded to a colleague in Clitheroe. The entry had the air of a letter that had not been unexpected, and had not been unwelcome.

The mill appointments grew fewer in spring. The last was on the fourteenth of May: *W.E. — mill — morning.* Four words. After that, nothing about the mill.

The entries became sparser and more domestic. Beckett here and there — the steward, the same name as in the strong-room register. A note about the south field. The insurance broker.

Prescott turned to August.

The fourteenth was a Saturday. The entry read: *Hot again. Beckett here this afternoon — the south field question — resolved.* And below, in a slightly smaller hand: *Neck troubling me this morning.*

That was the last entry. After it: blank pages, clean, through September and October and the remainder of the year.

Prescott read the entry a second time. It was the record of an ordinary day: no appointment beyond Beckett, no instrument made or directed, no reference to any testamentary act. A diary did not prove a negative. But it was a record, and the record said nothing.

---

He set the diary aside and lifted the correspondence bundle.

The administrator had divided it — formal on the left, household on the right. Prescott worked through the formal side first. Three letters to and from Garside & Prescott, all already in the firm's letter-book and accounted for there. A letter from a Ribchester solicitor on a tenancy matter. Two from the estate's insurance brokers. Nothing to or from Thurston & Marsh; nothing from any other firm on any question touching the will or the codicil; nothing that had not already been known from the letter-book side.

The household side he read more quickly. Family correspondence; replies to local matters; the magistrates' clerk again. He came, near the bottom of the right-hand bundle, to a letter in Josiah's hand — but a different hand from the instruments: softer, unguarded, the hand of a man writing to someone he was glad to write to. Addressed to Miss Nora Fairhurst, Bank Parade, Preston. Dated the third of April, 1926.

He read it carefully. Not long — three-quarters of a page, a correction in the second paragraph, a postscript about a book he had promised to send. It said nothing about the estate's disposition, nothing about instruments or codicils. But near the end Josiah had written:

*I am very glad we have the matter settled between us, and I mean it to stay settled. Your mother knew it. You know it. That is what I wished.*

He made a note of the letter and set it to one side for the exhibits bundle.

---

He had read the instrument register in full in December, and knew what it contained. He took it from the strong-room now for the same reason he had written the letter-book note the previous week: to fix the finding as a record item. He ran his eye down the Eccleston column from 1884 to the end.

The original lease of Vale Mill, 1884. A mortgage, 1889, discharged 1892. The deed of gift of the Ribchester farmland, 1903. The lease extension of 1908. The will, third of June 1919. And, in Garside's invariable hand, the last entry in the column: *First Codicil — J. Eccleston dec. — 15 March 1924.*

Nothing after it. Forty years of instruments for one estate, and then a line. He closed the register and returned it to the strong-room.

---

When he came back to the table, there was one more item in the bundle — flat at the bottom, below the register extracts and the attendance notes, easy to miss. A letter in Garside's hand, on plain notepaper rather than the firm's standard paper. Dated the fourteenth of March, 1924.

He sat down and read it.

Three sentences. The codicil was enclosed, properly engrossed and ready for execution; Mr. Eccleston would need to sign it in the presence of two witnesses, both present together at the same time, neither of whom took any benefit under the instrument; Garside would attend at the Hall if preferred, or if Mr. Eccleston wished to arrange the witnesses himself, the office would be glad to receive the executed original at his convenience.

Three sentences, and each one exact. The witness requirement stated in full for a man who had been signing instruments since 1884 and had not required instruction in forty years. The note about the executed original — not a request but an offer, *the office would be glad to receive it*, as if Garside had thought about the document's custody before the letter left his desk.

It had been written for the record. Not for Josiah.

Prescott held it a moment, then set it with the exhibits.

The whole file had that quality. Each letter a fraction more precise than the matter strictly required; each attendance note kept at the same level whether the occasion was routine or not; the register built to a standard that had no source in any statute or practice requirement, but had its source entirely in the man who had built it. The file was the work of a man who had never distinguished between what required a record and what deserved one.

And the file was going to prove a forgery.

---

He wrote the working note in the hand he used for formal file items, and read it back once before he dated it.

*No private record or correspondence contains any reference to any intention to revoke or alter the first codicil after its execution in March 1924. No instrument in the firm's register was made in the name of Josiah Eccleston after that date. The survey of instruments is complete: every instrument made by Josiah Eccleston for a period of forty years was made through the firm of Garside & Prescott, and the last was the first codicil.*

He dated it the twenty-seventh of January, 1927, and placed it at the front of the working file.

---

The strong-room smelled as it always did: clean paper, iron shelves, the dry compound of ink aged past sharpness into something denser and quieter. He set the register in its place, checked the order of the cabinet, and closed the door. The lock turned with its usual certainty.

He turned off the lamp and went out into Winckley Square, and home.

# Vale Mill

The motor took the road east out of Preston at half past eight on a Thursday morning in early March. The Ribble had been over its banks the previous week; the fields below the road still stood in water. Where the road fell toward the valley floor, the mud had crept across the lane, and the tyres moved with less assurance than Prescott preferred.

In September, Garside had driven and Prescott had been in the passenger seat with the Eccleston deed-box at his feet. An autumn morning, still warm; the family arranged in the Hall's drawing room when they arrived, and Garside's voice on the legal periods going exactly at the pace the instrument required. Prescott had sat with the box in his lap and thought about the quality of the light, and the draft from the windows, and nothing in particular. He had not been attending to the right thing.

He drove out of the valley at Longridge and back down into it again where the road turned toward Ribchester. The river showed through the trees as a grey-brown band, high for the season. Cold; the sort of day that refuses to lift.

---

Vale Mill stood on the hillside above the village on its own ground: stone-built, four storeys, a Victorian weaving shed of moderate scale. The engine-room chimney put out a thin plume of smoke, but the weaving shed was silent when Prescott came up through the gate. Late morning, between shifts; the looms not running; forty men in the village below waiting on the afternoon bell.

He left the motor on the road and went up through the yard. A mechanic crouched over something near the engine-room door and looked up without interest and looked back down. The counting house was through a plain wooden door at the ground level, glass-paned, with a card pinned to the frame: *Administrator — Estate of Josiah Eccleston, Decd.*

---

Mr. Hadfield was a precise, middle-sized man in a dark suit who had been working through the estate papers before Prescott arrived. He had the mill's accounts spread across the counting-house table — column books, receipt books, a sheaf of correspondence from the mortgage holder — and to one side of them, near the door, lay a printed mortgage instrument bearing the firm's name at its foot: *Garside & Prescott, Solicitors, Winckley Square, Preston.* At the bottom of the second page, Garside's signature was visible as the witnessing solicitor: small, exact, done for the record. Prescott had seen it ten thousand times at least. He looked back at the administrator.

"The figures for January," Hadfield said. He placed a single sheet across the table: the mill's income against its fixed charges for the month. The columns did not meet. "February is not better. I have interim figures — the month hasn't closed — but they follow the same direction."

Prescott looked at the income column. The mill was weaving at perhaps forty per cent of its former capacity; orders were there, in small parcels — work from a Blackburn merchant, some from a Bradford house — but not in the volumes that would cover the fixed charges. The mortgage interest was being met from the estate's capital reserves: capital in place of income, month by month.

"The mortgage is being met?"

"For the time being. I estimate the reserves will carry it for four more months at the present rate. Possibly five, if the March output holds."

Two hundred and eighteen days to the hearing. The reserves would last four months.

"The sale contract?"

"Still in place. The prospective purchaser has extended twice; his solicitors have indicated — not formally — that they will not extend again." Hadfield folded the income sheet. "The sale requires a grant of representation establishing the vendor's title. Until the action is resolved, that grant cannot issue."

Prescott knew this.

---

The connecting door between the counting house and the mill office stood ajar. While Hadfield went back toward the filing cabinets for a folder he had mislaid, Prescott stepped into the mill office and looked at the room.

A stone floor, like the counting house. Two metal filing cabinets against the far wall. A desk with the grain worn from its surface, a wooden swivel chair behind it, an inkstand without a pen. A window looking south over the yard. And on the desk, alongside the inkstand, a typewriter.

He had confirmed some weeks earlier that there was no machine at the Hall. Josiah had used the mill office for his correspondence — had made the twelve miles when he needed something typed — because there was nothing at the Hall on which a document could be set down in that form.

He did not touch it. He crossed to the desk and looked at the machine from a distance of eighteen inches: the carriage bearing the manufacturer's name on a small plate, the keys worn smooth on their faces, the type slugs visible in the slot. The plate read *Underwood Standard*. The lower-case *e* slug sat a fraction high; the full stop showed wear across its face. He took his pocket-book from his coat and wrote: *Mill office — Underwood Standard — e-slug high — full-stop worn — only machine in building — nothing at the Hall.*

Hadfield came back through the door. Prescott put the pocket-book away.

---

"I should like to know when Mr. Josiah Eccleston last visited the mill," Prescott said. "Whether there's a record of it."

Hadfield sent for the foreman.

Naylor was a wide, deliberate man who came in carrying the mill's daybook — a working log kept in the counting house, bound in green boards, entries in a single running hand. He set it on the table and found the page without being asked.

"The last time the old gentleman visited." He put his finger on the line.

*Mr. Eccleston visited, inspected the shed, attended the office; May 14, 1926.*

The entry sat between a 10 May note about a broken loom rod and a 16 May record of a delivery from the yarn merchant. The ink was continuous with the entries before and after it; the handwriting was the same throughout. A working notation made by a man with no reason to record anything beyond what occurred.

"He didn't visit after May?"

"He was ill," Naylor said. "He didn't travel much after summer. We had word he'd died in October, through Mr. Eccleston." He had the measured habit of a man who had specified, for fifteen years, which Mr. Eccleston he meant. "Mr. Walter Eccleston."

Prescott wrote in his pocket-book: *14 May 1926 — last confirmed visit — mill daybook, foreman's hand.*

The second codicil was dated the fourteenth of August 1926. Three months after the old man had last been in this building.

He did not write that second thought.

---

He was crossing back through the yard toward the gate when Walter Eccleston came out of the engine-room door on the far side.

Walter was heavier than Prescott had remembered from their meetings in Preston — a working man's build by now, not an office man's — in a flat cap and the working coat of a mill manager: the coat for the shed floor, not the office. He was speaking to a young mechanic as he crossed the yard, something brief and technical, and the mechanic nodded without looking up from his work. Walter did not look toward the counting house. He had not seen Prescott.

He moved through the yard with the ease of a man who understood every building in it — which level to walk, which door to take, where the ground would be slick near the engine room. Fifteen years of managing it; everything he had borrowed against was in these buildings, and his men were inside them. The mechanic said something back; Walter stopped and they both crouched over the same problem together. Then Walter stood and walked on, and the mechanic went back to his tools.

Prescott went out through the gate.

---

The road back to Preston ran west along the valley floor, the mill behind and above him on the hillside. He had the window open a fraction — enough to hear the valley — and above the road, faint through the wind noise, the looms had started their afternoon shift. A sustained, rolling sound: the weaving shed in motion, forty men. Prescott had the pocket-book on the seat beside him and did not open it. There was time for the office.

The road fell toward the Ribble crossing, the river still high, the light fading in the way it did in March before it had learned to last. The mill had gone behind a fold in the hillside. He drove west.
