# The Machine

The post arrived at twenty minutes to ten. Mr. Booth set it on the desk with the usual arrangement — circulars to the left, correspondence to the right — and then stood a moment longer than was necessary, which was his means of indicating that something in it required attention before anything else did.

"Manchester," he said. "By this morning's first."

Prescott looked at the envelope. His own name on the outside, the second line Garside & Prescott, then Winckley Square, and above the return address, printed in small capitals: *A. J. Croft, Document Examiner, Manchester.* He had engaged Croft in the last week of January, on the recommendation of a London firm that had used him twice; the comparison specimens — from the mill-office machine, from every solicitors' office the canvass had identified, and the necessary confirmation that the Hall contained no machine — had been arranged with Mr. Hadfield's assistance in the first fortnight of March.

Mr. Booth withdrew.

Prescott cut the envelope. The report ran to eleven pages. He had not expected eleven pages; he read from the first line regardless.

Croft identified himself for the record: practising as a document examiner since 1912, first trained in London, thereafter in Manchester. The examination covered: the propounded second codicil, marked as Exhibit B and provided by Thurston & Marsh; comparison specimens taken from the typewriting machine at Vale Mill office, Ribchester, on the twelfth of March 1927, by arrangement with Mr. Hadfield, administrator of the estate; comparison specimens from the typewriting machines at eight solicitors' offices in the county, supplied through the canvass and by separate arrangement; and a written confirmation from Mr. Hadfield, supported by a household statement, that no typewriting machine was present at or had been kept at Eccleston Hall.

Prescott made a mark beside the Hall confirmation. It was not a disputed point, but having it formally included placed it in the examiner's report rather than leaving it as an absence from the record — which was a different thing, evidentially.

Croft's method was set out in two stages. First, typeface design: the identification of the machine by the characteristics of its typeface, which varied by manufacturer and by series. Second, individual machine characteristics: the particular defects and displacements acquired by a specific machine over its working life, distinguishable from those of any other machine of the same manufacture.

On typeface design, the report was brief and precise. The typewriting of the second codicil was produced in the face of the Underwood Standard series — a face distinguishable, by the design of its descenders and the relative weight of its serifs, from the Remington, the Royal, and the L. C. Smith specimens in the comparison set, and distinct also from the two Yost machines identified among the solicitors' office specimens. The mill-office machine was an Underwood Standard. None of the comparison specimens from solicitors' offices was produced on an Underwood Standard. On the question of manufacture and series, the second codicil was consistent with the mill-office machine and with no other machine examined.

Prescott read that paragraph twice. What it said was what he had known in the mill-office doorway, looking at the machine from a distance of eighteen inches with his pocket-book in his hand; but knowing was not demonstrating, and demonstrating was the eleven pages.

The individual machine characteristics occupied six of the remaining pages. Croft had identified four concurrent defects in the typewriting of the second codicil, each of which appeared consistently in the mill-office comparison specimens and none of which appeared in the specimens from any other machine:

First: the lower-case *e* slug was displaced upward by a fraction, producing in the codicil's typewriting — and in the mill-office specimens without exception — a raised *e* perceptible in every line. Second: the full-stop key bore wear across the entirety of its face, the left impression lighter than the right, the pattern consistent across both sets of specimens. Third: the lower-case *d* had lost the upper terminus of its left-hand serif, leaving a squared end in place of a tapered one, visible under magnification in the codicil and reproduced in identical form in the mill specimens. Fourth: the lower-case *r* was displaced fractionally upward and to the left of its true base-line position, producing a letter whose right foot did not align with the surrounding characters — again, consistent between the codicil and the mill specimens, and absent in every other machine examined.

No individual defect appeared in any specimen from any solicitors' office. The four defects appeared collectively and individually in the second codicil and in the mill-office specimens only.

Croft's conclusion was set out on a separate page:

---

*It is my conclusion, reached from the foregoing examination and based upon both typeface design and individual machine characteristics, that the typewriting of the propounded second codicil was produced upon the Underwood Standard typewriting machine located in the office of Vale Mill, Ribchester. I was unable to identify any other machine examined as the source of the typewriting. The examination of typewriting specimens does not establish the identity of the operator or the date of production: those are matters beyond my evidence.*

---

Prescott read the last two sentences a second time, then set the report flat on the desk.

They were correctly stated. An examiner who claimed more than his evidence supported was an examiner whose cross-examination counsel would enjoy. The limits were as useful as the finding: they told Prescott where the examiner's evidence ended and where the record's other elements would need to carry the weight.

The weight they would carry was already in the file, or nearly so. Josiah's 1926 diary ran to the fourteenth of August — hot weather, the steward, a note about his neck — and was blank thereafter. Naylor the foreman's daybook gave the fourteenth of May as the last occasion Josiah had set foot in the building where the machine stood. What Croft could not say — when, and by whom — the depositions from the Hall would address: the household staff who had accompanied Josiah on his journeys in his last months, and who would testify that after May he had not left the Hall unescorted and had not been brought to the mill. Those depositions were being arranged.

Walter had told him, at the meeting in November, that Josiah must have typed the codicil himself — or had it typed — on one of his visits to the mill, then laid it in the despatch-box without telling anyone. The version required a visit; there had been no visit after May. The version required a machine; there was one machine, and it had stood in a room Josiah had not entered in the three months before the codicil's date. Croft could say the machine was the mill-office Underwood Standard and that no other machine was its source; the record already said the rest, and the depositions would close it.

The window gave onto the square. A solicitor's clerk crossed the flagstones below, folder in hand, walking with the specific pace of a man carrying something he had not read. Thurston & Marsh were not visible from this room; they faced the other way along the square, toward the garden in the centre, which at this time of year was bare. Prescott was not especially sorry that their windows pointed away from his.

He turned back to the desk and lifted the report again.

Croft had appended two supplementary pages on the paper. The stock used for the second codicil was a plain rag-content writing paper of medium weight — the kind kept for general office correspondence, unremarkable in quality. It was not consistent with the heavier, superior-quality engrossment paper standard in a solicitors' firm for the preparation of testamentary instruments; a sample of Garside & Prescott's own engrossment stock was appended for comparison. The papers were of different character and weight. The paper used for the second codicil was consistent with the class of plain writing paper maintained in mill and counting-house offices for routine correspondence, and with the specific stock observed in the Vale Mill office. Croft's supplementary note was as careful on its limits as the main report had been: consistent with, but not independently proving.

Prescott set the report aside and took a fresh sheet.

The note he wrote was eleven pages reduced to three sentences; that was the work.

---

*The second codicil (exhibited as B in this action) was typed upon the Underwood Standard typewriting machine at Vale Mill office, Ribchester. This finding is made by Mr. A. J. Croft, document examiner, Manchester, on the basis of typeface design and four individual machine characteristics concurrently identified in both the codicil's typewriting and in comparison specimens from the mill-office machine; no other machine examined produces a corresponding match. No typewriting machine was present at Eccleston Hall. Croft's report and supplementary paper note are filed at this page.*

---

He dated the note. In the left margin, in the smaller hand he used for working figures, he wrote: *200 days.*

The door was shut.

# The Sale Contract

The sale contract ran to forty-three pages. Prescott had been through the first twenty-one before he reached the clause that controlled everything else.

*Completion of this Agreement is in all respects conditional upon the vendor producing a grant of representation establishing his title to the said estate and hereditaments.*

Twelve lines. Standard post-1925 form; the purchaser's solicitors had drafted it without any particular expectation of difficulty. Two memoranda of extension were attached behind it — the first dated January 1927, the second dated the fifteenth of March — each granting a further eight weeks on the standard form. Clipped behind the second memorandum was a note from Thurston & Marsh to the purchaser's solicitors, advising that a third extension was not expected.

When the action concluded, the contract concluded with it.

---

He turned to the mortgage papers.

The mortgage had been prepared by the firm — Garside's drafting, March 1921, his hand in the instrument number at the head of the page and in the attestation clause set below the covenants as Garside had always set it — and Prescott read it with the economy of a man who knew the architecture before he reached the operative parts. Eight thousand five hundred pounds secured on the mill's plant and machinery and the business's goodwill; a Blackburn bank on one side, Josiah Eccleston on the other; four and a half per cent and the quarter-days for the interest.

Hadfield had confirmed in February that the last two quarter-days' interest had been paid from the estate's capital. The principal was untouched and would remain untouched unless the sale proceeded. Prescott did not write the remainder of that calculation.

---

The banking correspondence had arrived in Hadfield's second parcel, copies obtained through discovery in the action: nine letters from Walter Eccleston to his bank manager, Mr. Holt, running from the spring of 1924 to January 1927, and five replies from Holt, whose responses grew shorter as the correspondence ran on.

The record across all nine letters was consistent. A mill mortgaged, an inheritance expected, a codicil complicating matters — but not permanently, Walter had been at pains to explain, because the codicil was a soft mood and his uncle had spoken of putting it right. The bank should be patient. The estate would come through. In the letters from 1926 and early 1927, Walter had given up explaining and simply affirmed: the estate would come through, the grant would follow, the bank should wait.

Among the nine letters was one dated the eleventh of June 1925, written after Holt had asked for further security. Prescott set the other eight aside and placed this one on the desk.

---

*Dear Mr. Holt, — You ask what further security I can offer beyond the mortgage. My uncle has made a codicil, as I told you, in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst and her issue, but I am assured the arrangement will not stand; he made it in a soft mood and has spoken since of putting it right. My expectations are otherwise what they have always been. — Yours faithfully, WALTER ECCLESTON*

---

Prescott filed the letter with the mortgage and the sale contract. He opened Hadfield's monthly account, which had come with the second parcel.

The mill had lost a little over three hundred pounds against projected income in March. The wage bill was being met; the mortgage interest was not — Hadfield had paid the March quarter-day from the estate's capital reserves, following the same course as the two previous quarter-days. His estimate of the remaining reserves was not revised from his February communication: at the current rate, the estate's liquidity would be exhausted in approximately three months.

---

Prescott assembled the financial exhibits in order — the mortgage instrument, the sale contract with the two extension memoranda, all nine of the Holt letters, Hadfield's account — and clipped them into the brief.

One hundred and eighty-five days.

He had written the figure in the margin of his working notes that morning. The exhibits went behind it. Motive was clear and, now, documented. And then Josiah had died in October without putting it right, and within six days of the despatch-box being returned to the mill, a second codicil had appeared that put it right for him.

It explained the forgery. It proved nothing of the kind. For proof there was a typed document and a recital, and the recital quoted a text that had never left the strong-room at Winckley Square. That argument had not yet been made into the brief; it was the most work still remaining.

He stacked the exhibits and set the brief to one side. The witnesses folder lay open on the desk where Booth had left it that morning. There was the question of the commission — whether the Probate Division would grant one, and how long the application would take — and no settled answer to it yet.

He drew the folder toward him and turned to the first page.

# The Sale Contract

Booth had left the administrator's second parcel on the side of the desk — not quite at the centre and not at the edge, as he always placed things he considered likely to be unwelcome, as if the middle distance were the appropriate location for something he had no wish to be asked about. The brown paper was addressed to Prescott in Hadfield's careful hand, the knot tied in the practised way of a man who had been managing documents for thirty years and tied them the same way every time.

Prescott opened it after Booth had gone upstairs to the copying room. Four items: the mortgage instrument, the conditional sale contract, a bundle of banking correspondence bound in red tape, and the administrator's monthly account for March. He set them in order of origin — mortgage oldest, monthly account most recent — and began at the beginning.

---

The mortgage had been Garside's matter from the first. The instrument number at the head of the page was in his hand — the clean, deliberate numerals he had used for every instrument through this office since the year he established the register, each digit made the same way across three decades of files. The attestation clause below the covenants was set in the form Garside had preferred, the signature block indented a full measure from the covenant text and the witness clause arranged above it in a single clean sentence. Eight thousand five hundred pounds secured on the mill's plant and machinery and its goodwill, held by the County Bank in Blackburn at four and a half per cent, with the interest payable at each of the quarter-days in the year. The mortgage was made in the spring of 1921, when the mill had needed capital for plant renewal and Josiah had put up the security against the estate's credit rather than draw from his own reserves. The principal obligation was the estate's, not Walter's in his personal capacity, which was a distinction that mattered for the title but not for the question of who had depended on the estate's solvency to hold his position together.

Hadfield's February letter, already in the file, had confirmed that the most recent two quarter-days' interest had been met from the estate's liquid capital rather than from the mill's operating income. The mill's operating income had been insufficient to service the debt. The principal sat where it had sat since 1921: untouched, the whole sum outstanding, waiting on the sale. Under the conditional contract, the purchaser was taking the estate subject to the mortgage, with discharge from the proceeds of completion forming part of the closing transaction. If the sale completed.

---

The sale contract was a Manchester firm's work, commercial property men, and they had drafted it with the methodical confidence of solicitors who expected no difficulty with the condition they were inserting. Prescott read it through again from the recitals, which described the vendor's title by reference to a grant of representation that had not yet issued and that would not issue until the action was resolved. The condition was in clause twenty-four.

*Completion of this Agreement is in all respects conditional upon the vendor producing a grant of representation establishing his title to the said estate and hereditaments.*

Two memoranda of extension were clipped behind the contract: the first had been agreed in January, granting eight further weeks; the second was dated the fifteenth of March and granted eight more. A note from Thurston & Marsh to the purchaser's solicitors accompanied the second memorandum, advising that a further extension was not anticipated. The purchaser had been generous twice. Whatever patience had been available appeared to have been used.

Without the grant, the contract could not complete. Without the action being resolved — in one direction or the other — the grant could not issue. The administrator could collect the estate's income and pay its debts, but could not distribute or convey. The mill sat in this position as it sat in every other: the same short-time working, the same wage bill, the same mortgage interest being drawn from capital that was not being replenished. The purchaser's patience ran in one direction. The estate's capital ran in the other. The action ran between them.

---

The bundle of banking correspondence was nine letters from Walter Eccleston to his bank manager, Mr. Holt, running from the spring of 1924 through to January 1927. Five replies from Holt were tucked into the appropriate envelopes; four letters had no reply, or none that had been preserved. Prescott untied the red tape and set the letters in sequence.

The picture was consistent across three years — a record of how a man had explained his position to himself and to others under increasing pressure. The early letters explained. The codicil was a temporary arrangement, made in a soft mood by an old man who had spoken since of putting the matter right. The mill was carrying a mortgage, but mills carried mortgages; that was not peculiar to this mill. Walter's expectations were what they had always been, which was to say that he expected Josiah to do what Josiah had assured him he intended to do. The arrangement would not stand; it had not stood in any practical sense; the inheritance would come through as it had always been understood that it would.

Holt's replies grew shorter. By early 1926 he had begun asking questions about security. By the end of 1926 his replies were two lines where they had once been half a page, and they asked for answers Walter had already given once and could only give again. Walter gave them again, in longer versions of the same assurance: the estate would come through, the grant would follow, the bank should be patient.

Among the nine letters was one dated the eleventh of June 1925, written after Holt had put the security question to him directly. Prescott placed it on the desk.

---

*Dear Mr. Holt, — You ask what further security I can offer beyond the mortgage. My uncle has made a codicil, as I told you, in favour of my late cousin Mrs. Fairhurst and her issue, but I am assured the arrangement will not stand; he made it in a soft mood and has spoken since of putting it right. My expectations are otherwise what they have always been. — Yours faithfully, WALTER ECCLESTON*

---

He clipped it in sequence with the rest of the letters and opened Hadfield's March account.

---

The March figures were not an improvement on February's. Gross income from the mill was down sixteen pounds on the previous month; the wage bill was met; the March quarter-day on the mortgage interest had been paid from the estate's capital rather than its earnings, the same as the two quarter-days before it. The net loss against projected income was a little over three hundred pounds, and Hadfield's estimate of reserves — calculated on his February assumptions and not revised — showed approximately three months of liquidity remaining at the current rate of depletion. He noted this without recommendation. What happened after the estate's capital was exhausted was not a question he was authorised to answer from his position, and Prescott had no mechanism to answer it from his.

---

Prescott assembled the exhibits. The mortgage instrument first — the earliest document, the foundation of the financial position. The sale contract, with the two extension memoranda clipped behind it and the Thurston & Marsh note behind those. The nine letters from Walter to Holt, in date order, with Holt's five replies where they belonged. Hadfield's monthly account at the back, the most recent piece of the record.

He clipped the bundle and noted the reference on the cover sheet. One hundred and eighty-five days to the hearing; he had written the figure that morning, and it sat in the margin of his working notes where he had put it, the same way the earlier figures sat in earlier margins, each one smaller than the one before it.

Context was not proof. Motive explained the forgery; it did not establish that the forgery had been made, or by whom, or how. The proof was in the text of the second codicil and in the text it recited, and the argument that would be built from those two texts had not yet been assembled into the brief. It was the most work still remaining.

He stacked the financial exhibits and set the brief to one side.

# The Witnesses

> SIGNED by the said JOSIAH ECCLESTON as and for his last codicil in the presence of us both
> present at the same time who at his request in his presence and in the presence of each other
> have hereunto subscribed our names as witnesses:
>
> THOMAS BIRCH, Carrier, of Ribchester in the County of Lancaster.
>
> FREDERICK HALLETT, Gardener, of near Salesbury in the County of Lancaster.

Both men were in the instrument index.

The index was a bound ledger, red boards worn soft at the corners, in Garside's hand from its first
entry in 1906 to the last he had made before the autumn. It recorded witness by name, trade, address,
instrument number, and date — so that finding any given specimen was a question of reading a column
and walking to a shelf. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester: four entries, the earliest in 1912, the
latest in March 1921. Frederick Hallett, gardener, near Salesbury: one entry, the same March 1921
instrument.

Prescott noted the instrument numbers and wrote to the Ribchester registrar that afternoon. He
instructed Booth to pull both instruments from the file.

---

The registrar's reply arrived four days later. Thomas Birch, carrier, of Ribchester, had died on the
twenty-eighth of September 1926. The cause given was influenza. Prescott wrote by return for a
certified copy of the death certificate, and it came within the week.

He opened his attendance book and wrote the date.

The instruments Booth had found carried Birch's signature on both: the deed of cottage tenancy from
November 1914 and the property schedule from March 1921. The 1914 hand was angular and firm at the
ascenders; by 1921 it had settled, the loop of the g broader, the B somewhat taller. Consistent with
itself across seven years. Prescott had been present at the 1921 signing. He packaged both originals
with a covering note and posted them to Croft in Manchester, together with a photographic copy of the
attestation page of the propounded codicil.

The March 1921 property schedule bore one further signature as witness, below Birch's: Hallett's hand,
shorter in body, the letters more angled, a single specimen. He sent it to Croft under a second cover.

---

He had written to Atkinson at Ribchester on the same day as the registrar — Atkinson whose practice
was agricultural conveyancing and the kind of local inquiry that required knowing the farms east of
Langridge Moor.

Atkinson's reply took nine days and ran to two pages. Hallett had worked the previous spring and
summer for a farmer named Ogden on the Salesbury road — kitchen garden and light farmwork. In the
first days of October 1926, Hallett had given notice. He had left no address with Ogden, none with
any neighbour Atkinson could find, none with the post office, which had handled one redirected letter
and could not say where it had gone. Atkinson had then made inquiry at the shipping offices in Preston
and had found that in the second week of October 1926 a Frederick Hallett of Ribchester had taken
an assisted passage from Liverpool to Quebec aboard the *SS Aurania*.

No fixed address in Canada.

Prescott added the departure date to his attendance book below the first entry. Then the next two:
the last week of October, Josiah's death; the first days of November, the despatch-box opened with
Prescott present, no codicil in it. Six days at the mill. The four dates made a column and described
a shape, and the shape described a thing, and he drew his pen through the space where that thing
would have been written, because the brief was not a place for what was not evidence.

---

Croft's two reports arrived in the same cover, their dates of composition ten days apart. They were
written in the same form.

> *In the matter of the Estate of Josiah Eccleston, deceased. I have examined the attestation
> signature attributed to THOMAS BIRCH on a photographic copy of the propounded codicil and
> compared it with the two authenticated specimens submitted: the cottage tenancy deed of November
> 1914 and the property schedule of March 1921, both originals. The signature on the propounded
> instrument is consistent with both specimens in general formation, pen pressure, and the
> development that seven years' interval between specimens would naturally produce. Given that my
> comparison rests upon a photographic copy of the propounded instrument rather than the original,
> and that two authenticated specimens only are available, I am not in a position to offer a
> positive identification. I cannot exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction executed from
> comparison material of comparable quality to that submitted to me. — H. Croft, Document
> Examiner.*

The second report ran in the same terms. The Hallett attestation, compared against the single
1921 specimen, was consistent in general formation and character; a single specimen did not establish
the full range of a hand; Croft was unable to form a view on natural variation or development across
the intervening period; he was not in a position to offer a positive identification and could not
exclude the possibility of a skilled reproduction.

He put both reports in the file.

---

There was a practical consequence to Hallett being alive rather than dead, which was that a commission
might be applied for. If the Probate Division granted it, a judicial officer in Canada would take
Hallett's evidence on the question of due execution — if Hallett could be located. Prescott wrote to
Mitchell in London with the full position: the witness's identity; his last confirmed employment;
his departure from Ribchester in the first days of October 1926 and his assisted passage aboard the
*Aurania*; Atkinson's inquiries and their result; the confirmed absence of any traceable address.
Mitchell's reply came within the week. The power to issue a commission existed; the difficulty was
personal service, which required an address, which was not available; the commission, if granted,
would take time the calendar did not have. Nevertheless Mitchell recommended applying, disclosing
the difficulty in full.

Prescott agreed, and Mitchell filed the application in the last week of April.

One hundred and seventy-two days to the hearing. The draft of the application was in the file —
the instrument, the witness's identity and last known whereabouts, the absence of a fixed address
in Canada, the submission that his evidence on due execution could not otherwise be obtained. It
was a well-drawn piece of work.

He noted the date of filing in the margin of his attendance book and placed the file on Booth's
tray for the shelf.

# The Fairhursts

The parks were greener than in November. Prescott walked from Winckley Square in the early afternoon, the river visible below Miller Park where the path curved west, the trees in full leaf and the light long enough to reach the far bank. He had not particularly noticed it was spring until today.

The Fairhurst house on Bank Parade showed its south face to the afternoon. The stone was less shuttered than it had been in autumn, the terrace looking lighter, almost sandy, in the May light. He arrived at a quarter past two and Nora Fairhurst opened the door before he could use the bell.

She showed him into the parlour. The room was recognisable — the dark sideboard, the pair of chairs either side of the empty grate — though the curtain at the window was drawn back today and the light came in across the parks. She went to call her father.

Edgar Fairhurst came in with George a step behind him. George was taller than Prescott had remembered, or had grown since November; he sat in the chair at the window while his father and Prescott arranged themselves at the table.

---

The April account was three pages from Hadfield: a loss of just under three hundred pounds against projected income; mortgage interest from capital for the third consecutive quarter-day; the mill working three and a half days in a normal week, wages stable. Prescott set the sheets between them.

Edgar read with his elbows on his knees and did not speak for a moment. He had learned to read a balance sheet in the course of a legal action he had not expected and would not have chosen.

"Is this typical?" he said.

"It is consistent with the preceding months," Prescott said. "Hadfield expects no improvement before late summer."

Edgar looked at the sheets a moment longer, then set them aside. "I suppose I am asking how confident you are."

"The record is building. The hearing date is fixed. The firm is confident, and when I am in a position to say more than that, I will say it."

He sat back in his chair.

George turned from the window then.

"What happens to the mill?" he said. "If the action fails."

Prescott looked at him. Sixteen; and he had put the question in the terms his father had not.

"The estate passes to Mr. Walter Eccleston under the second codicil," Prescott said. "His sale contract completes upon a grant of representation establishing his title. When that happens, the mill is sold. The proceeds go to Mr. Eccleston and, in large part, to his creditors."

"The men lose their jobs."

"In all probability, yes."

George turned back to the window. He said nothing more.

---

Nora brought the tea things through and poured without being asked. They worked through the remaining items — a letter requiring Edgar's signature on the administrator's quarterly renewal; a question from Mitchell in London about the form of the children's instructions, which Edgar answered clearly and in three sentences.

One hundred and fifty-five days to the hearing. Prescott wrote the figure in his attendance book and said nothing in the room.

He was gathering the signed papers when Nora said, setting down her cup, that Walter Eccleston had come to call last week.

Prescott looked up.

"He wrote first," she said. "He asked whether he might — he said he understood if not — and Father said he supposed there was no reason he should not. He came on a Tuesday."

"And was it—"

"He was kind. He seemed genuinely fond of Mother. He told us what Mother had been to receive — what the codicil meant for us. He said grandfather had made a codicil giving everything to Mother and her issue, which meant us. He said grandfather had always meant to put it right, and that he was sorry it had come to this." She was quiet a moment. "He was sorry in the way people are when they have done something they believe they had to do. It was not performed."

Prescott wrote the substance: Walter's visit; Tuesday, approximately the eighth of May; what Walter had said about the codicil's terms. He asked whether she was sure of the date and she said the eighth or the ninth, and he wrote the eighth with a small query beside it. He moved on to the matter of the signed letter.

---

The letter was in order. He sorted the papers and clipped them into their sequence. Nora sat with her cup.

"I think Mother would have been uncomfortable," she said, "being made the subject of an action. She was not a person who liked to be the reason for anything. She would have been glad it was being done and would not have wanted to know the detail."

"That is not unusual," Prescott said, which was true, and insufficient.

"I hope the record is enough."

"I believe it is."

"Grandfather wrote to her," Nora said. "When he made the codicil. I found the letter after she died, in a box she kept in the wardrobe. The tone of it was—" She stopped. "It was kind. It was not a man saying he had done something to settle an obligation."

Prescott knew the letter. He had carried it out of this house in November, Exhibit A in Garside's envelope. He said: "Yes."

He fastened his bag and stood. He declined tea — he had a brief to review that evening — and Edgar showed him to the door.

---

The light was still long over Miller Park. He went back the way he had come, the river running below in the afternoon between the trees, the path along the top of the bank occupied in a loose and leisurely way that seemed to belong to a different order of time from the one in which he was working. An old man on a bench with a newspaper folded against the wind. Two children crossing the path with a dog that briefly considered Prescott and decided against it.

He had the letter in the brief. He had had it since November — Garside's envelope, the fold marks of a document kept in a wardrobe rather than a file, read and returned to rather than put away. He had read it then and filed it under A and thought of it as a document, which it was.

He walked to the station. The train ran south along the river for twelve minutes, and he sat with his bag on the rack above him and the evening beginning outside the window, and he did not think about anything in particular until the town came back around him and he got off at Preston.

# The Date

The hearing brief had been growing for three days. Mr. Booth had laid the exhibits in numbered order on the long table in the outer office — each document confirmed against the schedule, the index number pencilled in the upper right corner, the relevance notation entered in the right-hand column. Prescott had been working through them in sequence, transferring the verified bundles to the briefcase that would travel to London at the end of the month. It was the second week of July; the square outside was light until nine, and the office without its winter coal fire felt opened out, the iron grate cleaned and cold.

He had accounted for twenty-two exhibits. The twenty-third was the firm's notice letter of the second of November 1926 to Thurston & Marsh of Church Street.

He laid it on the desk and read it as a document rather than as something he had written.

The letter gave notice of the will and of the first codicil, the codicil described as *dated the 15th March 1924 which materially affects the disposition of the residue.* Those were the words: a date, and a bare statement of material effect. No text of the codicil; no identification of the beneficiary; no operative language. It was what solicitors wrote to other solicitors at the outset of an estate matter, when what was required was notice rather than disclosure.

The letter-book carbon confirmed the transmission. The copy was in its correct position in the letter-book, dated and addressed, sequenced between the first of November and the fourth. Garside had established the letter-book system the year Prescott had come into the office as an articled clerk, and nothing about it had varied since. The letter of the second of November had been sent; its contents had reached Thurston & Marsh on or about the third; from shortly after that date the date of the first codicil — *the 15th March 1924* — had been in their client's hands in writing.

Before the second of November, what had been available?

The September reading. On the nineteenth of September 1926, Garside had fetched the first codicil from the strong-room and driven to Eccleston Hall; the strong-room register recorded the fetch and the same-day return in Garside's hand. In the drawing room at the Hall, Garside had read the instrument entire to the assembled family: the gift, the date, the form of words, the revocation of clause 4. Prescott had been in the room, carrying the deed-box. Walter Eccleston had been in the room. The date of the first codicil had been spoken in that room: *the fifteenth of March 1924.* Walter had heard it once, in September, amid a great deal else.

Five weeks later, in the days before R5 arrived — in the days the despatch-box stood at the mill — memory of a single occasion was the only source. After the second of November, memory was supplemented by writing.

Prescott drew the second codicil from exhibit envelope two and read the recital.

---

WHEREAS by a codicil to my said will dated the fifteenth day of March 1924 I gave the residue of my estate unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely NOW I HEREBY REVOKE the said codicil in its entirety and I confirm my said will dated the third day of June 1919 in all respects as if the said codicil had not been made.

---

The date in the recital was *the fifteenth day of March 1924.* The date in the firm's notice letter was *the 15th March 1924.* The same figures in two conventions: the abbreviated form a notice letter would use, and the written-out style a drafter would set into the recital of an executed instrument. The correspondence was exact.

The operative words in the recital were *unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely.*

The firm's notice letter had not given operative words. It had given the date and the bare fact of material effect. The letter-book record showed that no text of the operative clause of the first codicil had been transmitted from this firm in writing; the profession canvass of the previous August had established that no solicitor in the county had been asked to advise on the codicil's terms. If the operative words in the recital had reached the drafter from any written source, that source was not in evidence and was not in the record.

The operative words of the executed first codicil were *unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst of Bank Parade Preston or her issue absolutely.* The recital's version — *and her issue* — was not those words. It was the version that appeared in exhibits already filed: in Walter Eccleston's letter to his bank manager on the eleventh of June 1925, in Walter's own hand, fourteen months before the codicil's stated date; and in the attendance note recording Nora Fairhurst's account of what Walter had told the children in early May. Three instances of the same version across three years. The version was consistent; it was Walter's version.

Prescott set the notice letter and the second codicil side by side and took up a fresh sheet.

The working note occupied two pages.

---

*Working note — exhibit 23 (R5, notice letter, 2 Nov. 1926) — 16 July 1927*

*The firm's notice letter to Thurston & Marsh of 2 November 1926 (R5, exhibit 23) gave the date of the first codicil as "the 15th March 1924." It gave no operative text of the codicil. The letter-book carbon (exhibit 7) confirms transmission on 2 November 1926. The date of the first codicil was not in writing from this firm or from any other established source before that date.*

*The recital of the second codicil (R3, exhibit 2) recites the first codicil as "dated the fifteenth day of March 1924" and as giving the residue "unto my niece Margaret Fairhurst and her issue absolutely." The date in the recital ("the fifteenth day of March 1924") corresponds exactly to the date in R5. The operative words in the recital ("and her issue") do not correspond to the operative words of the executed first codicil ("or her issue" — R2, exhibit 1). They correspond to the version documented in the hand of Walter Eccleston as at 11 June 1925 (R4, exhibit 14) and in the attendance note of 13 May 1927 (exhibit 21).*

*The recital reproduces the element of the first codicil that was supplied in writing by this firm's correspondence (the date). It does not reproduce the element that was not so supplied (the operative text); it reproduces instead a version of the operative words documented as Walter Eccleston's own, derived from a spoken account and not from the executed instrument.*

*Taken alone, this does not establish authorship. Combined with the foreclosures established by exhibits 1–22 — the machine, the presence, the witnesses, the profession, the firm's own record, the habit, the despatch-box, the September reading — it establishes that the recital was composed by a person who had the date from R5, had the operative words from memory of a spoken account, and had no access to the executed first codicil at any point.*

*A.P., 16.vii.27*

---

He filed the working note behind exhibit twenty-three. He returned the second codicil to its envelope and set it back in its position. Twenty-four was the extract from the strong-room register.

Ninety days to the hearing. The asymmetry was in the record: the date had been in writing; the text had not.

# Solemn Form

He had the deed-box under his arm by nine. He had been awake at half past three, had read through the authorship section of the brief by the bedside lamp, found no errors in it, and put it face-down on the desk. He did not sleep again until after five. The walk from the hotel to the Royal Courts of Justice was twenty minutes along the Strand, and the October morning was cold enough that he was glad of it — the room had been warm and small, and he had done everything in it that could be done.

The Royal Courts of Justice stood at the eastern end of the Strand — the particular Victorian Gothic of the State announcing its intentions in stone and pinnacles — and it was the third time Prescott had been inside it on Garside & Prescott business, the first two being a chambers meeting and a matter that had settled before argument and been no business of the court at all. The building had not diminished in the interval. He crossed the forecourt with the deed-box and found the corridor for the Probate, Divorce and Admiralty Division, which already held the morning's population of barristers in gowns, their solicitors at their elbows, each pair apart from the next with the composed patience of people who do this regularly and have learned that patience is part of the work. The smell of the place was distinctive — old stone, varnished wood, coal smoke from the court fires working behind closed doors — the smell of a building that has held the same proceedings for fifty years and taken the character of them into its walls.

Their counsel found him before ten. Keane was a tall man of about forty-five, considered in manner, who had acknowledged the brief in August with a letter of three sentences and who had since written twice with questions about the exclusion section. He had the unhurried confidence of a man who has read the brief and finds it sufficient. He shook Prescott's hand and asked whether the originals were in the deed-box.

Prescott confirmed they were.

They stood together in the corridor while it filled further. The courtroom doors had not yet opened; through the gap where a latch had not quite caught, Prescott could see the brass rail of the witness box and the bench above it, both empty.

---

Counsel for the defendant came across to them at ten minutes to ten. His name was Ardern, and Prescott knew from the action papers that he had been at the bar for twenty-five years. He was a shorter man, compact, who moved through the corridor with the ease of long practice.

The request was framed correctly. Whether the plaintiff's solicitor might permit the defendant a few minutes to examine the executed original of the first codicil, before the judge took his seat — purely for the purposes of instruction, Ardern said, and Prescott's side would retain custody throughout. It was said without the tone of a man asking a favour, and without the tone of a man who expected to be refused.

Keane looked at Prescott, briefly, because it was Prescott's deed-box.

Prescott set it on the bench beside him and opened the lid. The Eccleston papers were arranged as he had laid them in Preston the week before: the custody list on top, the originals beneath in exhibit order. He lifted the custody list, and beneath it, in a folded envelope marked in his own hand — *R2. First Codicil (executed original)* — was the instrument that had been in the strong-room since the fifteenth of March 1924.

He handed the envelope to Ardern without speaking.

---

Walter Eccleston was standing eight or ten feet away, beside a young man from Thurston & Marsh that Prescott did not recognise. He had come into the building while Prescott and Keane were talking; Prescott had noted his arrival at the edge of his attention without looking at him directly. He looked at him now. Walter was watching Ardern cross the corridor with the envelope.

Ardern held the envelope out. Walter took it. He opened it carefully — he was a careful man — and drew out the codicil. Rag paper, folded twice, typewritten, a single page. He unfolded it and began to read.

He read it the way a man reads a document he expects to confirm what he knows: quickly, his eyes moving across the type.

And then he slowed.

He went back a line, read it again; went back further; came to rest at a particular point in the instrument and stayed. He read it again from that point, deliberately, his head very slightly inclined. Then he read it a third time and was quite still.

He was fifty or thereabouts, broad-shouldered, a man whose presence had always been larger than his physical size. He was not large now. He held the instrument and stood without moving, and something in the set of his shoulders was different from a moment before.

---

Prescott watched and did not speak.

Walter had never been in a room with the executed text before this moment. He had been wrong since March 1924 and had not known it.

Prescott kept his face composed and his hands at his sides. There was nothing to say.

After some moments, Walter spoke briefly to Ardern — low, inaudible at the distance. Ardern put a hand once on Walter's arm, professional and brief, and withdrew with him down the corridor. Two men, twenty feet away, a conference too quiet to follow.

Keane stood beside Prescott and did not speak, which was correct.

A barrister passed between them on his way to another court, acknowledged Keane with a nod, and moved on.

Three minutes, or a little more.

When Ardern returned, his manner was composed in the way of a man who has instructions he does not enjoy executing but who will execute them precisely.

"My client is not in a position to proceed," he said. "I am instructed to apply for a withdrawal of the claim."

---

The matter came before the judge at a quarter past ten: the application to withdraw; Keane's assent on behalf of the plaintiff in solemn form; the brief exchange of counsel establishing the disposition of the instruments and the question of costs. The judge was a spare man of about sixty with a dry manner and a habit of precise speech who had clearly had the brief — his questions were exact — and who received the application without visible surprise.

The second codicil had not been proved; accordingly it was not to be admitted to probate. The instruments of 1919 and 1924 stood. Letters of administration with the will annexed would be sought in due course through the Principal Registry.

The handwriting evidence: two opinions, directly irreconcilable — one finding the signature genuine, one finding it not. The judge noted that the decision had not rested on either. He added one observation, speaking to the courtroom at large rather than to either set of counsel: that in cases of this kind the most reliable witnesses were frequently the most ordinary — a letter-book entry, a register note, a word in a recital — because ordinary documents do not accommodate themselves to what comes after. He said it in the same flat tone he had used throughout, and moved to the costs.

The costs were to be paid by the defendant. Garside & Prescott, which had carried the action at its own risk from the caveat onward, would recover them in full.

---

By eleven the corridor was nearly empty. The matter had gone quickly — as matters go quickly, Prescott knew, once the decision has been made before it reaches the court.

Keane gave him his hand and said that it had been well conducted. That was the right amount to say. Prescott thanked him, and they parted.

He opened the deed-box and replaced the first codicil, in its envelope, in its place in the exhibit order. He noted the custody on the list: *R2. Returned from use. RCJ, 14 Oct. 1927. A.P.* He closed the lid.

He would telephone Mr. Booth from the hotel before midday. He would write to Edgar Fairhurst this afternoon.

He picked up the deed-box and walked toward the entrance.

# Reader — Act 1 Assessment
## Chapters 01–07: The Strong-Room through The File

---

### Overall

Act 1 is doing its job with considerable skill. The register holds from the first sentence, the fair-play plant lands cleanly and without flagging, the compounding mechanism is visible and building, and the displacement mechanism — Prescott finding Garside in the file — earns its first full beat by chapter 7. This is the right first quarter: the two codicils surface, the caveat is entered, Garside dies, the first foreclosures are made. The act earns its pace through procedural precision rather than event, as the brief requires.

---

### Brief-Adherence Checks (Act 1 scope)

**1. Fair-play contract (R2 and R3 on the page before discovery):**
R2 ("or her issue") appears verbatim as a set-off passage in Ch 1. R3 ("and her issue" in the recital) appears verbatim in Ch 2. Both are printed exactly as registered, unglossed, before any discovery. ✓ No document fidelity failure in Act 1.

**2. Walter's misquotation — first plant in place:**
Plant 2 (Walter to Prescott at the caveat meeting) lands precisely as briefed — mid-sentence in his account of Josiah's intentions, unremarked by the narration: *"He always said the arrangement for Margaret and her issue wouldn't stand as he'd left it."* The phrasing is natural, the occasion is his plausible cover story, and the narration neither repeats it back nor reacts to it. Plant 1 (R4 as financial exhibit) and plant 3 (Walter to the children) are correctly deferred to later acts. ✓

**3. Single POV discipline:**
Clean throughout. No passage accesses another character's interior. Events at the Hall and the mill are relayed through documents (the despatch-box attendance note, the strong-room register, later the diary). Walter is observed and recorded, never internalized. ✓

**4. Compounding mechanism:**
- Ch 1: Door (g) — despatch-box inventoried, no codicil; September reading established (door h seeds). ✓
- Ch 2: Cover story on record; both witnesses identified as beyond reach; the notice letter's scope fixed (date only, no text). ✓
- Ch 3: Door (f) — forty years of instruments, all through the firm; the attendance note of 15 March 1924 establishes "or her issue" as deliberate legal form, not careless drafting. ✓
- Ch 4: Exhibit A (Josiah's March 1924 letter to Margaret) forecloses "soft mood he meant to revise" — door (f) corroborated with new documentary evidence. ✓
- Ch 5: September register entry established formally, with full text and "instrument read entire, including date." ✓
- Ch 6: Door (e) — no request for the codicil's text ever reached the firm; R5 gave only the date. ✓
- Ch 7: Door (f) extended — August 14 diary entry shows an ordinary Saturday, no testamentary act; correspondence is silent. ✓ (See mild concern below.)

**5. Calendar monotonicity:**
Hearing date set in Ch 5 (290 days). Ch 6: 265 days (mid-chapter). Ch 7: 257 days (opening). Monotonically decreasing. Chs 1–4 correctly lack a countdown, as the hearing date is not yet fixed when they occur. ✓

---

### What's Working

**The register.** The opening sentence of Ch 1 places everything correctly: *"The deed box was on the table when Prescott arrived: black painted steel, 'ECCLESTON' lettered in white on the lid, the label in Garside's copper-plate facing up across the room."* Inference is in the observation. Garside's hat is still on — Prescott reads the room through professional signs, never by naming what the signs mean. This continues throughout the act without a significant slip.

**The death of Garside (Ch 5).** The whole shock is delivered through Mr. Booth's position in the passage. *"In sixteen years Prescott had never seen Mr. Booth standing in the passage."* No death scene, no direct grief, no announcement. The two-sentence paragraph — *"He was thirty-eight. He had worked beside this man for sixteen years."* — placed after the practical arrangements and before *"By the afternoon the office was working again, because it had to"* — is the register at its best. These sentences are exactly what the style guide means by the plain sentence that carries disproportionate weight because everything around it is controlled.

**The displacement beat in Ch 7.** The act's culminating Garside moment: Garside's cover letter to Josiah about the draft codicil, written for the record rather than for Josiah. *"The file was the work of a man who had never distinguished between what required a record and what deserved one."* Followed by: *"And the file was going to prove a forgery."* This is not a gloss — it's consequence, not explanation — and it properly pivots to the case rather than naming the grief. The displacement mechanism is working as intended.

**Nora Fairhurst (Ch 4).** *"She stood the way a person stands who has decided not to sit until she understands what is happening."* One sentence; she's alive from it. Her questions — *what was our mother to have had* and *how long will it take* — are exact without being aggressive, and Prescott answers without softening. The brief's requirement that the children remain people and not a cause is met here.

**Fair-play subtlety.** The "and her issue" plant in Ch 2 is buried exactly right in Walter's cover story, a single phrase in a plausible account of Josiah's intentions. A reader paying close attention will feel the charge against R2 read an act earlier; a reader not paying close attention will hear Walter's account and find it plausible. The narration never signals the variance. ✓

**The Garside attendance note in Ch 3.** The marginal note *"Or her issue: collateral; substitutional form required. — H.G."* is a genuine exhibit. It closes not only the habit door but a possible defense: that "or" was a typist's error for "and." Garside recorded the legal rationale at the time of execution. This is the compounding mechanism working exactly as the brief envisions: a prior act of professional exactitude becoming a later foreclosure.

**Document inserts.** Every set-off passage is clean: the document stands, the prose resumes from the same narrative level, nothing following explains what the document "really" meant. R1, R2, R3, R5 — all correctly deployed. R5 quoted twice (Ch 2 and Ch 6) is within the ceiling and neither instance functions as filler.

---

### Concerns

**Mild re-walk in Ch 7 (instrument register).** Chapters 3 and 7 both cover the instrument register and both arrive at the same conclusion: every instrument of Josiah's adult life through this firm, ending with the first codicil. Ch 3 does this through the full index and the earlier wills; Ch 7 does it again by walking the register and naming the same sequence. The diary entry for August 14 and the letter to Nora Fairhurst are genuinely new in Ch 7 — they carry the chapter and close door (f) on its "diary and correspondence silent" side. But the instrument register passage in Ch 7 (*"The original lease of Vale Mill, 1884... Nothing after it."*) re-establishes a fact already established in Ch 3 without materially narrowing or extending it. This is a mild concern — not a full re-walk, and the new material in Ch 7 justifies the chapter — but the register walk repeats.

**Four routine-procedure openings in seven chapters.** Chapters 1, 2, 3, and 6 all open in the same texture: Prescott at a desk or table, beginning to work through documents. Chapters 4 (transit), 5 (arrival/summons), and 7 (arrival by post) provide variation. For a procedural novel in this register this is expected, and the content of each procedure is distinct, but the accumulation is noticeable. Within Act 1 it is not a problem; if the pattern continues across Act 2's middle-movement chapters, it will become one.

**Bank Parade's atmospheric close (Ch 4) runs slightly long.** The park walk — the Ribble, the heron, the lit window — is earned and the period texture is right. But the lit-window closing image comes after an already complete emotional beat (Prescott's realization that *"The file had always had an address in it — Bank Parade, Preston — but it had been a legal address"*) and adds a second atmospheric gesture that slightly diminishes the first. A very minor rhythm issue; the chapter's core is excellent.

---

### Thread Check (Act 1)

All six threads properly introduced and advancing:
- **Thread 1 (firm's risk)**: entered Ch 2, advancing Chs 3, 5, 6, 7. ✓
- **Thread 2 (Garside in the file)**: entered Ch 5, first full displacement beat Ch 7. ✓
- **Thread 3 (the children)**: entered Ch 4, humanized correctly. ✓
- **Thread 4 (Walter's logic)**: entered Ch 2 (cover story, first plant), context Ch 3. ✓
- **Thread 5 (witness trap)**: entered Ch 2. ✓
- **Thread 6 (one-word variance)**: R2 Ch 1, R3 and plant 2 Ch 2. ✓

**No thread is missing. No door is walked twice within Act 1** (the instrument register re-mention in Ch 7 is an extension, not a full re-walk). No fair-play violation.

---

### Voice Check

The failure modes from the style guide are largely avoided. No "sentence after the sentence" is egregious — the narration generally stops rather than glosses. No passage of direct grief for Garside beyond the two controlled sentences in Ch 5. Period-legal vocabulary (substitutional form, letters of administration with the will annexed, solemn form, the recital) is used correctly and without gloss throughout; the prose trusts context to carry it.

One watch point: **Walter's plausibility in Ch 2.** His cover story is presented through Prescott's attendance note and observed behavior — the *ease of a man who had spent twenty years at home in other people's offices*, the brief nod accepting the solicitor's non-answer. This is exactly right. The risk, as the middle movement develops, will be maintaining this human complexity while the record closes around him. Thread 4 is building correctly.

---

### Verdict

A very strong first act. The register is clean, the fair-play plants are correctly placed and unannounced, the compounding mechanism is visible and building, Garside's death lands with full weight in exactly the right register, and the displacement mechanism is earning its first real moment by chapter 7. The mild instrument-register re-walk in Ch 7 and the slightly elongated atmospheric close in Ch 4 are worth watching in revision but do not damage the act. The book is doing what it promised.

# Reader Act 2 Assessment
## Chapters: 08-the-gazette, 09-vale-mill, 10-the-machine, 11-the-sale-contract, 12-the-sale-contract, 12-the-witnesses, 13-the-fairhursts

---

### Overview

Act 2 is, by and large, the compounding mechanism working as the brief intends. Each chapter advances the record; the legal vocabulary is used as furniture, not display; and the prose stays in register without faltering. The act's high point is **09-the-gazette** through **09-vale-mill** — a one-two sequence where the negative canvass closes a door cleanly, and then the mill visit delivers the book's best single chapter so far. The act's central problem is structural and requires attention before synthesis: there are **two draft versions of the sale-contract chapter**, both in the story arc, both containing R4 in full.

---

### What's Working

**09-vale-mill is the act's standout chapter.** The opening memory — Garside driving, Prescott in the passenger seat with the deed-box at his feet, thinking "about the quality of the light, and the draft from the windows, and nothing in particular. He had not been attending to the right thing" — is exactly what the brief calls for in the displacement thread. The sentence does not explain itself; it doesn't need to. The mill visit carries all four threads Prescott is weaving: the Hadfield figures advancing the firm's exposure (Thread 1), the mortgage instrument in Garside's hand on the counting-house table (Thread 2), Walter observed crossing the yard with the ease of a man who had earned his understanding of every building in it (Thread 4), and Josiah's last dated visit — "May 14, 1926" — pulled from the foreman's daybook without ceremony. The final note of the chapter — "He did not write that second thought" — is the register working perfectly. The literary-fade ending (Prescott driving west, the looms audible, the mill behind a fold in the hillside) is one of the act's best sentences.

**10-the-machine handles its technical material without losing the voice.** Croft's eleven-page report could easily become a dry inventory; instead the act of reading it is rendered in Prescott's register throughout. "What it said was what he had known in the mill-office doorway, looking at the machine from a distance of eighteen inches with his pocket-book in his hand; but knowing was not demonstrating, and demonstrating was the eleven pages." That sentence earns its place. The limits of Croft's evidence — "The examination of typewriting specimens does not establish the identity of the operator or the date of production" — are correctly given in set-off rather than paraphrased, and the prose does not explain why those limits are actually useful to Prescott. He understands it; the reader is trusted to follow.

**08-the-gazette is patient procedural work that doesn't drag.** Booth's two-column list, the forty-six firms, the careful phrasing of the notice, the weeks-long wait, the final summary memo placed at the front of the file — all of it moves at exactly the pace a negative canvass should move. "The Gazette produced nothing" as a section heading carries the dry wit the brief licenses, and the closing paragraph — the cover story requiring a solicitor who had vanished from the professional record without a letter-book carbon or a bill rendered — is a clean, satisfying door-closing that earns its last sentence: "The door was locked."

**13-the-fairhursts lands all three of its required beats.** Thread 3 (the children as people) is renewed at the case's midpoint through George's question — "What happens to the mill?" and "The men lose their jobs" — which is the best Thread 3 beat in the book so far: a sixteen-year-old asking the question his father didn't, and settling for the answer in silence. The third fair-play misquotation is planted correctly via Nora's report of Walter's visit: "grandfather had made a codicil giving everything to Mother and her issue, which meant us." The narration doesn't flag the "and"; the chapter doesn't remark on the word; it moves on to the signed letter. And Nora's portrait of her mother — "She was not a person who liked to be the reason for anything" — followed by Prescott's "That is not unusual, which was true, and insufficient," is the act's most precise moment of the displacement register working at its best.

**The Garside thread accumulates correctly through the act.** The instrument index in Garside's hand in 12-the-witnesses ("red boards worn soft at the corners, in Garside's hand from its first entry in 1906"). The mortgage instrument at the counting-house table in 09-vale-mill, "Garside's signature visible as the witnessing solicitor: small, exact, done for the record. Prescott had seen it ten thousand times at least." These are exactly the kind of specific professional discoveries the brief requires — more precise than the occasion required, accumulating without announcement.

---

### The Structural Problem: Duplicate Sale-Contract Chapter

The act contains two drafts of the same chapter. **11-the-sale-contract.md** and **12-the-sale-contract.md** cover identical ground: the £8,500 mortgage in Garside's drafting, the conditional sale contract and its two extension memoranda, Walter's nine letters to Holt, R4 (the June 1925 bank letter) quoted verbatim, and Hadfield's March account at a loss of approximately £300, with three months of reserves remaining. Both chapters end with 185 days to the hearing. Both appear in the story-arc digest with near-identical one-line summaries. The longer version ("12-the-sale-contract") is more thoroughly rendered — the mortgage reading is fuller, the banking correspondence more developed — but they describe the same professional act on the same day.

**This is a structural failure that must be resolved before synthesis.** It creates two consequences. First: R4 appears verbatim twice in the manuscript — once in the "11" version, once in the "12" version. The fair-play brief pins the second plant of the misquotation as R4 quoted once as a financial exhibit, unremarked. Two full quotations of R4 do not technically over-signal the variance (the narration remarks on neither), but the duplicate makes the intent ambiguous and could shade toward over-planting for a careful reader. Second: the chapter numbering is now broken — "12-the-sale-contract.md" and "12-the-witnesses.md" share the same number, and the story arc has logged both "12" chapters as well as a duplicate entry for "12-the-witnesses."

**The likely resolution:** one version of the sale-contract chapter should be canonical (almost certainly the longer "12" version, which is more fully developed), and the other removed. If the "11" number is vacated, the chapter ordering through the act needs to be re-sequenced. This is a human call, not a repair-agent call. No agent should attempt to reconcile the two.

---

### Minor Concerns

**The sale-contract chapter does not strictly close one of the nine enumerated doors.** The brief requires each chapter to close or materially narrow a named innocent explanation of the second codicil. The sale-contract chapter documents motive and formally installs R4 in the brief — essential work, and not orbiting — but the nine doors are: machine, Josiah's presence, witnesses, profession, firm, habit, despatch-box, September reading, date asymmetry. Motive isn't on the list. The chapter's foreclosure contribution is indirect: it narrows the despatch-box door by establishing what Walter needed the codicil to do and when he needed it, but it doesn't explicitly close it. This is a softer concern than the duplicate-chapter problem; the chapter earns its place through Thread 4 and the fair-play plant. But on strict compounding-mechanism audit, the brief's requirement is not fully met for this chapter in either version.

**One very minor voice-register note in 09-vale-mill.** The sentence "Fifteen years of managing it; everything he had borrowed against was in these buildings, and his men were inside them" is Prescott observing Walter — it's technically through Prescott's external noticing, which is permitted, but "his men" leans slightly toward inhabiting Walter's perspective rather than observing it. The effect is close enough to the line that it registers, though the passage does not tip into POV breach.

---

### Thread Development in This Act

All six threads advance on schedule. The witness trap (Thread 5) opens its irreversibility in 12-the-witnesses — Croft's attestation reports are "consistent but unbreakable," the commission is submitted with no address in hand — positioning the refused commission (Thread 5's permanent close) correctly for Act 3. The Garside displacement thread accumulates through three separate acts of professional discovery across the act's seven chapters, precisely as the brief requires. Walter's logic (Thread 4) is the act's most humanizing thread, receiving its three best moments: the mill visit (ch.09), the financial desperation laid bare (ch.11/12), and the kindly visit with the wrong word (ch.13). The six-thread weave is intact.

---

### In-Act Pacing

The act covers approximately February through May 1927. Chapter lengths are appropriate to their tasks; no chapter feels padded or rushed. The calendar countdown is named in every chapter and decreases monotonically — except for the duplicate problem, where both sale-contract chapters mark "185 days," leaving the calendar static between them. Once the duplicate is resolved, the calendar is clean. The act ends at 155 days, with the firm's record substantially built and the only remaining paths being the Hall depositions, the date asymmetry chapter, the commission refusal, and the discovery. The pacing into Act 3 is correctly set.

---

### Summary

The act is working. The prose is in register, the threads are advancing, and the compounding mechanism produces genuine accumulation — the reader at 13-the-fairhursts has more on the page than at 08-the-gazette, and they know it. The duplicate sale-contract chapter is the act's one genuine problem and requires a human decision on canonical version before the book can be considered structurally sound. Everything else is either working or minor enough to leave alone.
